why_incorrect.D: Model versions are pinned by ID; the pattern of offline gains that vanish in production points to evaluation design.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance plans to use Claude Sonnet 5.5 as an LLM judge to grade claim-summary quality on a 1–5 scale. Early results show the judge rarely gives scores below 4.
questions.question: Which TWO steps most improve the judge's reliability? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Ask the judge to output its score first and then a justification, so the score is not anchored by its own explanation
options.B: Normalise each judge score against the batch mean so that scores spread across the full 1–5 range on every run
options.C: Replace the vague 1–5 scale with a rubric defining concrete criteria for each level, or binary pass/fail per criterion
options.D: Switch the judge to Claude Opus 5.5, since a more capable model should be stricter and spread its scores across the scale
options.E: Measure agreement between the judge and human-labelled summaries and refine the rubric until agreement is acceptable

questions.explanation: LLM judges need a precise rubric with concrete descriptions of each score level (or a binary pass/fail per criterion), and they need calibration against human labels to measure agreement. Asking the judge to reason before scoring and grading one criterion at a time also helps. Swapping the judge model or rescaling its scores does not fix an undefined scale or show that the judge agrees with people.

why_incorrect.A: Reasoning before scoring tends to improve judge reliability; scoring first removes that benefit and leaves the vague scale in place.
why_incorrect.B: Forcing a spread changes the distribution, not the accuracy; a batch of good summaries would be marked down arbitrarily.
why_incorrect.D: Leniency comes from the undefined scale; a different model without a rubric or calibration may be just as lenient, at higher cost.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail wants to A/B test a new system prompt for its live shopping assistant. The primary metric is the add-to-cart rate after an assistant interaction.
questions.question: Which TWO design choices are most important for a valid test? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Randomise assignment at the user or session level so each user consistently sees one variant
options.B: Assign variants per message within a conversation so both prompts see the same users and the comparison is fully paired
options.C: Pre-register the primary metric and sample size from a power calculation, and run to that size rather than stopping on an interim lead
options.D: Run variant B in week one and variant A in week two, so each variant receives the full traffic in its period
options.E: Check the add-to-cart rate daily and stop once one variant leads with p < 0.05, to limit exposure to a worse prompt

questions.explanation: Valid A/B tests randomise at the right unit (usually the user or session, so one person does not see both variants), fix the primary metric and sample size in advance from a power calculation, and run until that size is reached rather than stopping when results look good. Running variants in different weeks or switching variants mid-session confounds the results.

why_incorrect.B: Within-conversation switching contaminates both variants, since each turn depends on the other prompt's earlier replies.
why_incorrect.D: Sequential periods confound the prompt with the week: promotions, seasonality and traffic mix differ between them.
why_incorrect.E: Repeated peeking and stopping early inflates false positives.

questions.scenario: Coho Winery's team iterates on a tasting-note generator. Each week they change several prompt sections at once, and quality sometimes improves and sometimes regresses without anyone knowing why.
questions.question: Which iteration practice would most improve their process?

options.A: Run an automated prompt optimiser each week that rewrites sections and keeps whichever version scores highest on the eval
options.B: Version-control prompts, change one element at a time, run the same eval suite on each change, and keep or revert based on the results
options.C: Batch changes into a monthly release with a full eval run, so each release is tested thoroughly and there are fewer experiments to track
options.D: Have the prompt author compare ten outputs before and after each change and record a judgement in the change log

questions.explanation: Effective iteration changes one thing at a time, runs the full offline eval suite on each change, records the result against a version-controlled prompt, and keeps or reverts based on evidence. This makes improvements attributable and regressions reversible. Bundled releases, small hand-picked comparisons and unreviewed automated rewrites hide cause and effect.

why_incorrect.A: Unreviewed rewrites change several things at once and optimise against the same eval, which removes traceability and invites overfitting.
why_incorrect.C: Testing each release thoroughly still bundles changes, so a regression cannot be attributed to the change that caused it.
why_incorrect.D: Ten author-chosen outputs are too few and too biased to detect regressions reliably.

questions.scenario: Relecloud wants to compare Claude Opus 5.5 at `medium` effort with the same model at `low` effort for its ticket-triage agent. Each eval run costs real money and takes an hour.
questions.question: Which experiment design gives a trustworthy answer at reasonable cost?

options.A: Compare `low` effort on Claude Haiku 5.5 with `medium` effort on Claude Opus 5.5, since a cheaper model may beat both ideas at once
options.B: Run a two-week online A/B test with live tickets split between the two effort levels, since production traffic is the true benchmark
options.C: Run each configuration on a different random sample of 50 cases, so the comparison covers twice as many distinct tickets for the same cost
options.D: Run both effort levels on the same representative eval set (a paired comparison), compare quality, latency and cost per completed task, and apply a pre-agreed decision rule

questions.explanation: A paired comparison on the same representative eval cases isolates the effect of the single changed variable (effort) and needs fewer cases than unpaired comparisons. Tracking quality, latency and cost per completed task gives the full trade-off, and agreeing the decision rule in advance avoids rationalising results. Unpaired samples add noise, going straight to an online test spends time and risk before offline evidence exists, and comparing different models at once confounds the result.

why_incorrect.A: Changing model and effort together confounds the result.
why_incorrect.B: An online test is slower, costlier and exposes live tickets to an untested configuration; an offline paired comparison should come first.
why_incorrect.C: Different samples add case-to-case noise that can swamp the real difference; pairing removes it for the same budget.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Toys ran an online A/B test of two prompts for 48 hours. Variant B's satisfaction score was 2 points higher with a p-value of 0.04, but traffic during the test was mostly a weekend holiday sale.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Roll out variant B, since p < 0.05 means the improvement is statistically established and further testing delays the benefit
options.B: Discard variant B, because a 2-point gain is within the normal week-to-week noise of satisfaction scores on this assistant
options.C: Re-analyse the existing data across other metrics, such as conversion and session length, to see whether they independently confirm the satisfaction result
options.D: Treat the result as provisional, because the sample was unrepresentative; extend or rerun the test across typical traffic before full rollout

questions.explanation: A statistically significant result can still fail to generalise if the sample is unrepresentative. A short test dominated by atypical holiday-sale traffic may not reflect normal usage, so the result should be confirmed over a period that covers typical traffic (or analysed by segment) before rollout. Statistical significance alone does not guarantee practical or general validity, and mining the same data for confirming metrics does not fix the sample.

why_incorrect.A: Significance on an unrepresentative sample does not establish that the effect generalises to normal traffic.
why_incorrect.B: The p-value already addresses noise within this sample; the issue is representativeness, and small effects can matter at scale.
why_incorrect.C: Testing more metrics on the same holiday-skewed data inflates false positives and leaves the sampling problem untouched.

questions.scenario: Meridian Clinics' referral-letter assistant sometimes cites specialist clinics that do not exist. The prompt includes a directory of 400 clinics, and errors cluster on letters for rare specialties.
questions.question: Which TWO interventions most directly address this hallucination pattern? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Move the 400-clinic directory to the top of the system prompt under a heading, so the model attends to it more closely
options.B: Require the clinic to be chosen by ID from the directory, through a lookup tool or schema constraint, and validate the ID before sending
options.C: Instruct the assistant to say when no listed clinic matches the specialty, rather than inventing one
options.D: Add few-shot examples of well-written referral letters that each name a clinic from the directory correctly
options.E: Replace the directory with retrieval that returns the five clinics most similar to the requested specialty

questions.explanation: Fabricated entities near the edge of the provided data usually mean the model is filling gaps instead of admitting none match. Two direct fixes: give the model explicit permission and a defined way to say no matching clinic was found, and constrain the output so the clinic must be chosen from the directory (for example a schema enum or a lookup tool returning valid IDs), then validate it. Moving the directory, adding examples or narrowing it with similarity search does not close the gap.

why_incorrect.A: Placement may help attention slightly, but it gives the model no sanctioned way to say no clinic matches and no validation of the result.
why_incorrect.D: Examples that always find a clinic reinforce the habit of naming one, and do not cover the rare specialties where errors occur.
why_incorrect.E: For rare specialties the nearest matches may not fit, and without a 'no match' path or validation the model can still invent or misuse a clinic.

questions.scenario: Margie's Travel's visa-advice assistant performs well in English but poorly on questions asked in Portuguese. The eval set contains only English cases.
questions.question: What is the best first diagnostic step?

options.A: Translate Portuguese questions into English before sending them, then translate the answers back for the customer
options.B: Add Portuguese few-shot examples to the system prompt, then compare complaint rates from Portuguese-speaking users before and after the change
options.C: Switch the Portuguese route to the most capable model, which handles less common languages more robustly than smaller tiers
options.D: Add Portuguese cases mirroring the English eval and measure which stage fails (retrieval, reasoning or output) on that slice

questions.explanation: Before changing prompts or models, extend the evaluation to cover the failing slice: build a Portuguese test set with the same scenarios and measure where performance drops (retrieval of Portuguese sources, reasoning, or output language). Diagnosis needs data on the failing segment. Switching models, translating everything or adding examples without evidence may fix the wrong thing.

why_incorrect.A: This is a fix chosen without diagnosis, adds two translation steps that can lose nuance, and may not address the failing stage.
why_incorrect.B: Examples are a fix rather than a diagnosis, and complaint rates are slow, noisy evidence compared with a targeted eval slice.
why_incorrect.C: This may help but is unverified and expensive; without a Portuguese eval you cannot confirm it or know what failed.

questions.scenario: Trey Research's contract-analysis prompt worked well on an older model. After migrating to a current model, outputs are longer, the model asks clarifying questions the old one never asked, and one rule ('ALWAYS list every clause') causes very long lists of trivial clauses.
questions.question: Which diagnosis best explains these symptoms?

options.A: The new model reasons more by default; lower effort and request shorter answers so outputs return to the old model's length and style
options.B: The contracts exceed the new model's effective attention span, so it compensates by listing every clause and asking questions
options.C: The new model uses a different tokenizer, so the old `max_tokens` setting now permits much longer responses than the team originally intended
options.D: The prompt was tuned for the old model; the new one follows instructions more literally, so absolute rules over-trigger and verbosity defaults differ. Revise and re-evaluate

questions.explanation: These are signs of model mismatch: the prompt was tuned for an older model's behaviour. Newer models follow instructions more precisely, so absolute rules written to overcome weaker adherence now over-trigger, and they may be calibrated differently on verbosity and clarification. The fix is to revisit the prompt for the new model, removing dated emphasis, stating what 'relevant' means and specifying the desired length and when to ask questions, then re-running the eval.

why_incorrect.A: Lower effort may shorten output, but it leaves the absolute rule that causes trivial clause lists and does not address the clarifying questions.
why_incorrect.B: Nothing indicates a context problem; over-applying an explicit 'ALWAYS' rule is a prompt-model mismatch, not a capacity limit.
why_incorrect.C: Tokenizer changes can shift counts, but `max_tokens` is a cap rather than a target, and it cannot explain clarifying questions or over-applied rules.

questions.scenario: An architect at Alpine Ski House is triaging a list of assistant failures and wants to classify each by root cause before choosing fixes.
questions.question: Which pairing of symptom and most likely root cause is correct?

options.A: An answer contradicts a policy document present in the context: a grounding or prompt-structure problem
options.B: A response ends mid-sentence: the rate limiter cut generation short during a traffic spike, so add backoff
options.C: The model picks the wrong one of two near-identical tools: stale tool definitions served from the prompt cache
options.D: JSON output occasionally fails to parse: the context window is nearly full, so the model compresses its output

questions.explanation: Matching symptoms to causes guides the fix. An answer that contradicts a document present in the context points to a prompt or grounding problem (for example the document is buried or the instructions do not prioritise it). Truncated output points to `max_tokens`, malformed JSON points to missing structured-output constraints, and wrong tool choice between overlapping tools points to tool design. Attributing these to rate limits or caching is a mismatch.

why_incorrect.B: Truncation mid-sentence is typically `max_tokens`; rate limits return errors rather than partial responses.
why_incorrect.C: This points to overlapping tool design; caching reuses identical input processing and does not serve stale definitions.
why_incorrect.D: Parsing failures point to missing format constraints such as structured outputs, not to context pressure.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail runs a nightly job that generates 80,000 personalised email drafts using a shared 6,000-token brand guide followed by per-customer data. Nobody reads the drafts until the next morning.
questions.question: Which TWO optimisations most reduce cost without affecting quality? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Set `max_tokens` to 150 so each draft's output cost is capped at a predictable level
options.B: Put the shared brand guide first with a cache breakpoint and the per-customer data after it
options.C: Run the job synchronously with fast mode so it finishes within an hour and frees capacity for the morning
options.D: Move the job to Claude Haiku 5.5, since email drafts are simple enough for the smallest current model
options.E: Submit the nightly job through the Message Batches API and key results by custom ID

questions.explanation: For latency-insensitive bulk jobs, the Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at a discount. Placing the shared brand guide first with a cache breakpoint lets requests reuse the cached prefix, reducing input cost further, while per-customer data follows the breakpoint. Shrinking `max_tokens` risks truncation, switching models without evaluation risks quality, and paying for speed buys nothing overnight.

why_incorrect.A: A tight cap risks truncated drafts, which affects quality.
why_incorrect.C: Fast mode charges a premium for speed, and an overnight job gains nothing from finishing sooner; batch processing is discounted instead.
why_incorrect.D: A model change made without evaluating draft quality risks quality, which the requirement excludes.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments switches effort between `low` and `high` on alternate turns of a long agent conversation to save money. Afterwards, cache reads on the conversation history drop sharply and costs rise.
questions.question: What explains the cost increase, and what is a better approach?

options.A: Low-effort turns make more tool calls to compensate, so the conversation grows faster and every later turn costs more
options.B: Changing top-level effort mid-conversation invalidates the cached history; pin effort per route, or use per-message effort where supported
options.C: Alternating effort changes the thinking blocks in history, which shifts the prefix; disable thinking on the low-effort turns instead
options.D: Route the low-effort turns to Claude Haiku 5.5 instead, which is far cheaper per token and leaves the main model's cached history untouched

questions.explanation: Thinking and effort settings are part of what the cache keys on, so changing the top-level effort between requests invalidates the cached message history. Pin effort per route instead, or, on models that support it, use the per-message effort mechanism, which changes effort without that invalidation (a beta feature as of 2026-10-24). Switching models would also break the cache, because caches are model-scoped.

why_incorrect.A: Lower effort generally means fewer, more consolidated tool calls, and it would not explain the sharp drop in cache reads.
why_incorrect.C: Toggling thinking is itself a setting change that invalidates the message cache, and some current models reject disabled thinking; the trigger is the top-level change.
why_incorrect.D: Caches are model-scoped, so every Haiku turn reads the full history uncached, and the switch back adds further misses.

questions.scenario: Litware's dashboard reports one latency figure: mean end-to-end response time across all its Claude calls, which fell from 3.4 to 2.9 seconds last month. Yet complaints about the streaming support chat rose, mostly at peak hours. The same figure also averages in thousands of short, non-streaming classification calls.
questions.question: Which latency metrics should the team define for the support chat?

options.A: Per-route time to first token with p95 and p99 percentiles for the chat, tracked by hour alongside full completion time
options.B: Mean end-to-end latency for the chat route on its own, sampled every minute instead of daily so peak spikes are visible
options.C: Median end-to-end latency per route with the slowest 5% of requests excluded as outliers, so the trend is not distorted
options.D: Average output tokens per second for each route, since generation speed determines how quickly users can read complete answers

questions.explanation: Users of a streaming chat feel the wait before text appears, so time to first token is the primary latency metric for that route, and complaints concentrated at peak hours point to the tail rather than the mean. Defining metrics per route stops fast, high-volume classification calls from masking the chat, and percentiles such as p95 and p99 expose the slow experiences that means and medians hide.

why_incorrect.B: Separating the route helps, but a mean still hides the slow tail and does not measure the wait before text appears.
why_incorrect.C: The excluded slowest requests are exactly the poor experiences that are driving the complaints.
why_incorrect.D: Output speed matters once text is flowing; it captures neither the wait before the first token nor tail behaviour.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending is moving a document-classification service to production. Leadership wants early warning if quality degrades, for example after input formats change.
questions.question: Which TWO monitoring practices provide the best early warning of quality degradation? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Re-run the full offline eval suite every quarter and before each prompt or model release, comparing against the baseline
options.B: Track cost per thousand documents weekly, since degraded outputs often trigger retries and reprocessing that raise spend
options.C: Alert on drift in input and output distributions, such as document types, label proportions and stop-reason rates
options.D: Monitor API error rates and p95 latency per endpoint, alerting when either moves outside its normal operating range
options.E: Continuously score a sample of live traffic with automated checks or an LLM judge, calibrated by periodic human review

questions.explanation: Quality monitoring in production needs both a direct and an indirect signal. Running an LLM judge or rule checks on a sampled slice of live traffic, with periodic human review to keep the judge honest, measures quality directly. Tracking input and output distribution drift (document types, lengths, label proportions, refusal and `max_tokens` stop rates) gives early indicators even before quality labels arrive. Service health, cost and scheduled offline evals do not detect quality changes as they happen.

why_incorrect.A: Release-time evals are essential but do not see input-format changes that arrive between releases, so they give no early warning.
why_incorrect.B: Cost is a lagging, indirect signal and says little about classification quality.
why_incorrect.D: Errors and latency show service health, not whether classifications are correct; a format change can degrade quality with no error at all.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance's dashboards show a sudden rise in HTTP 429 responses from the Claude API every weekday at 09:00 when batch-style back-office jobs start alongside interactive traffic.
questions.question: Which response best addresses the problem?

options.A: Attribute usage by workload, move back-office jobs to the Batch API or off-peak, and use backoff that honours `retry-after` for interactive retries
options.B: Put all traffic behind one shared queue that releases requests at the rate limit, so 429 responses stop appearing entirely
options.C: Raise the SDK's `max_retries` to 10 with short fixed delays, so interactive requests eventually succeed during the morning peak
options.D: Request a higher rate-limit tier for the organisation, since sustained 09:00 peaks show that demand has outgrown the current allocation for both workloads

questions.explanation: 429 responses indicate rate limits are being exceeded. Monitoring should break usage down by workload so the cause is visible, and the fix is to separate and shape traffic: move back-office jobs to the Batch API or schedule them off-peak, honour `retry-after` with exponential backoff, and request higher limits if sustained demand justifies it after that. Aggressive retries make contention worse, and a shared queue trades errors for interactive latency.

why_incorrect.B: A single queue stops 429s by making interactive users wait behind back-office jobs, which moves the problem into user-facing latency.
why_incorrect.C: More retries with short fixed delays add load during contention and ignore `retry-after`, prolonging throttling.
why_incorrect.D: More headroom may be justified later, but it pays to absorb back-office work that could move to batch or off-peak, and it does not separate the workloads.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank wants its monitoring to detect possible prompt-injection or data-exfiltration attempts against its customer-facing assistant.
questions.question: Which monitoring signal is most useful for this purpose?

options.A: A classifier that scans each user message for known injection phrases and records the matches in the security log
options.B: The daily count of refusals and safety-classifier stops, trended against a baseline to spot campaigns probing the assistant
options.C: Daily token usage per customer account, with alerts when an account's consumption exceeds three times its 30-day average
options.D: Alerts on anomalous tool use, such as unusual data-access sequences, bulk record retrieval or calls to unapproved destinations, correlated by session

questions.explanation: Security monitoring for LLM applications should look at behaviour, not only at volumes. Alerting on anomalous tool-use patterns, such as unusual sequences of data-access tools, bulk retrieval of records, or attempts to reach unapproved destinations, catches injection and exfiltration attempts that have bypassed prompt-level defences. Token volumes are too coarse, phrase matching on user input misses indirect injection, and refusals are a partial signal.

why_incorrect.A: Indirect injection arrives through documents and tool results rather than user messages, and known phrases are easy to rephrase; it also says nothing about impact.
why_incorrect.B: Successful attacks often do not trigger refusals, so this misses the most important cases.
why_incorrect.C: Token volume is coarse: exfiltration can use few tokens, and many benign spikes would trigger alerts.

questions.scenario: Coho Vineyard's support team A/B tested a new escalation prompt for one week with 500 conversations per arm. First-contact resolution was 20.0% for the control and 21.6% for the variant (two-sided p ≈ 0.53). The product owner says this proves the prompt makes no difference, but the team considers a 2-percentage-point gain worth shipping.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate conclusion and next step?

options.A: The test is underpowered for a 2-point effect; size it with a power calculation (about 6,500 per arm) and rerun
options.B: The variant has no effect, since p is far above 0.05; keep the control prompt and test a different idea next week
options.C: Ship the variant, since its rate is higher and a non-significant difference still points in the right direction
options.D: Extend the current test day by day and ship the variant as soon as the running p-value drops below 0.05

questions.explanation: A non-significant result from a small sample is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. Detecting a 2-point lift from a 20% baseline with 80% power at a two-sided 5% significance level needs roughly 6,500 conversations per arm, so 500 per arm could reliably detect only much larger effects. The right step is to size the test for the smallest effect worth shipping and run it to that pre-set size.

why_incorrect.B: Failing to reject the null with low power does not show the effect is zero; a worthwhile 2-point gain could easily be missed at this size.
why_incorrect.C: The observed difference is well within chance variation at this sample size; shipping on direction alone risks adopting a prompt that is no better.
why_incorrect.D: Checking repeatedly and stopping on the first significant reading inflates the false-positive rate; the stopping point should be fixed in advance.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments is designing guardrails for a merchant-support assistant that can look up transactions and issue small goodwill credits up to a fixed limit.
questions.question: Which THREE controls form a sound layered guardrail design? (Choose 3.)

options.A: Log every credit the assistant issues and have finance reconcile totals against the limits at month end
options.B: Enforce credit caps and daily per-merchant totals in the credit tool's backend, independent of the model
options.C: Put the credit limits in a dedicated system-prompt section and instruct the assistant to refuse any request above them
options.D: Screen inputs with a lightweight classifier for abuse and injection patterns before the main model call
options.E: Scan outputs for sensitive data such as full card numbers before they reach the user

questions.explanation: Effective guardrails are layered and the strongest ones are deterministic. Input screening (for example a fast classifier for abuse or injection patterns) reduces risk early. Hard limits enforced in the credit tool's backend (amount caps, per-merchant daily totals) hold regardless of what the model says. Output checks for sensitive data such as full card numbers stop leakage. Limits stated only in the prompt are guidance rather than enforcement, and month-end reconciliation detects overspend only after it has happened.

why_incorrect.A: Reconciliation is a useful detective control, but it finds overspend weeks after the money has gone rather than preventing it.
why_incorrect.C: A prompt rule is guidance the model can be talked out of; the limit has to be enforced in the backend where the credit is issued.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's public chatbot occasionally gets attempts to make it write abusive content about competitors. The team wants a cheap pre-screen before the main model runs.
questions.question: Which design is most appropriate?

options.A: Add a firm instruction to the main system prompt telling the assistant to decline requests for abusive content about competitors
options.B: A fast, low-cost model call that classifies each input against a defined policy and routes flagged inputs to a safe fallback
options.C: A maintained blocklist of competitor names and abusive terms, updated weekly from flagged chats, that rejects matching messages before the main model runs
options.D: Let the main model answer every message, then run a moderation classifier on the output and swap any abusive reply for a polite refusal

questions.explanation: A common harmlessness-screening pattern is a fast, low-cost model call that classifies user input against a defined policy and returns a structured verdict, with flagged inputs routed to a safe response or review. It runs before the main model, adds little latency and can be tuned and evaluated independently. Blocklists alone are easy to evade, screening only after generation wastes cost, and an instruction in the main prompt is not an independent screen.

why_incorrect.A: A prompt instruction relies on the main model itself, so it adds no cheap independent check that can be tuned and evaluated separately.
why_incorrect.C: Keyword lists are evaded by paraphrase and also block legitimate questions that mention competitors by name.
why_incorrect.D: Output screening is a useful second layer, but it is not a pre-screen: every abusive prompt still pays for a full main-model generation.

questions.scenario: Proseware's coding agent runs shell commands in CI. A security review asks how to prevent it from exfiltrating secrets to arbitrary internet hosts if it is manipulated by malicious content in a dependency's README.
questions.question: Which guardrail is most effective?

options.A: Route every shell command through a second model that checks whether it looks like exfiltration before the command runs
options.B: Scan CI logs after each run for outbound requests to unknown hosts and rotate any secret that appears to have been exposed
options.C: Run the agent in a sandbox whose egress is restricted to an allowlist of required hosts, with only the minimum secrets available
options.D: Add a system-prompt rule forbidding the transfer of credentials and tell the agent to treat dependency READMEs as untrusted data

questions.explanation: Network and filesystem isolation enforced by the environment is a hard boundary that holds even if the agent is manipulated. Running the agent in a sandbox whose egress is restricted to an allowlist of required hosts, with no secrets mounted beyond those strictly needed, prevents exfiltration regardless of the model's behaviour. Prompt warnings and post-hoc log review do not prevent the action, and a second model reviewing commands can itself be fooled by obfuscation.

why_incorrect.A: A model-based reviewer is probabilistic and can be fooled by obfuscated commands; it is not a hard boundary.
why_incorrect.B: Detection and rotation after the run limit damage but do not prevent the secret from leaving.
why_incorrect.D: Good hygiene, but instructions can be overridden by injected content; they do not block network access.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency's guardrail classifier blocks 6% of legitimate questions about domestic-violence support services, frustrating vulnerable users.
questions.question: What is the best response?

options.A: Add legitimate sensitive-topic queries to the guardrail eval, refine the policy with allowed and disallowed examples, and give borderline cases a helpful safe reply
options.B: Add domestic-violence keywords to an allowlist so matching queries skip the guardrail and go straight to the main model, with weekly spot checks of the bypassed traffic
options.C: Keep the hard block but rewrite the refusal message so it lists the support hotlines that blocked users should call instead
options.D: Lower the classifier's blocking threshold across the board until the false-positive rate on support questions falls below one per cent

questions.explanation: Guardrails have false positives as well as false negatives, and both need measurement. The team should build an evaluation set that includes legitimate sensitive-topic queries, tune the policy and classifier prompt with examples of allowed versus disallowed requests, and route borderline cases to a safe, helpful response (for example signposting support services) rather than a hard block. Loosening the threshold everywhere or adding a keyword bypass trades one harm for another, and a friendlier refusal still blocks the question.

why_incorrect.B: A keyword bypass is easily abused by anyone who includes the phrase, and weekly spot checks find misuse only afterwards.
why_incorrect.C: Signposting helps, but legitimate questions are still refused; the policy and classifier causing the false positives are left unchanged.
why_incorrect.D: A global threshold change trades false positives for false negatives on every topic, letting genuinely harmful requests through.

questions.scenario: Adatum Pharma's research agent can browse the web, read internal documents and send email. A threat-modelling workshop is identifying the most serious failure mode.
questions.question: Which risk combination is most serious and why?

options.A: Stale internal documents, because the agent may combine outdated procedures with current web content and give researchers conflicting guidance
options.B: Unbounded browsing loops, because the agent can fetch hundreds of pages per task and exhaust the monthly API budget
options.C: Hallucinated citations in research summaries, because scientists may rely on fabricated papers in regulatory submissions
options.D: Untrusted web content, access to internal documents and the ability to email externally together enable injection-driven data exfiltration

questions.explanation: The most dangerous combination in agentic systems is access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. Together they allow an indirect prompt injection in a web page to instruct the agent to read internal documents and email them out. Breaking any leg of that combination, for example by removing external email or isolating untrusted content from private data access, sharply reduces risk.

why_incorrect.A: Content freshness affects answer quality, but it does not combine untrusted input with a path for data to leave the company.
why_incorrect.B: Runaway cost is a genuine operational risk, but it is bounded by spend caps and is recoverable, unlike leaked data.
why_incorrect.C: A real quality risk, but it is caught by citation checks and review; it is far less severe than silent data exfiltration.

questions.scenario: A product manager at Wingtip Toys says 'Claude is deterministic if we use the same prompt, so we can skip regression testing after we change unrelated code'.
questions.question: Which TWO statements correct this misunderstanding? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Regression testing can be limited to model version changes, because application code outside the prompt does not affect outputs
options.B: Prompt caching returns stored outputs for repeated prompts, so identical requests give identical responses until the cache expires
options.C: Changes to surrounding code such as retrieval or templates change the model's inputs, so regression evaluation is still needed
options.D: Setting `temperature` to 0 makes outputs repeatable, so the team needs to re-test when the prompt text changes but not after code changes
options.E: Outputs can vary between runs with identical inputs, so quality should be measured statistically over a test set rather than by exact matching

questions.explanation: LLM outputs can vary between runs even with the same input, and current models do not accept sampling parameters such as `temperature` to force determinism. Systems should therefore be evaluated statistically over a test set rather than by exact output matching. Separately, changes to surrounding code (retrieval, tool results, templates) change what the model sees, so regression tests remain necessary.

why_incorrect.A: Code outside the prompt, such as retrieval or templating, changes what the model receives, so it can change outputs.
why_incorrect.B: Prompt caching reuses the processed input prefix to cut cost and latency; it does not store or replay outputs.
why_incorrect.D: Current models reject sampling parameters such as `temperature` with an error, and even where accepted it never guaranteed identical outputs.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance's claims agent runs unattended overnight. One night it loops on a failing tool for six hours, consuming a large share of the monthly budget.
questions.question: Which TWO controls address this failure mode? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Enable server-side compaction so the agent keeps a summary of its earlier failed attempts in context during long runs
options.B: Switch to a more capable model at higher effort so the agent recognises repeated failures and changes its approach
options.C: Enforce per-task caps on iterations, elapsed time and spend outside the model, with alerting on abnormal usage
options.D: Move the job to business hours so an operator can watch the usage dashboard and cancel runaway tasks by hand
options.E: Return explicit error results from failing tools and define when the agent should stop and escalate

questions.explanation: Unbounded consumption is a recognised LLM risk. Agents need hard limits on iterations, wall-clock time and spend per task, enforced outside the model, plus alerting when usage deviates from normal. Tools should return clear error results so the agent can stop or escalate rather than retry blindly. More capable models, context management or manual supervision do not reliably prevent runaway loops.

why_incorrect.A: Compaction manages context length; it does not cap iterations, time or spend.
why_incorrect.B: A stronger model may loop less often, but nothing bounds the run when it does; limits have to be enforced outside the model.
why_incorrect.D: Manual watching is unreliable and gives up the overnight capacity the team wanted; automated caps and alerts do the job.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing's summarisation tool sometimes produces summaries of long manuscripts that omit the final chapters, while still reading confidently.
questions.question: Which limitation is most likely at play, and how should it be mitigated?

options.A: Prompt caching is serving a stale prefix from an earlier, shorter draft; disable caching for manuscript requests and re-run them
options.B: Uneven coverage of long inputs or silent truncation; check the full text is sent, then summarise per chapter and merge results
options.C: The output limit is cutting the summary short; raise `max_tokens` so the model has room to cover the final chapters as well
options.D: The context window is too small for whole manuscripts; move to a model with a larger window and resend the full text in a single request

questions.explanation: Long-input tasks can suffer from uneven attention or from inputs that exceed what was actually sent (for example, the pipeline silently truncating to fit). The first check is whether the full manuscript reached the model; then decompose summarisation by chapter and merge, which gives each section full attention and makes omissions detectable. A confident tone is not evidence of completeness.

why_incorrect.A: Caching matches an exact prefix, so it cannot substitute a different draft; it does not change what the model reads.
why_incorrect.C: An output cut-off would end mid-sentence with a `max_tokens` stop reason; these summaries finish confidently but skip content.
why_incorrect.D: It skips the check of what was actually sent, and a single pass over a very long input still risks uneven coverage.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank's operations agent prepares wire-transfer corrections. Regulators expect a human to approve each correction, and analysts complain that approval screens show only 'Approve correction?'.
questions.question: Which human-in-the-loop design is most effective?

options.A: Group corrections by customer and let analysts approve each group in one step, with the full list of transfers behind an expandable link
options.B: Let the agent execute corrections straight away and give analysts a same-day review screen showing each transfer and its evidence, with one-click reversal for any they reject
options.C: Show the exact action, its evidence, the policy rule applied and any uncertainty, after deterministic validation, and record each approver's decision and rationale
options.D: Auto-approve corrections when the model reports confidence above 95% and send the lower-confidence ones to analysts for approval

questions.explanation: Approval is only meaningful if the reviewer has what they need to decide. The approval step should present the exact action (accounts, amounts, before and after), the evidence the agent used, the policy rule applied and any uncertainty, and should record the approver's decision for audit. Deterministic validation runs before the human sees it. Approving in bulk or relying on the model's confidence undermines oversight.

why_incorrect.A: Group approval hides the detail behind a click and encourages rubber-stamping, weakening the per-correction approval regulators expect.
why_incorrect.B: Approval after execution is not approval, and wire transfers are not reliably reversible.
why_incorrect.D: Regulators expect a human to approve each correction, and model confidence is not a calibrated measure of correctness.

questions.scenario: Meridian Clinics uses Claude to draft responses to patient portal messages. Clinical staff review every draft, but review time is now the bottleneck.
questions.question: Which approach best reduces review burden without weakening oversight of risky messages?

options.A: Remove clinician review once drafts score above 90% on the eval, and reinstate it if patient complaints rise above the current baseline
options.B: Add a second Claude pass that checks each draft against the clinic's guidelines, sending flagged drafts to clinicians and unflagged ones straight to patients
options.C: Have clinicians review a random 10% sample of drafts each day, and send the rest directly to patients with an AI-drafted label
options.D: Tier review by risk: full clinician review for symptom or medication drafts, lighter review or sampling for admin replies, and monitoring of the classifier

questions.explanation: Risk-based review focuses human attention where it matters. Classify messages by risk (for example clinical symptoms versus appointment logistics), require full clinician review of high-risk categories, and allow lighter review or sampling for low-risk administrative messages, with monitoring to verify the classification. Removing review, sampling at random or letting a second model decide what clinicians see ignores where the risk sits.

why_incorrect.A: A 90% aggregate score still means unreviewed errors on clinical messages, and complaints are a lagging signal of patient harm.
why_incorrect.B: Model review can help prioritise, but letting it decide which clinical drafts humans see removes oversight where it matters most.
why_incorrect.C: Random sampling treats a medication question like an appointment change, so most high-risk drafts reach patients unreviewed.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending added human approval to an agent's account-closure tool. Audits show approvers accept 99.7% of requests and median review time is four seconds.
questions.question: Which TWO actions best address this automation-bias risk? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Remove the approval step and replace it with a weekly audit of sampled closures, since approvers are not adding value
options.B: Require approvers to confirm the specific facts that justify closure, shown alongside the evidence, rather than a single approve button
options.C: Display the model's confidence score and reasoning prominently so approvers can focus on low-confidence requests
options.D: Require two independent approvers for every closure so that one inattentive reviewer cannot approve alone
options.E: Seed the approval queue with known-incorrect requests and measure reviewer catch rates

questions.explanation: Very high acceptance with very short review times suggests rubber-stamping. Countermeasures include presenting the evidence and requiring approvers to confirm specific facts (not just click approve), inserting known-bad test cases to measure whether reviewers catch them, and tracking reviewer accuracy. Adding approvers, foregrounding the model's confidence or removing the step does not restore meaningful oversight.

why_incorrect.A: Closures happen before the audit sees them; the fix is to make approval meaningful, not to drop it.
why_incorrect.C: Foregrounding the model's confidence anchors reviewers on it and tends to increase automation bias.
why_incorrect.D: Two rubber-stampers are no better than one and double the cost; the problem is how reviewers engage, not how many there are.

questions.scenario: An architect at Alpine Ski House is deciding which agent actions in a booking system should require human confirmation.
questions.question: Which principle should guide the decision?

options.A: Require confirmation for every write action, including holds and notes, so a human sees each change before it reaches the booking system
options.B: Base it on reversibility and impact: irreversible, high-value or externally visible actions need approval; read-only and reversible ones proceed with logging
options.C: Require confirmation for any action above a fixed monetary value, such as refunds over $500, and let every other booking action proceed automatically with logging
options.D: Require confirmation when the model's self-reported confidence is low, so humans see the decisions most likely to be wrong

questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop effort should scale with the consequences of an action: irreversible, high-impact or externally visible actions (refunds above a threshold, cancellations affecting other guests, messages to many customers) need confirmation, while read-only or easily reversible actions can proceed automatically with logging. Requiring confirmation for everything creates fatigue; requiring it for nothing removes oversight.

why_incorrect.A: Confirming trivial, reversible writes creates approval fatigue, which erodes attention on the actions that matter.
why_incorrect.C: A value threshold misses irreversible or externally visible actions with no price, such as cancelling other guests' bookings or mass messages.
why_incorrect.D: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and says nothing about consequences; a confident mistake can still be irreversible.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health is planning a Claude-based clinical documentation assistant in the United States that will process protected health information (PHI).
questions.question: Which TWO steps are prerequisites from a HIPAA perspective? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Obtain the provider's SOC 2 Type II report, which demonstrates the safeguards HIPAA requires of business associates
options.B: Configure the integration for zero data retention, which removes the need for a BAA because the provider stores no PHI
options.C: De-identify notes with a pattern-matching pass for names and dates, which takes the data outside HIPAA so no agreement is needed
options.D: Design for minimum-necessary PHI, with access controls, audit logging and encryption across the data flow
options.E: Execute a Business Associate Agreement with the provider that covers the specific services and features to be used

questions.explanation: Under HIPAA, a covered entity sending PHI to a vendor needs a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) covering the specific services used, and the architecture must apply the minimum-necessary principle along with administrative, physical and technical safeguards (access control, audit logging, encryption). Zero data retention, an audit report or ad hoc de-identification does not substitute for the contractual and technical requirements. Confirm current eligibility of specific features with the provider, as of the date of design.

why_incorrect.A: An audit report is useful due diligence but is not the contractual BAA that HIPAA requires.
why_incorrect.B: Zero data retention reduces exposure, but the provider still processes PHI, so a BAA covering the services used is still required.
why_incorrect.C: Pattern matching does not meet HIPAA de-identification standards, and a documentation assistant needs identified clinical detail anyway.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail operates in the EU and wants Claude to personalise marketing emails using customer purchase history. The DPO asks for GDPR-aligned design.
questions.question: Which design choice best reflects GDPR principles?

options.A: Rely on consent captured in the general terms of service at sign-up, and send product categories rather than full order histories
options.B: Send only the attributes needed for personalisation, document the lawful basis and processor terms, and suppress customers who have objected to direct marketing
options.C: Pseudonymise customers by hashing names and emails before sending order histories, which takes the processing outside GDPR's scope
options.D: Send full purchase histories under a signed data processing agreement, since the agreement makes the provider responsible for minimising and protecting what it receives

questions.explanation: GDPR requires a lawful basis for processing, purpose limitation and data minimisation, among other principles. The design should send only the attributes needed for personalisation (for example product categories rather than full order history with addresses), document the lawful basis and processor arrangements, and honour objections to direct marketing. Sending everything 'in case it is useful' violates minimisation, and pseudonymised data remains personal data.

why_incorrect.A: Minimising to categories is right, but consent bundled into general terms is not valid consent, and objections to marketing are ignored.
why_incorrect.C: Hashed or pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR, and the rest of the history is sent unminimised.
why_incorrect.D: A processor agreement is needed, but data minimisation remains the controller's duty; it does not justify sending everything.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency is a US government body that requires FedRAMP-authorised cloud services for production systems handling citizen data. A team has prototyped on the Claude API directly.
questions.question: What should the architect do before production?

options.A: Verify which Claude deployment path holds the required FedRAMP authorisation for this data as of the decision date, and use it
options.B: Deploy through any major cloud marketplace listing for Claude, since the cloud provider's FedRAMP authorisation extends to every service in its catalogue
options.C: Encrypt prompts client-side before sending them, so the service handles nothing but ciphertext and FedRAMP scope does not apply
options.D: Proceed on the direct API, because the provider's SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reports cover the control families that FedRAMP assesses

questions.explanation: Government compliance regimes such as FedRAMP apply to the specific service and deployment used. The architect should confirm which Claude offering and deployment path (for example a cloud platform's government region or an authorised offering) holds the required authorisation level for the data involved, as of the decision date, and adjust the architecture accordingly. A prototype's success or the model's capability does not establish authorisation.

why_incorrect.B: FedRAMP authorisations apply to specific services, regions and impact levels, not to everything a cloud provider lists.
why_incorrect.C: The model must read plain text to process it, so client-side encryption of prompts is not workable and does not change authorisation scope.
why_incorrect.D: Overlapping controls are not an authorisation; FedRAMP requires the specific service to hold the required level.

questions.scenario: Harbourline Credit Union must ensure that model inference for EU members' data runs in a specified geography. The team is choosing between building a self-hosted proxy and using a provider-level control.
questions.question: Which approach is most appropriate, as of 2026-10-24?

options.A: Store prompts and responses in EU databases with a short retention period, so members' data at rest stays inside the region
options.B: Run inference through a cloud platform's regional endpoint or inference profile in the required geography, and keep that configuration as evidence
options.C: Pseudonymise member identifiers before each request so the data sent for inference no longer counts as personal data
options.D: Route every request through a self-hosted proxy in an EU region, and record in the data protection impact assessment that model traffic now originates inside the EU

questions.explanation: Use the provider's own control for where inference runs rather than building around it. As of 2026-10-24 the Claude API's `inference_geo` parameter offers only `"us"` and `"global"`, so it cannot pin inference to the EU. Cloud platforms can: on Amazon Bedrock and Google-managed Claude models on Google Cloud, the endpoint or inference profile you call determines the inference region, and that deployment configuration is the audit evidence. A home-grown proxy cannot change where the provider runs inference, and keeping stored data in the EU says nothing about where inference ran.

why_incorrect.A: Data at rest in the EU is useful, but the requirement is about where inference runs, which this does not control.
why_incorrect.C: Pseudonymised data is still personal data, and the residency requirement applies regardless.
why_incorrect.D: Where traffic originates does not change where the provider runs inference.

questions.scenario: Northwind Lending uses Claude to summarise applicant files for underwriters. An internal review asks whether the summaries could introduce bias.
questions.question: Which TWO practices best address bias and fairness risk? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Remove underwriters' discretion and approve or decline automatically from the summary so decisions are applied consistently
options.B: Run counterfactual tests that vary only protected or proxy attributes and check whether summaries change materially
options.C: Rely on the provider's published fairness evaluations and model card, which cover demographic bias across common tasks
options.D: Have the model add a fairness self-assessment to each summary so underwriters can see whether bias was detected
options.E: Exclude protected characteristics and known proxies from the summarisation inputs unless legally required

questions.explanation: Fairness risk is measured, not assumed. Counterfactual testing (varying only protected or proxy attributes such as name, gender or postcode and checking whether summaries change materially) detects differential treatment. Excluding protected characteristics and known proxies from the summary's inputs where they are not legally required reduces the chance of influence. Relying on the model's general training or removing human underwriters does not address the risk.

why_incorrect.A: Consistency is not fairness; automating decisions removes oversight and can apply a biased summary at scale.
why_incorrect.C: General evaluations do not measure this prompt, data and use case; fairness has to be tested in context.
why_incorrect.D: A model's self-assessment is not a reliable measure of its own bias.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail's customer-facing assistant answers product questions. Legal asks how to meet transparency expectations.
questions.question: Which practice best supports transparency to end users?

options.A: Add a notice under each answer that it is AI-generated and may be inaccurate, and ask users to verify everything independently
options.B: Disclose that users are talking to an AI, cite sources for factual answers where possible, and offer an easy route to a human
options.C: Publish the full system prompt and model version on a help page so users can see exactly how the assistant is instructed
options.D: Give the assistant a friendly human name and persona, and disclose AI involvement in the privacy policy that is linked from every page footer

questions.explanation: Transparency means users know they are interacting with an AI system, understand its limitations, and can reach a human or verify important information. Clear disclosure, citations or links to the source of factual answers, and an obvious escalation path achieve this. Burying the disclosure, publishing prompt internals or adding a generic disclaimer is not the transparency users need.

why_incorrect.A: Labelling helps, but without sources or a route to a human it shifts the whole burden of verification onto users.
why_incorrect.C: Prompt internals are not what users need to make informed decisions, and publishing them aids prompt attacks.
why_incorrect.D: A human persona with disclosure buried in a policy page misleads users about who they are talking to.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency's document-extraction step performs worse on applications written in non-standard English, leading to more requests for additional information from those applicants.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Measure accuracy by applicant segment, add representative cases to the eval, improve the prompt and examples, and send uncertain extractions to human review for now
options.B: Keep optimising the overall accuracy metric, which already exceeds its target, and document the weaker results for non-standard English in the system's public model card
options.C: Route applications detected as non-standard English to manual processing indefinitely, and leave the extraction step unchanged for others
options.D: Translate every application into standard English with a preprocessing step before extraction, then re-measure overall accuracy

questions.explanation: This is a disparate-impact problem: performance differs across groups in a way that creates burden. The response is to measure performance by segment with an eval set representing those applicants, address the cause (prompt guidance, examples, or translation where appropriate), and add human review for low-confidence extractions to prevent harm while improvements are made. Ignoring segment performance or only fixing the aggregate metric hides the problem.

why_incorrect.B: Documenting the gap is not fixing it; the aggregate metric hides the burden on the affected applicants.
why_incorrect.C: Permanent manual handling slows those applicants down without measuring or fixing the cause.
why_incorrect.D: Translation may help but is untested here, can introduce its own errors, and is judged on the aggregate metric that hid the problem.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' risk committee requires that model inference for a new dispute-analysis service run on Amazon Bedrock under the company's existing AWS agreements and controls. The prototype, built on the Claude API, uses prompt caching, strict tool use, citations on policy PDFs, the server-side web search tool for current card-network bulletins, and the Files API to upload policy PDFs once and reference them by ID.
questions.question: Which TWO parts of the design must be re-planned before committing to Bedrock, as of 2026-10-24? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Prompt caching of the shared system prompt and the policy documents
options.B: The server-side web search tool for current card-network bulletins
options.C: Strict tool use to keep dispute-record tool arguments schema-valid
options.D: Uploading policy PDFs once through the Files API and citing them by ID
options.E: Citations on the policy PDFs so analysts can trace claims to a page

questions.explanation: Feature availability differs by platform, so a compliance-driven platform choice must be checked against the design. As of 2026-10-24, Amazon Bedrock supports prompt caching, structured outputs and strict tool use, PDF input and citations, but not Anthropic's server-side web search tool or the Files API. The team needs another source of current bulletins, such as its own retrieval tool, and must send the PDFs in each request. Claude Platform on AWS, which Anthropic operates, is a separate offering whose fit with the committee's requirement would need its own review.

why_incorrect.A: Prompt caching is supported on Amazon Bedrock.
why_incorrect.C: Structured outputs and strict tool use are supported on Amazon Bedrock.
why_incorrect.E: PDF input and citations are supported on Amazon Bedrock.

questions.scenario: Harbourline Credit Union's COO asks you to 'add AI to the loan process'. You have two weeks of discovery before a design review.
questions.question: Which discovery activity should come first?

options.A: Map the current loan workflow with the staff who run it, measuring where time, errors and cost concentrate and which decisions are regulated today
options.B: Shortlist candidate models and deployment platforms against the credit union's security requirements so that procurement can run in parallel
options.C: Survey loan officers and underwriters about which AI features they would find most useful, then rank the requests by popularity
options.D: Build a working prototype on a few sample loan files so the COO and loan officers can react to something concrete early

questions.explanation: Structured discovery begins by understanding the current process and its pain points: map the workflow with the people who do it, measure where time, errors and cost concentrate, and identify which decisions are regulated. This grounds the use-case shortlist in evidence and establishes baselines for later value measurement. Choosing a platform, building a prototype or collecting a feature wish-list first anchors the project on solutions before the problem is understood.

why_incorrect.B: Choosing a platform before the problem is understood anchors the project on a solution and may not fit the eventual use case.
why_incorrect.C: Staff input matters, but a feature wish-list is not evidence of where time, errors and cost concentrate.
why_incorrect.D: Prototypes are useful later, but building one before mapping the process tests an unvalidated guess and skips the baseline.

questions.scenario: During discovery for Meridian Clinics' referral-triage project, you are compiling non-functional requirements.
questions.question: Which THREE questions are most important to resolve during discovery because they constrain the architecture? (Choose 3.)

options.A: Which model has the highest published benchmark scores for medical question answering this quarter
options.B: What latency and availability levels the clinics need, and what happens when the AI component is unavailable
options.C: Which triage decisions require clinician sign-off and what audit evidence is needed
options.D: Which interface clinicians prefer for reviewing triage suggestions, such as a sidebar in the record or a separate queue
options.E: What data classifications and regulatory regimes apply, including PHI and data residency

questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements that constrain architecture should be surfaced early: data classification and regulatory scope (PHI, residency) determine the deployment path and controls; latency and availability expectations shape model, serving and fallback choices; and the required human oversight for clinical decisions determines workflow design. Interface layout preferences and public benchmark rankings do not constrain architecture in the same way.

why_incorrect.A: Model choice follows from the requirements and your own evaluation; public benchmarks are not a requirement.
why_incorrect.D: Interface layout is a design detail resolved with users later; it does not constrain the deployment path, controls or serving design.

questions.scenario: Six weeks into building a contract-review assistant for Lucerne Publishing, the legal team says the output 'is not what we needed': they wanted risk scores per clause, not summaries. The original requirement said 'help lawyers review contracts faster'.
questions.question: Which discovery practice would most likely have prevented this?

options.A: Write a detailed requirements specification listing every feature the assistant should have, and have it signed off by the head of the legal team
options.B: Benchmark several models on contract summarisation quality during discovery and pick the best performer before design starts
options.C: Agree concrete success criteria with users, with worked examples of the desired output, and make them the first eval cases
options.D: Hold weekly demos with the legal team from the first sprint so they can watch progress and redirect the work if it drifts

questions.explanation: Vague goals such as 'review faster' need to be turned into concrete, testable success criteria during discovery, ideally with examples of the desired output agreed by users (for example annotated sample contracts showing clause-level risk ratings). Those examples double as the first evaluation cases. Longer specifications, more demos or model benchmarks without agreed examples of the output do not resolve the ambiguity.

why_incorrect.A: A longer feature list can still say 'faster review' without defining the output; worked examples expose the misunderstanding.
why_incorrect.B: This optimises the assumed task; nobody had confirmed that summaries were what the lawyers needed.
why_incorrect.D: Frequent demos would catch the drift sooner, but they correct it after work is built rather than defining success up front.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' discovery has produced 18 candidate Claude use cases. Leadership wants three to pursue first.
questions.question: Which TWO criteria are most appropriate for prioritisation? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Technical ambition: which use cases best stretch the team's skills with agents and multistep tool use
options.B: Expected measurable value against a baseline, such as volume and time or cost saved
options.C: Strategic visibility: which use cases would make the strongest announcement to customers and investors
options.D: Competitive parity: which use cases competitors have already launched, to avoid falling behind
options.E: Feasibility and risk, including data availability, how easily outputs can be verified and the cost of errors

questions.explanation: Use-case prioritisation should weigh measurable value against feasibility and risk. Value includes volume, time saved and strategic importance against a measured baseline. Feasibility and risk include data availability, how verifiable outputs are, regulatory exposure and the cost of errors. Announcement value, competitor launches or technical ambition are weak signals.

why_incorrect.A: Technical complexity raises risk and cost; it is not a reason to prioritise a use case.
why_incorrect.C: Announcement value is a weak proxy for measurable business value and ignores feasibility.
why_incorrect.D: A competitor's launch says nothing about this company's baseline, data or risk.

questions.scenario: You must explain to Woodgrove Bank's risk committee why the design uses a workflow with human approval instead of a fully autonomous agent.
questions.question: Which communication approach is most effective for this audience?

options.A: Cite industry research showing that autonomous agents still make frequent errors, and recommend the workflow on that basis
options.B: Give a live demo of the workflow approving and rejecting sample cases, then take questions on anything the committee members want to explore further
options.C: Present the options considered, the risks and value of each, the controls chosen and evaluation evidence, in business terms
options.D: Walk the committee through the agent architecture, tool schemas and API request flow so they can see exactly how the design works

questions.explanation: Executive and risk audiences need decisions framed in terms of business risk, controls and outcomes, not implementation detail. Presenting the options considered, the risk and value of each, the controls in the chosen design and the evidence from evaluation lets the committee make or endorse the decision. Deep technical detail, generic research or a demo of hand-picked cases does not answer their questions.

why_incorrect.A: Generic research does not show the options considered for this system, its controls or its own evaluation evidence.
why_incorrect.B: A demo shows behaviour on chosen cases but does not frame the trade-off, the residual risks or the evidence behind the choice.
why_incorrect.D: Implementation detail does not answer a risk committee's questions about risk, controls and outcomes.

questions.scenario: Proseware's architecture team decides to use MCP for internal tool integration rather than per-application custom tools. Six months later, new engineers keep asking why.
questions.question: Which artefact best preserves this decision and its trade-offs?

options.A: An Architecture Decision Record capturing context, the decision, alternatives considered, consequences, and conditions for revisiting it
options.B: A pinned thread in the architecture team's chat channel summarising the discussion, with links to the original messages
options.C: A detailed comment block at the top of the MCP server's main source file explaining how each tool is registered, configured and authenticated
options.D: The original design-review slide deck, saved to the shared drive alongside the meeting recording and list of attendees

questions.explanation: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures the context, the decision, the alternatives considered, and the consequences (both positive and negative) in a short, version-controlled document. It answers 'why' for future engineers and records when a decision should be revisited. Chat threads, slide decks and code comments are hard to find or explain 'how' rather than 'why', and rarely capture alternatives and consequences.

why_incorrect.B: Chat threads are hard to find later and rarely record the alternatives considered or the consequences.
why_incorrect.C: A code comment explains how the server works, not why MCP was chosen over the alternatives.
why_incorrect.D: A deck captures the presentation, not a concise, versioned record of alternatives and conditions for revisiting.

questions.scenario: The CFO of Bluefin Grocers asks why the proposed design uses a more expensive model for one step when a cheaper one 'seems fine'.
questions.question: Which explanation best communicates the trade-off?

options.A: Agree to trial the cheaper model in production for a month and switch back if users complain about the quality of results
options.B: Show eval results for both models on that step, the cost of the cheaper model's errors and the resulting cost per completed task, with a plan to re-evaluate
options.C: Show the per-request price difference against projected monthly volume, and point out that the extra annual spend still fits within the approved project budget
options.D: Explain that the larger model scores higher on public reasoning benchmarks, so it is the safer choice for a step this important

questions.explanation: Trade-offs land with finance stakeholders when they are framed as total cost and risk per business outcome, with evidence. Showing eval results for each model on that step, the error cost (for example manual rework per error) and the resulting cost per completed task makes the choice transparent, and committing to re-evaluate when new models arrive shows discipline. Appeals to benchmarks, budget headroom or a trial in production do not justify spend.

why_incorrect.A: Using customers as the test set exposes them to errors, and complaints are a slow, incomplete signal.
why_incorrect.C: This shows the cost side only; without error rates and rework cost the CFO cannot see what the extra spend buys.
why_incorrect.D: Public benchmarks do not measure this step; the CFO needs evidence on the actual task and its error cost.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health's clinical leaders and its security team disagree: clinicians want the assistant to read full patient histories for better summaries, while security wants minimum-necessary data.
questions.question: Which TWO actions best help resolve the disagreement? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Evaluate summary quality with full versus scoped histories to quantify the actual clinical benefit
options.B: Implement full-history access for clinicians, since they are accountable for patient outcomes and are the primary users
options.C: Launch with full histories for a pilot group and decide the long-term scope after reviewing complaints and incidents
options.D: Present options with their residual risks, controls and costs to the accountable decision-makers, and record the outcome in an ADR
options.E: Adopt the security team's minimum-necessary design, since the regulatory duty sits with security and overrides clinical preference

questions.explanation: Conflicting requirements are resolved with evidence and explicit trade-offs, not by picking a side. Running an evaluation that compares summary quality with full versus scoped histories quantifies the clinical benefit, and presenting options with their residual risks and controls lets accountable owners decide. Implementing one side's preference, or deciding through a production pilot, undermines trust.

why_incorrect.B: Picking a side without data ignores the regulatory requirement and undermines trust with security.
why_incorrect.C: This exposes full histories before the decision is made and measures harm through incidents rather than evaluation.
why_incorrect.E: Minimum necessary is a principle to apply with evidence, not a veto; this ignores the clinical benefit that has not been measured.

questions.scenario: Two weeks after launch of Tailspin Insurance's claims-summary assistant, adjusters say it 'sometimes gets things wrong', but feedback comes through hallway conversations.
questions.question: Which feedback mechanism is most useful?

options.A: A thumbs-up and thumbs-down button on each summary, with the daily ratio shown on the team's quality dashboard
options.B: An in-product flag with error categories and an optional note, stored with the trace ID so the team can reproduce it and add it to the eval set
options.C: A quarterly satisfaction survey of adjusters with free-text questions about where the assistant gets things wrong
options.D: A shared mailbox where adjusters can email screenshots of poor summaries with a short description, triaged every week by the claims product owner

questions.explanation: Useful feedback is structured, captured in context and actionable. An in-product control that lets adjusters flag a summary, choose an error category and add a note, stored with the trace ID, lets the team reproduce, categorise and prioritise issues and turn them into eval cases. Informal channels, periodic surveys and bare ratings lose the specifics.

why_incorrect.A: A ratio shows trend but carries no error category or trace, so it is hard to act on or turn into eval cases.
why_incorrect.C: Quarterly surveys arrive late and lose the specific request needed to reproduce the issue.
why_incorrect.D: Screenshots detach feedback from the trace, so the team cannot reproduce or categorise issues reliably.

questions.scenario: Alpine Ski House's executive sponsor expects the new booking assistant to be '100% accurate' from day one.
questions.question: Which TWO actions best set realistic expectations? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Explain how errors are detected and corrected, and share a roadmap for improving quality after launch
options.B: Explain that generative output cannot be scored, so quality will be judged from user satisfaction after launch
options.C: Commit to the 100% target in the sponsor's report and track the actual error rate internally until it improves
options.D: Present the model provider's benchmark accuracy figures to show the assistant will be highly accurate at launch
options.E: Agree measurable quality targets per task based on evaluation, with zero-tolerance areas enforced by deterministic controls

questions.explanation: LLM-based systems have error rates that must be measured and managed. Setting expectations means agreeing measurable targets per task (for example 95% correct bookings on the eval, with zero tolerance for payment errors enforced by deterministic checks), explaining how errors are caught, and sharing a plan for improvement over time. Promising perfection, borrowing benchmark figures or refusing to measure sets the project up to lose trust.

why_incorrect.B: Task quality can be measured with evaluations; relying on satisfaction alone gives no agreed target.
why_incorrect.C: Promising perfection while tracking a different number privately sets the project up to lose trust.
why_incorrect.D: Provider benchmarks do not measure this booking task and imply a level of accuracy the system has not demonstrated.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail's support organisation wants an SLA for its Claude-powered order-status assistant. The assistant depends on the Claude API, an order-management API and a retrieval index.
