questions.question: Which approach to defining the SLA is most sound?

options.A: Commit to a 99.99% SLA and add automatic retries with exponential backoff on every dependency so transient failures do not reach users
options.B: Define user-facing SLOs end to end, decompose them across the model, order API and retrieval index, measure each, and set graceful degradation and an error budget
options.C: Adopt the model provider's published availability target as the assistant's SLA, since the model is the least proven dependency
options.D: Use the lowest availability figure among the three dependencies as the end-to-end SLA, since the assistant can be no more available than its weakest single dependency

questions.explanation: A sound SLA is defined end to end from the user's perspective, decomposed into service level objectives for each dependency, and backed by measured indicators. It accounts for dependency availability and rate limits, defines graceful degradation (for example show order status from the order API directly when the model is unavailable) and sets an error budget. Quoting one dependency's figure, the weakest component's figure or a target with no measurement is not an SLA.

why_incorrect.A: Retries help with transient errors but cannot meet a target that was never derived from the dependencies or measured.
why_incorrect.C: One dependency's figure ignores the order API and retrieval index and is not measured from the user's perspective.
why_incorrect.D: Serial dependencies compound, so end-to-end availability is lower than the weakest component; it also lacks measurement and degradation.

questions.scenario: Six months after launch, Relecloud's users say the knowledge assistant 'got worse'. Nothing in the application has changed, but the knowledge base has grown from 2,000 to 15,000 documents and new departments have joined.
questions.question: What is the best way to respond to this feedback?

options.A: Reply that the application has not changed since launch, and ask users for specific examples so the team can check whether a regression exists
options.B: Re-run evaluation on current content and recent real queries, compare with the launch baseline by department, and share a remediation plan
options.C: Upgrade to the newest model generation, since a larger corpus needs stronger reasoning, and monitor whether the complaints decrease
options.D: Re-index the knowledge base with smaller chunks to improve retrieval precision across the larger corpus, then announce the improvement to the affected departments

questions.explanation: When users report degradation, confirm it with data before acting. Production monitoring and the eval set should be re-run with current traffic and content; growth in the corpus and new user groups can shift retrieval quality and query mix. Communicating findings and a remediation plan to stakeholders closes the loop. Dismissing feedback or making untested changes erodes trust.

why_incorrect.A: Examples help, but the system's inputs have changed a great deal, so 'nothing changed' is wrong and the burden belongs with the team.
why_incorrect.C: An untested model change may not address a retrieval or query-mix problem and makes the cause harder to isolate.
why_incorrect.D: Re-chunking might help, but announcing an untested fix before measuring the degradation risks making things worse.

questions.scenario: Your design for Northwind Lending's document-intake system is being handed to an implementation team in another region.
questions.question: Which documentation set gives the most useful implementation guidance?

options.A: A detailed functional specification of every screen and user story, with the model IDs and environment configuration to use
options.B: The steering committee's slide deck plus recorded walkthroughs from the lead architects, so the new team hears the reasoning behind each decision first hand
options.C: Read access to the original team's repository and chat history, with the architects available for questions for one month
options.D: Data-flow diagrams with trust boundaries, ADRs for key decisions, versioned prompt and tool specifications, the eval suite with thresholds, and runbooks

questions.explanation: Implementation guidance should let another team build and operate the system correctly without the original architects: architecture diagrams with data flows and trust boundaries, ADRs explaining key decisions, prompt and tool specifications under version control, the evaluation suite and acceptance thresholds, and operational runbooks. Slide decks, functional specifications or raw project history leave too many decisions open.

why_incorrect.A: Functional detail omits trust boundaries, decisions, evals and operations, which the implementing team needs most.
why_incorrect.B: Walkthroughs convey intent but leave decisions, specifications and acceptance thresholds undocumented.
why_incorrect.C: Raw history is unstructured and the temporary access expires before the team has to operate the system.

questions.scenario: Proseware is documenting its agent platform for internal teams. Security reviewers want the documentation to support threat modelling.
questions.question: Which TWO elements should the architecture documentation include for that purpose? (Choose 2.)

options.A: A breakdown of token usage and cost per agent so reviewers can spot agents with unusual consumption
options.B: The full text of every system prompt, published on the company-wide wiki so anyone can review it
options.C: A summary of the business capabilities each agent provides and the teams that rely on them
options.D: Data-flow diagrams marking trust boundaries, including where untrusted content such as retrieved documents and tool results enters
options.E: An inventory of each agent's tools, permissions, credentials and approval requirements

questions.explanation: Threat modelling needs to know where trust changes and what each component can do. Data-flow diagrams marking trust boundaries (user input, retrieved content, tool results, external services) and an inventory of each agent's tools, permissions and credentials let reviewers analyse injection paths and excessive agency. Capability summaries, cost tables and widely published prompts are useful elsewhere or risky, but not what threat modelling needs.

why_incorrect.A: Cost data supports operations, not analysis of injection paths or excessive agency.
why_incorrect.B: Prompts are less important to threat modelling than data flows and permissions, and publishing them widely creates its own risk.
why_incorrect.C: Business capabilities help scoping but do not show where trust changes or what each agent is permitted to do.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Toys' prompts are currently embedded as strings in application code across six services, and nobody knows which version is in production.
questions.question: Which practice gives the clearest implementation guidance for managing prompts?

options.A: Collect every prompt on a central wiki page with a named owner per prompt, and ask engineers to copy the latest text into their services
options.B: Keep prompts in version control with review, record eval results for each change, and log the prompt version per request
options.C: Move prompts into a shared configuration service that service owners can edit live, so fixes reach production without a deploy
options.D: Consolidate the six services' prompts into one shared library module so every service uses identical prompt text

questions.explanation: Prompts are part of the system's behaviour and should be treated like code: stored in version control, reviewed, tied to the eval results that justified each change, and deployed with an identifiable version that is logged with each request. This makes changes auditable and regressions traceable. Live editing, copying from a wiki or consolidating without versioning loses that traceability.

why_incorrect.A: Copying from a wiki recreates the drift between documented and deployed versions.
why_incorrect.C: Live edits without review, eval evidence or version logging make it impossible to tell which prompt caused a regression.
why_incorrect.D: Consolidation reduces duplication, but without review, eval records and per-request version logging the deployed version is still unknown.

questions.scenario: An on-call engineer at Kestrel Payments receives an alert that the dispute assistant's refusal rate jumped from 1% to 12%. There is no runbook and the original team has moved on.
questions.question: Which runbook content would have helped most?

options.A: A system overview describing the assistant's purpose and architecture diagram, the model and prompt versions in use, and the downstream teams that depend on it, with their contacts
options.B: Alert-specific diagnosis steps (dashboards, traces by stop reason), checks of recent prompt, model and config changes, rollback and escalation
options.C: Links to the provider's API reference and status page, plus a table of the HTTP error codes and retry behaviour the assistant's client handles
options.D: The project charter and launch-readiness checklist, including the original acceptance criteria, the eval results from launch and the sign-off record

questions.explanation: Runbooks turn architecture knowledge into operational steps: what each alert means, where to look (dashboards, traces filtered by `stop_reason`), recent changes to check (prompt, model or configuration versions), how to roll back, and when to escalate and to whom. A design overview, vendor documentation or launch paperwork does not give the on-call engineer a path to resolution.

why_incorrect.A: Useful context, but it gives the on-call engineer no steps for diagnosing or resolving this alert.
why_incorrect.C: A refusal spike is not an HTTP error; vendor references do not explain what changed in this system.
why_incorrect.D: Launch documents describe the original intent, not how to diagnose and roll back a production change.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing's translation assistant has been in production for a year. A newer model generation has been released, and the provider has announced a retirement date for the model currently in use.
questions.question: Which lifecycle approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Pin the current model ID and negotiate an extended support arrangement with the provider, deferring migration until the next major release
options.B: Switch to the new model ID now across environments, since newer generations score higher on benchmarks, and watch user feedback for problems
options.C: Keep the current model until the announced retirement date, then switch the model ID in a single planned release, since newer generations are backward compatible with old prompts
options.D: Run the eval suite on the new model, adjust prompts for behaviour changes, compare quality, latency and cost, and roll out gradually with a rollback path before retirement

questions.explanation: Model upgrades are a planned lifecycle activity: run the existing eval suite on the new model, review and adjust prompts for behavioural differences, compare quality, latency and cost, roll out gradually (for example a canary or A/B) with monitoring, keep a rollback path, and complete the migration before the retirement date. Waiting for retirement, deferring migration or switching blindly all create avoidable risk.

why_incorrect.A: Retirement dates are set by the provider; deferring only compresses the same migration work into less time.
why_incorrect.B: Benchmarks do not measure this translation task, and a blanket switch without evaluation or a canary risks a silent regression.
why_incorrect.C: New generations often change behaviour and request parameters; a last-day switch leaves no time to evaluate or roll back.

questions.scenario: Civic Benefits Agency asks how its Claude solution will be handled after the initial build team hands over to an operations team.
questions.question: Which TWO elements are most important to include in the handoff phase? (Choose 2.)

options.A: A support contract keeping the build team on call for escalations during the first three months
options.B: A recorded walkthrough of the system by the build team for operations staff to watch before go-live
options.C: A final project report summarising scope, budget, delivered features and lessons learned for the steering group
options.D: Named owners and a change-management process for prompts, models, tools and knowledge sources
options.E: Runbooks, dashboards, alerts and the evaluation suite, with training on how to use them

questions.explanation: Handoff should transfer both knowledge and ownership: operational runbooks, dashboards and alerts, the eval suite and how to run it, and a clear owner for prompts, models and data changes with an agreed change-management process. Without these, the system degrades silently. A recording, a closure report or temporary build-team cover does not equip the operations team.

why_incorrect.A: Temporary cover delays the handoff rather than completing it; ownership still has to move to operations.
why_incorrect.B: A recording transfers some knowledge but not the tools, ownership or change process needed to operate the system.
why_incorrect.C: Closure reporting serves the sponsors, not the operations team that must run the system.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's team proposes a lifecycle plan that ends at launch: discovery, design, build, launch. The sponsor asks what is missing.
questions.question: Which addition makes the lifecycle plan complete for a Claude-based system?

options.A: A formal post-launch review after one month that compares results with the business case and then closes the project
options.B: Ongoing monitoring, feedback collection, eval-set growth and periodic iteration, including model upgrades
options.C: A two-week hypercare period after launch with the build team on standby, followed by formal project closure
options.D: A longer build and hardening phase so the system reaches its quality targets before launch and needs fewer changes afterwards

questions.explanation: LLM systems need continuing lifecycle phases after launch: monitoring of quality, cost and safety; collecting feedback and new eval cases; periodic iteration on prompts, retrieval and tools; and planned model upgrades. Inputs, users and models change over time, so a plan that ends at launch leaves the system to drift. A longer build phase, a hypercare period or a one-off review does not address that.

why_incorrect.A: A single review is useful but is not ongoing monitoring, eval growth or planned model upgrades.
why_incorrect.C: Hypercare covers launch issues but still ends the lifecycle; drift after the first weeks goes unmanaged.
why_incorrect.D: Inputs, users and models keep changing after launch, so no amount of pre-launch hardening removes the need to monitor and iterate.

questions.scenario: Woodgrove Bank is rolling out Claude Code to 400 engineers. Security requires that no developer can allow Claude Code to read files under `secrets/` or run `curl` to arbitrary hosts, regardless of their personal settings.
questions.question: Which configuration approach enforces this?

options.A: Put the deny rules in managed settings on every machine, which take precedence over user, project and local settings
options.B: Distribute a standard user settings file containing the deny rules through the dotfiles repository that every engineer installs
options.C: Write the restrictions into each project CLAUDE.md and the onboarding guide so that Claude and engineers both know the policy
options.D: Add the deny rules to a checked-in `.claude/settings.json` in every repository, with a CI check that fails if the file is changed

questions.explanation: Claude Code applies settings in a precedence order, and managed settings (delivered through a `managed-settings.json` file, MDM policy or server-managed settings) sit at the top: nothing in a developer's user, project or local settings, or a command-line flag, overrides a managed key. Putting deny rules for the sensitive paths and commands in managed settings therefore enforces the policy organisation-wide. Project or user settings can be overridden or edited by developers, and CLAUDE.md guidance is only advisory.

why_incorrect.B: User settings have the lowest precedence and each engineer can edit them.
why_incorrect.C: CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude reads, not an enforced permission rule.
why_incorrect.D: A checked-in project settings file only covers that repository, and developers can edit or remove it in their own working copy. Only managed settings are enforced centrally and cannot be changed by the developer.

questions.scenario: Fabrikam Retail's platform team wants every Claude Code session in its monorepo to know the build commands, coding conventions and the rule that database migrations need a reviewer, without each developer configuring anything.
questions.question: Which TWO mechanisms are most appropriate? (Choose 2.)

options.A: A checked-in `.claude/settings.json` with shared permission rules and hooks for the migrations directory
options.B: A project CLAUDE.md checked into the repository with build commands and conventions
options.C: Each developer's `CLAUDE.local.md` file, populated from a template the platform team publishes
options.D: A user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` that each developer copies from the platform team's template with the build commands
options.E: A shared prompt snippet that developers paste at the start of each session from the team wiki

questions.explanation: A project CLAUDE.md checked into the repository gives every session the shared commands and conventions automatically. Team-shared settings in `.claude/settings.json` (also checked in) let the team define permission rules and hooks consistently, for example requiring approval for edits under the migrations directory. Personal `CLAUDE.local.md` or user-level files depend on each developer setting them up, and pasting instructions into each session does not scale.

why_incorrect.C: Local files are personal and normally git-ignored, so each developer must set them up and they drift.
why_incorrect.D: User-level memory applies across all projects and depends on each developer copying and updating it; the requirement was no per-developer setup.
why_incorrect.E: Pasting instructions into each session depends on every developer remembering, and it does not scale.

questions.scenario: Contoso Health wants Claude Code to block any command that writes to production database hosts, even if a developer approves it by mistake, and to log the attempt centrally.
questions.question: Which mechanism best meets this requirement?

options.A: A CLAUDE.md rule forbidding production connections, backed by a quarterly audit of developers' shell histories
options.B: Deny rules for commands containing the production host names, added to each repository's project settings so that Claude Code refuses to run any of them
options.C: A `PreToolUse` hook, deployed through managed settings, that inspects commands, blocks those targeting production database hosts and logs the attempt
options.D: A `PostToolUse` hook that sends an alert to the security team whenever a command touches a production database host

questions.explanation: Hooks run deterministic code at defined points in Claude Code's lifecycle. A `PreToolUse` hook can inspect each tool call before it executes and block it, and the same hook can emit a log event. Deployed through managed settings, it applies to every developer. Instructions in CLAUDE.md are advisory, prefix-based deny rules in project settings are easy to bypass, and a `PostToolUse` hook fires only after the command has run.

why_incorrect.A: CLAUDE.md is advisory, and a quarterly audit finds the write months after it happened.
why_incorrect.B: Bash permission patterns are fragile for constraining arguments such as host names buried in arbitrary commands, and nothing records centrally what was blocked.
why_incorrect.D: A `PostToolUse` hook runs after the command has executed, so it can alert but not block.

questions.scenario: Lucerne Publishing's engineering manager wants to control Claude Code spend across teams while keeping developers productive.
questions.question: Which approach is most effective?

options.A: Set a hard monthly token quota for every developer that blocks Claude Code once reached, sized from average usage across the engineering teams
options.B: Have each team lead review the monthly invoice line by line and ask the heaviest users on their team to justify their usage at the next sprint retrospective meeting
options.C: Enable usage telemetry by team, set organisation model defaults in managed settings, and coach efficient context habits such as clearing context between tasks
options.D: Make the smallest available model the managed default for every task, and let developers request exceptions through a ticket

questions.explanation: Cost management starts with visibility: enabling telemetry or usage reporting by team shows where spend goes. From there, teams can set sensible defaults (for example which models are available through managed settings), share efficient practices such as clearing or compacting context between unrelated tasks, and review outliers. Arbitrary quotas, forced model downgrades or after-the-fact invoice reviews, without data, hurt productivity.

why_incorrect.A: A quota sized from an average, without data on why usage differs, blocks heavy legitimate users mid-task and hurts productivity.
why_incorrect.B: Invoice review is late, coarse and lacks the per-team visibility needed to change habits.
why_incorrect.D: Forcing the smallest model on hard tasks can raise cost per completed task through retries and rework.

questions.scenario: Wingtip Toys wants Claude to review every pull request automatically for missing tests and obvious security issues, posting comments on the PR.
questions.question: Which integration is most appropriate?

options.A: Have the tech lead paste each day's merged diffs into a Claude chat and file follow-up issues for any problems found
options.B: Add a pre-commit hook that runs Claude Code locally on each developer's staged changes and prints review findings in the terminal
options.C: Run Claude Code in CI on each pull request, via GitHub Actions or headless mode, with a set review prompt and scoped permissions
options.D: Run Claude Code in CI on each pull request with full repository permissions, and let it approve and merge changes that pass its own automated review checks

questions.explanation: Running Claude Code non-interactively in CI, for example through the Claude Code GitHub Actions integration or headless mode, lets the review run on every pull request with a defined prompt and scoped permissions and post comments back. It remains a supplement to human review. Local hooks are easy to bypass, after-merge review comes too late, and letting the bot approve and merge removes human review.

why_incorrect.A: Reviewing after merge misses the chance to fix issues before they land and is a manual, inconsistent step.
why_incorrect.B: Local hooks can be skipped, do not post to the pull request and depend on each developer's setup.
why_incorrect.D: Automated review supplements human review; granting merge rights and broad permissions removes that oversight and widens the blast radius.

questions.scenario: Relecloud's developers use Claude Code for large refactors. Results are inconsistent: sometimes it edits dozens of files before anyone notices a wrong approach.
questions.question: Which TWO workflow practices most improve outcomes? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Turn off permission prompts for refactors so long edit sequences are not interrupted
options.B: Give Claude tests or build commands it can run to verify each step as it goes
options.C: Keep instructions brief and high level so Claude can choose the most idiomatic approach
options.D: Have Claude explore the code and propose a plan for review before it makes any edits
options.E: Ask for the whole refactor in one detailed message so Claude has full context from the start

questions.explanation: For larger changes, asking Claude to explore and propose a plan before editing (for example using plan mode) lets the developer correct the approach early. Giving Claude a way to verify its work, such as tests or a build command it can run, lets it check changes as it goes. Turning off permissions for speed or giving vaguer instructions increases the chance of large, wrong changes.

why_incorrect.A: Removing checkpoints lets a wrong approach spread across more files before anyone notices.
why_incorrect.C: Vaguer instructions increase the chance Claude picks an approach the team did not intend.
why_incorrect.E: Detail helps, but asking for everything in one go without a reviewed plan still lets a wrong approach run across dozens of files.

questions.scenario: Fourth Coffee's teams repeat the same multistep workflows in Claude Code: creating a service from a template, writing release notes and running a security checklist. Each developer prompts these differently.
questions.question: Which mechanism best standardises these workflows across teams?

options.A: Collect each team's best prompts into a shared snippets library on the wiki, with a named owner for each workflow
options.B: Package each workflow as a Skill, shared through the repository or a team plugin, as one version-controlled procedure
options.C: Write the three workflows out step by step in every repository's CLAUDE.md, so the full procedures are loaded into each session automatically
options.D: Run training sessions with recorded examples showing the recommended way to prompt each of the three workflows

questions.explanation: Reusable workflows can be packaged as Skills (and shared through plugins), giving a consistent, version-controlled procedure that Claude loads when relevant or that developers invoke by name. Distributing them as a plugin or through the repository keeps every team on the same version. Wiki snippets, training or bloating every CLAUDE.md do not standardise the workflow as well.

why_incorrect.A: Snippets still depend on developers copying them correctly, and versions drift between the wiki and use.
why_incorrect.C: Loading full procedures into every session wastes context on unrelated work, and copies drift across repositories.
why_incorrect.D: Training improves skill but does not give everyone the same executable, version-controlled procedure.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' on-call engineer uses Claude Code to investigate a production incident. The service's logs are large and the engineer is worried about context filling with log noise.
questions.question: Which TWO practices are most effective? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Run `/compact` after each log read so a summary replaces the raw output and the context stays small
options.B: Paste the full log files into the conversation once at the start so Claude has the complete picture before investigating
options.C: Ask Claude to search logs with targeted filters, such as the request ID and incident time window, instead of reading entire files
options.D: Delegate log searches to a subagent that returns a condensed summary, keeping the main context focused
options.E: Give Claude Code read and write access to the production hosts so it can inspect live state and apply a hotfix quickly

questions.explanation: Subagents run with their own context window, so delegating log searches to a subagent that returns only a condensed finding keeps the main session focused. Asking Claude to filter logs with targeted commands (grep for the request ID or time window) rather than reading whole files reduces noise further. Pasting full logs, compacting after reading whole files or granting production write access adds noise or risk.

why_incorrect.A: Compacting after the fact still pulls whole files into context first and can drop details the investigation needs.
why_incorrect.B: Full logs fill the context with noise, which is the problem the engineer wants to avoid.
why_incorrect.E: Production write access adds risk without addressing context noise.

questions.scenario: A developer at Northwind Lending reports that an MCP server configured for Claude Code is not available in their session, while it works for colleagues.
questions.question: What is the most effective first diagnostic step?

options.A: Reinstall Claude Code and clear its cache on the developer's machine so the MCP configuration is reloaded from scratch
options.B: Copy a colleague's working `~/.claude.json` onto the developer's machine so their MCP configuration matches the team's
options.C: Ask the platform team to restart the MCP server process on the shared host, then check its logs for errors from the developer's connection attempts in the session
options.D: Run `claude mcp list` to check each server's status and scope, including whether a project-scoped server awaits the developer's approval or needs authentication

questions.explanation: Start with the tool's own diagnostics. `claude mcp list` shows each configured server with a health status (for example connected, needs authentication, failed to connect, or pending approval for a project-scoped server from `.mcp.json` that this developer has not yet approved). That reveals whether the server is configured in a scope the developer's session uses and why it is unavailable. Reinstalling, copying another person's configuration or restarting a server that works for others does not target the likely causes.

why_incorrect.A: Reinstalling is disruptive and does not reveal whether the cause is scope, approval or authentication.
why_incorrect.B: Overwriting the developer's configuration with a colleague's discards their own settings and credentials without diagnosing the cause.
why_incorrect.C: The server works for colleagues, so the fault is likely in this developer's configuration, not the server process.

questions.scenario: Tailspin Insurance runs Claude Code headlessly in a nightly job that triages failing tests. Some nights the job hangs and never produces output.
questions.question: Which change most improves the job's operational reliability?

options.A: Run the job interactively in a terminal multiplexer so an engineer can attach and answer any permission prompts that appear
options.B: Run the job with every permission check bypassed inside the CI container so no prompt can block it, relying on the container's isolation instead
options.C: Wrap the job in a watchdog that restarts Claude Code whenever it produces no output for thirty minutes, up to five attempts a night
options.D: Pre-approve the headless run's allowed tools, set turn and time limits, request structured output, and fail visibly on timeout

questions.explanation: Unattended runs need explicit bounds and pre-approved permissions: a headless run has no one to answer permission prompts, so the allowed tools should be configured in advance, with a turn or time limit and structured output that the job checks. Logging the run and failing loudly on timeout makes hangs visible. Running interactively, bypassing all permissions or restarting blindly defeats the purpose, adds risk or hides the cause.

why_incorrect.A: Needing a human to attach defeats the purpose of an unattended nightly job.
why_incorrect.B: Bypassing every check widens what the job can do, and still sets no turn or time limit or structured output to detect hangs.
why_incorrect.C: Restarting repeats the same hang without fixing its cause, and burns time and spend.

questions.scenario: Proseware Analytics wants every engineer who clones its data-platform repository to get the same internal ticketing MCP server in Claude Code, without running setup commands by hand. The server needs a per-user API token, and security forbids tokens in version control.
questions.question: Which configuration approach best meets both requirements?

options.A: Define the server at project scope in a checked-in `.mcp.json`, reading each engineer's token from an environment variable
options.B: Commit the server definition to `.mcp.json` with a shared service-account token inline, so it works the moment the repository is cloned
options.C: Publish a wiki page telling each engineer to add the server at user scope with `claude mcp add` and paste in their own token
options.D: Configure the server at local scope on one reference laptop, then copy that machine's `~/.claude.json` to every engineer's laptop

questions.explanation: Project-scoped MCP servers live in `.mcp.json` at the repository root and are meant to be checked into version control so the whole team gets the same tools. `.mcp.json` supports environment variable expansion, so each engineer supplies their own token from their environment and no secret is committed. Claude Code asks each developer to approve project-scoped servers in interactive sessions.

why_incorrect.B: This puts a credential in version control, which security forbids, and a shared token removes per-user accountability.
why_incorrect.C: Manual per-developer setup is exactly what the team wants to avoid, and configurations drift between engineers.
why_incorrect.D: Local scope is per-user state in `~/.claude.json`; copying that file between machines is brittle and spreads one person's credentials.

questions.scenario: Litware Labs' developers often ask Claude Code to fix an urgent bug while a long feature task is still running in another Claude Code session in the same checkout. The two sessions' edits collide, and developers keep stashing and restoring work to untangle them.
questions.question: Which workflow change best addresses this?

options.A: Pause the feature session, run `/clear`, fix the bug in that same session and checkout, then restart the feature
options.B: Keep both sessions in one shared checkout, but tell each session in its prompt exactly which files it is allowed to modify
options.C: Run each task in its own git worktree, for example with `claude --worktree <name>`, so sessions edit separate checkouts
options.D: Hand the bug fix to a subagent inside the feature session so that both tasks are coordinated by one main session

questions.explanation: A git worktree is a separate checkout on its own branch, so parallel Claude Code sessions in different worktrees cannot overwrite each other's edits. Claude Code supports this directly with `claude --worktree`, letting the bug fix and the feature proceed in parallel and merge through normal review.

why_incorrect.A: Clearing context discards the feature session's progress and serialises work that could safely run in parallel.
why_incorrect.B: Prompt-level file boundaries are not enforced, and both sessions still share one working tree and branch, so changes still mix.
why_incorrect.D: A subagent works in the same working directory, so the bug fix still lands in the feature branch's uncommitted changes.

questions.scenario: Adatum Software's platform team added a `PostToolUse` hook to the repository's `.claude/settings.json` to run the code formatter after Claude edits a file, using the matcher `edit|write`. Developers report that edited files are never formatted, and no hook error appears in the transcript.
questions.question: What is the most effective way to diagnose and fix the problem?

options.A: Use `/hooks` to confirm the hook loaded under `PostToolUse`, then correct the case-sensitive matcher to `Edit|Write`
options.B: Add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to run the formatter itself after every edit, and remove the hook from settings entirely
options.C: Move the hook from `PostToolUse` to `PreToolUse` so the formatter runs reliably on every file before Claude writes to it
options.D: Make the formatter script exit with code 1 after it succeeds, so Claude Code prints its output in the transcript

questions.explanation: The `/hooks` menu shows which hooks are loaded, for which event and from which settings file, which confirms whether the configuration is being read. Hook matchers compare against tool names as written and are case-sensitive, so `edit|write` never matches the `Edit` and `Write` tools; correcting the matcher fixes the silent failure.

why_incorrect.B: A CLAUDE.md rule is advisory rather than deterministic, and it abandons the hook without finding the root cause.
why_incorrect.C: `PreToolUse` fires before the edit, so it would format the old file contents, and it leaves the matcher bug in place.
why_incorrect.D: Exit code 1 signals a non-blocking error rather than success, and it does nothing to make the hook fire in the first place.

questions.scenario: Orrin Analytics runs its research coordinator with the Agent SDK's query() function. An engineer proposes ending the run when the coordinator writes 'REPORT COMPLETE' in its text, so the service can return quickly. Runs sometimes stop because of the configured turn or spend limits.
questions.question: How should the service decide that a run has ended and whether it succeeded?

options.A: Treat the run as ended when the SDK yields the ResultMessage, and branch on its subtype to tell success from a turn or budget limit
options.B: Set maxTurns to ten and treat reaching that limit as completion, since a cited report rarely needs more than ten tool-use turns to finish
options.C: Watch the output directory and treat the run as complete once a report file appears, then cancel the query to save tokens
options.D: Tell the coordinator to finish with 'REPORT COMPLETE', and stop reading the stream as soon as that phrase appears in its text

questions.explanation: In the Agent SDK the loop runs until Claude produces a response with no tool calls, then the SDK yields a ResultMessage. Its subtype says whether the run succeeded or stopped on error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd or an execution error, and it carries cost and session_id for resumption. Text markers, iteration counts and side effects are unreliable proxies for that signal.

why_incorrect.B: Hitting maxTurns ends the run with an error_max_turns result; it signals an unfinished task, not a completed one.
why_incorrect.C: A file can appear before the agent has finished revising it, and cancelling loses the final result, its status and the session ID needed to resume.
why_incorrect.D: Parsing natural-language markers is fragile, and stopping early discards the ResultMessage with its subtype, cost and session ID.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Home Goods runs a support agent on a hand-written Messages API loop. The loop ends as soon as a response contains a text block. Customers often see the agent say 'Let me pull up that order for you' and then nothing further happens, even though the same response also requested an order-lookup tool.
questions.question: How should the loop's control flow be changed?

options.A: Keep the text check, and add a system prompt rule telling the model never to write any text before it calls a tool
options.B: Cap the loop at eight iterations, and also stop early whenever the reply text includes a closing phrase such as 'anything else'
options.C: Drive the loop from stop_reason: run the requested tools and send their results back while it is "tool_use", and finish on "end_turn"
options.D: Strip text blocks from any response that also has tool_use blocks, so the text-based exit condition only fires on genuine final answers

questions.explanation: A response can contain explanatory text and a tool_use block together. The reliable signal is stop_reason: while it is "tool_use" the loop executes every requested tool, appends the results as tool_result blocks, and calls the model again; "end_turn" means the model has finished. Checking for text, matching phrases or capping iterations are the anti-patterns that cause exactly this stall.

why_incorrect.A: The model can still write text alongside a tool call, and a prompt rule only lowers the rate; the exit condition itself remains wrong.
why_incorrect.B: Iteration caps and phrase matching are both proxies; neither tells the loop that the model has asked for a tool and is waiting for its result.
why_incorrect.D: This still keys termination on content shape instead of stop_reason, drops the model's own words from history, and ignores cases such as max_tokens.

questions.scenario: Larchmont Utilities is building a billing-support agent on the Messages API with its own loop. The model often requests two or three lookups in one response (meter reads, payment history, tariff), and the payments backend occasionally throws exceptions.
questions.question: Which TWO loop behaviours should the team implement? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Send each parallel tool result back in its own user message, in completion order, so the model reasons about one result at a time
options.B: When a tool throws, return a tool_result with is_error set and the failure detail, so the model can decide what to do next
options.C: When a tool throws, remove that tool_use block from the history and resend the request, so the model can try again from a clean state
options.D: Return each result as a tool_result block that references its tool_use_id, with all results from one turn in a single user message
options.E: Use a hard cap of three iterations as the main stopping rule, because most billing questions are answered in a few tool calls

questions.explanation: Tool results are how the model learns what happened, so each requested call needs a matching tool_result (linked by tool_use_id), and all results for one assistant turn go back together in a single user message. A failed tool should still produce a result, flagged with is_error and a useful message, so the model can retry, choose another route or tell the customer. Hiding failures or capping iterations removes information the model needs.

why_incorrect.A: Results from one turn belong in one user message; splitting them breaks the expected structure and discourages the model from making parallel calls.
why_incorrect.C: Editing the model's own turn out of history hides the failure from the model and leaves it unable to reason about or explain what went wrong.
why_incorrect.E: A fixed cap is a safety net, not the stopping mechanism; it cuts off legitimate longer investigations and says nothing about whether the model finished.

questions.scenario: The Meridian Public Health Observatory's research coordinator sends every query through web search, document analysis, synthesis and report subagents. Many queries are simple, such as 'Which year does our stored regional survey cover?', and the answer is already in one indexed document. Cost per query is three times the budget.
questions.question: What change best reduces cost without weakening complex research?

options.A: Keep the full pipeline for every query but move each subagent to the cheapest model tier, so simple questions cost less
options.B: Merge the four subagents into one generalist agent with every tool, so simple questions finish inside a single context
options.C: Put a keyword router in front of the coordinator that sends questions containing 'year' or 'who' down a cheap single-call answer path
options.D: Have the coordinator judge what each query needs and invoke only those subagents, with descriptions that say when each one applies

questions.explanation: A coordinator should analyse each request and decide which subagents to invoke, rather than always running the whole pipeline. Clear subagent descriptions help it match tasks to agents. Simple lookups then use one subagent (or none), while complex questions still get the full decomposition.

why_incorrect.A: This still pays for four agents on trivial questions and degrades the quality of the complex research that needs stronger models.
why_incorrect.B: Collapsing roles removes the context isolation and specialised tool sets that keep complex research reliable.
why_incorrect.C: Keyword routing misclassifies easily and bypasses the coordinator's judgement about what a question actually needs.

questions.scenario: In Brackenfield Insights' research system, the document-analysis subagent sends its findings straight to the report subagent, and the report subagent asks the web-search subagent for extra sources directly. When a hand-off fails, the coordinator never learns of it, and engineers cannot trace which findings reached the report.
questions.question: What should the architect change?

options.A: Route every hand-off through the coordinator, which receives each result, handles failures and decides what to pass on next
options.B: Add a shared message bus that every subagent writes to and reads from, so hand-offs stay direct but leave a trace
options.C: Keep the direct calls between subagents but require each one to append its outgoing payload to a central log file for later audit
options.D: Merge document analysis and report writing into one subagent, so the particular hand-off that loses errors disappears

questions.explanation: A hub-and-spoke design makes the coordinator the only route between subagents. That gives one place for observability, consistent error handling and controlled information flow, and it lets the coordinator decide what each subagent receives.

why_incorrect.B: A bus adds logging but still lets subagents act on each other's output with no single place handling errors or deciding routing.
why_incorrect.C: After-the-fact logs help forensics but do not let anything react to failures or control what information flows where.
why_incorrect.D: This removes one failure point but leaves the other direct links and loses the separation between analysis and writing.

questions.scenario: Halvard Policy Institute's clients send a written scope checklist with each research request, for example costs, staffing impact, legal constraints and international comparisons. The coordinator fans the work out and passes subagent results to synthesis. A client audit finds that about a third of briefings silently omit one checklist item, usually one where a subagent came back with nothing useful.
questions.question: Which TWO changes address the root cause? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Have the coordinator check results against the checklist before synthesis and re-delegate any item with no findings
options.B: Raise every subagent's turn limit, so each one is more likely to find at least something for every checklist item
options.C: Ask the synthesis agent for a longer report, so that each section of the client's checklist has more room in the text
options.D: Have the briefing mark each checklist item as covered, partial or not found, so gaps are stated, not dropped
options.E: Let subagents message one another directly to divide up the checklist items among themselves without the coordinator

questions.explanation: The coordinator holds the client's checklist, so it is the place to evaluate coverage: comparing returned results with each item before synthesis and re-delegating targeted work for empty items catches the gap early. Where a gap remains after a retry, the briefing should state it explicitly per item rather than leave it out, so the client sees what was not found instead of an incomplete report that looks complete.

why_incorrect.B: More turns do not make anyone check coverage; an item can still come back empty and be dropped without notice.
why_incorrect.C: Length does not create findings. An item with no results still has nothing to say, and the omission stays silent.
why_incorrect.E: Peer-to-peer coordination bypasses the hub that holds the checklist and weakens observability, so no one owns the coverage check.

questions.scenario: During a schema change at Pinecrest Freight, the main Claude Code conversation spends an hour discussing which three tables are altered and why. It then delegates to a custom migration-checker subagent with the prompt 'verify the migration is safe'. The subagent reports no issues after checking unrelated tables.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Write the delegation prompt with the migration file path, the three tables and the safety criteria to check
options.B: Tell the subagent in its prompt to review the main conversation, since subagents can read the parent's history
options.C: Set memory: project on the subagent so it inherits the main conversation's discussion of the altered tables
options.D: Set model: inherit on the subagent so that it shares the main conversation's model and its context window

questions.explanation: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context and none of the parent conversation. The delegation prompt is the channel for task context, so it must carry the specific files, tables and acceptance criteria.

why_incorrect.B: A subagent cannot read the parent's conversation history; it starts with a fresh context, so an instruction to review it has nothing to point at.
why_incorrect.C: The memory field gives the subagent its own persistent memory directory. It does not pass the parent conversation into the subagent.
why_incorrect.D: model: inherit selects the model only. The subagent still starts with its own fresh context.

questions.scenario: Ironbark Logistics built a headless Agent SDK tool that explores legacy code. The options set allowedTools to ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"] and define a call-graph-tracer agent in agents. Logs show the main agent's attempts to call the Agent tool being refused, while Read and Grep calls succeed.
questions.question: What change most directly fixes this?

options.A: Add "Agent" to each AgentDefinition's tools list so that each subagent is allowed to be spawned by others
options.B: Add "Agent" to the main query's allowedTools so subagent invocations are approved in the headless run
options.C: Set permissionMode to "acceptEdits" so that the Agent tool is approved together with file edits
options.D: Move the agent definitions into .claude/agents/ files, since programmatic agents need interactive approval

questions.explanation: Claude invokes subagents through the Agent tool (formerly Task). In a headless run, that tool must be approved, and listing "Agent" in the main query's allowedTools does this, as the SDK examples show.

why_incorrect.A: A subagent's tools list governs what that subagent can do, not whether the main agent may call the Agent tool.
why_incorrect.C: acceptEdits auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands. It does not cover the Agent tool.
why_incorrect.D: Programmatic definitions are the recommended SDK approach and take precedence over files with the same name. The issue is permission to call the tool.

questions.scenario: In an Agent SDK pipeline at Ironbark Logistics, a dependency-scanner subagent finds risky library calls. A separate report-writer subagent then produces the engineer-facing report. Reviewers complain that the report's claims cannot be traced: file paths, line numbers and commit hashes are missing.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Tell the report-writer to read the scanner's transcript, since subagents in one session share their memory
options.B: Give the report-writer the scanner's tools so it can re-scan the repository and collect locations for itself
options.C: Have the coordinator pass the scanner's full findings to the report-writer as records with separate location fields
options.D: Add 'always cite your sources' to the report-writer's prompt so that it includes file paths and line numbers

questions.explanation: Subagents receive only what the coordinator puts in their prompt. Passing complete findings in a structured form that keeps content apart from metadata (file, line, commit) lets the report-writer keep attribution intact.

why_incorrect.A: Non-fork subagents start with fresh context and do not share memory or transcripts with sibling subagents.
why_incorrect.B: Re-scanning duplicates work and cost, and the two scans may disagree. The scanner already produced the data.
why_incorrect.D: An instruction cannot conjure locations the report-writer never received. The data has to be passed in.

questions.scenario: An exploration agent at Fernhill Education needs four independent analyses of a legacy repository: HTTP endpoints, database access, feature flags and scheduled jobs. Today the coordinator spawns one subagent, waits, then spawns the next. The subagents also follow rigid step lists and fail when a directory layout is unusual.
questions.question: Which TWO changes improve this design? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Give each subagent the goal and what a complete answer must contain, instead of a fixed step list
options.B: Merge the four analyses into one general-purpose subagent with a combined checklist to cut overhead
options.C: Emit all four Agent tool calls in a single coordinator response so the subagents run concurrently
options.D: Fork the coordinator's conversation into each subagent so that every one can watch the others' progress
options.E: Specify exact search commands and directory order in each prompt so that the results are deterministic

questions.explanation: Independent subtasks should be launched together, as multiple Agent calls in one response, so they run in parallel. Prompts that state goals and quality criteria let each subagent adapt to the repository's real layout.

why_incorrect.B: One combined subagent loses both parallelism and context isolation, and its context fills with four unrelated investigations.
why_incorrect.D: A fork copies the conversation at that moment. It does not give live visibility into sibling subagents, and it adds context each analysis does not need.
why_incorrect.E: More rigid procedures make the layout-sensitivity problem worse rather than better.

questions.scenario: For a market-entry study, Sorrel Partners' coordinator needs web research on five independent regions. Logs show it spawns the first regional search subagent, waits for its report, then spawns the next, so the study takes five times as long as one search.
questions.question: What change shortens the run most directly?

options.A: Have the coordinator launch all five independent regional searches in one turn, then combine their reports
options.B: Lower each search subagent's turn limit, so every sequential run finishes sooner and the total wall-clock time drops
options.C: Move the regional searches into the coordinator itself, so no time is spent starting a subagent between regions
options.D: Merge the five regions into one web-search subagent prompt, so a single subagent covers every region during one run

questions.explanation: Subagents can run concurrently, so independent subtasks finish in roughly the time of the slowest one rather than the sum. The coordinator should start all independent subagents together (multiple subagent calls in one response) and aggregate their reports, rather than serialising work that has no dependency between parts.

why_incorrect.B: Shorter runs cut research depth and may end searches unfinished, while the serial structure that causes the delay remains.
why_incorrect.C: Start-up time is not the bottleneck, and doing the searches inline floods the coordinator's context with raw results.
why_incorrect.D: One subagent works through the regions serially in one context, so the run stays slow and the context fills with all five regions' material.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Research's coordinator spawns a synthesis subagent with the prompt 'Synthesise the findings from the analysis we just did into a cited summary.' The summary that comes back is generic and cites none of the twelve documents the analysis subagent processed earlier in the run.
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Set the synthesis subagent's model to 'inherit', so it shares the coordinator's context and sees the earlier analysis
options.B: Move the synthesis instructions into the coordinator's system prompt, so the subagent picks them up when it is spawned
options.C: Pass the analysis and search findings, with their source metadata, in the prompt used to spawn the synthesis subagent
options.D: Give the synthesis subagent web-search tools, so it can find the sources again when the earlier findings are missing

questions.explanation: A (non-fork) subagent starts with a fresh context: its own system prompt plus the prompt string the parent passes when spawning it. It does not see the parent's conversation history or earlier tool results, so 'the analysis we just did' refers to nothing. The coordinator must pass the findings, ideally structured with source URLs and document names, directly in that prompt.

why_incorrect.A: The model setting only chooses which model runs; it does not give the subagent the parent's conversation history.
why_incorrect.B: Subagents do not receive the parent's system prompt, and instructions are not the missing piece; the findings are.
why_incorrect.D: This repeats work, may find different sources, and gives the synthesis role tools outside its specialisation.

questions.scenario: Orrin Analytics is defining AgentDefinition entries for its document-analysis, web-search and synthesis subagents. Shared citation rules apply to all three, and the document-analysis subagent must never reach the web.
questions.question: Which TWO configuration choices are correct? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Give the document-analysis subagent a tools list with only its document tools; tools left out are simply not in its session
options.B: Omit the tools field on the synthesis subagent to make it read-only, because a subagent with no tools listed gets none
options.C: Rely on subagents inheriting the coordinator's system prompt, so the shared citation rules only need to be written once there
options.D: Put the current research brief in each subagent's prompt field, so every run automatically receives the user's latest query
options.E: Write each subagent's description to say when to use it, because the coordinator matches tasks to subagents using those descriptions

questions.explanation: AgentDefinition's description tells the coordinator when to delegate to that subagent, and the tools list restricts what it can do: a tool not listed is not in its session at all. Omitting tools gives broad access, the prompt field is a fixed system prompt rather than a per-task brief, and the parent's system prompt is not inherited.

why_incorrect.B: Omitting tools gives the subagent every tool available to subagents; restriction requires an explicit list.
why_incorrect.C: Subagents do not receive the parent's system prompt, so the citation rules must be in each subagent's own prompt or another loaded source.
why_incorrect.D: The prompt field is the subagent's standing system prompt; per-task details are passed in the prompt string when it is spawned.

questions.scenario: Fernvale Mobile's support agent escalates billing disputes to a human queue. Human agents work in a separate ticketing tool and cannot see the AI conversation. Today's handoff note usually reads 'Customer unhappy about bill, please assist', and humans spend several minutes re-asking questions.
questions.question: What should the handoff contain?

options.A: The agent's confidence score and the customer's sentiment rating, so the human queue can sort incoming tickets by urgency and by doubt
options.B: A short note in the customer's own words, so the human hears the complaint without the agent's interpretation
options.C: A structured summary with account ID, disputed charges, root cause found, actions already taken and a recommended resolution
options.D: The full raw transcript attached to the ticket, so the human can read everything the customer and agent said

questions.explanation: Because the human cannot see the conversation, the handoff must carry what they need to act at once: identifiers, the verified facts and root cause, what the agent has done, and its recommended next step. A structured summary avoids repeated questions and gives the human a clear place to start.

why_incorrect.A: Scores may help sorting but tell the human nothing about the account, the charges or what has been tried.
why_incorrect.B: It omits the IDs, findings and actions the agent already has, so the human still has to repeat the investigation.
why_incorrect.D: The transcript has the facts but makes the human dig for them, and it gives no verified root cause or recommendation.

questions.scenario: Pinecrest Pharmacy Online's support agent can book routine refills with schedule_refill, but policy says refills of controlled medicines must go to a pharmacist through escalate_to_pharmacist. The system prompt states this. Reviews show the agent occasionally books a controlled refill itself when a customer pushes hard for speed.
questions.question: What should the team implement?

options.A: A PreToolUse hook on schedule_refill that denies controlled drugs and points the model to escalate_to_pharmacist
options.B: Removal of schedule_refill from the agent, so that a pharmacist has to handle every refill request, routine or controlled
options.C: A nightly job that cancels any controlled refill booked without pharmacist sign-off and emails the affected customers
options.D: Few-shot examples of pushy customers being escalated, placed at the very top of the system prompt in capital letters

questions.explanation: A policy that must hold every time needs a deterministic gate, not stronger wording. A PreToolUse hook can check the requested drug against the formulary and return a deny decision with a reason that points the model to escalate_to_pharmacist, so controlled refills are blocked and handed off correctly while routine refills still flow.

why_incorrect.B: This enforces the rule by removing a capability routine refills legitimately need, pushing every request onto pharmacists.
why_incorrect.C: After-the-fact cancellation lets the wrong booking happen first and creates a worse customer experience than prevention.
why_incorrect.D: Prompt changes may lower the failure rate, but compliance stays probabilistic for a rule that must hold every time.

questions.scenario: A Kestrel Home Goods customer writes: 'I was charged twice for order 5521, the lamp in order 5530 arrived cracked, and can you change the delivery address on order 5547 before it ships?'
questions.question: Which TWO design choices handle this message best? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Resolve the first issue the customer mentioned, then ask them to open a new conversation for each of the remaining issues
options.B: Keep one shared case record of account, orders and amounts that each issue's investigation reads and updates
options.C: Escalate every message with several issues to a human, since multiple concerns in one message indicate a complex case
options.D: Split the message into separate issues, investigate each with the right tools, then send one reply that resolves all three
options.E: Handle the issues in order of the amount involved, closing each with its own separate reply before starting the next

questions.explanation: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, investigated (in parallel where they are independent) against a shared set of case facts, and then answered in one unified resolution. The shared record keeps amounts and order IDs consistent across the three investigations.

why_incorrect.A: This pushes work back to the customer and ignores two problems the agent could handle in the same conversation.
why_incorrect.C: Several routine issues are not a policy exception or a blocked case; escalating them all wastes human capacity.
why_incorrect.E: Sequential replies fragment the conversation, and ordering by amount ignores the time-sensitive address change.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' incident-explorer agent gets timeline data from three MCP servers. One returns Unix epoch seconds, one ISO 8601, and one DD/MM/YYYY strings. The agent sometimes orders events wrongly when it merges them.
questions.question: What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Add a PostToolUse hook for those MCP tools that converts every timestamp to ISO 8601 with updatedToolOutput
options.B: Add a PreToolUse hook that appends a format=iso parameter to every call made to the three MCP servers
options.C: Ask the agent to write and run a small conversion script through Bash each time it merges the timelines
options.D: Add a system-prompt section explaining the three formats and asking the agent to convert them before sorting

questions.explanation: A PostToolUse hook runs deterministic code on tool results before the model sees them. Normalising timestamps there removes the chance of misreading a format, rather than relying on the model to convert correctly each time.

why_incorrect.B: Adding a parameter the servers may not support does not guarantee consistent output, and it may cause tool errors.
why_incorrect.C: Generating a script on each run adds variability and cost. The normalisation belongs in fixed code on the result path.
why_incorrect.D: Prompt guidance is probabilistic. Mixed formats keep causing occasional misreads, which is the failure being seen.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Payments' boilerplate-generator agent writes scaffolding files. The team wants every Write to land under ./generated/, and wants every MCP tool call logged to an audit service without slowing the agent.
questions.question: Which TWO hook designs are correct? (Choose 2.)

options.A: A PostToolUse hook on Write returns updatedInput, which moves the file into ./generated/ after it has been written
options.B: An audit hook with matcher ^mcp__ returns an async output, so the agent continues without waiting for the logging call
options.C: A PreToolUse hook on Write returns updatedInput with the rewritten file_path, with an allow decision or normal permission checks
options.D: The audit hook returns a systemMessage for each call, because that field is how hooks give Claude context
options.E: When PreToolUse hooks disagree the first registered decision wins, so register the audit hook after the others

questions.explanation: PreToolUse can modify a tool's input through updatedInput before execution, either auto-approved with allow or passed through normal permission evaluation. Hooks used only for side effects such as logging can return async output so the agent does not wait for them.

why_incorrect.A: updatedInput applies to PreToolUse, before the call runs. A PostToolUse hook cannot change where a file was already written.
why_incorrect.D: systemMessage is shown to the user, not the model. additionalContext is the field that passes context to Claude.
why_incorrect.E: Matching hooks run in parallel and the most restrictive decision applies (deny before defer, ask and allow). Registration order does not decide it.

questions.scenario: Brightwater Logistics' platform agent can run Bash to help engineers with infrastructure chores. Policy says it must never run terraform apply or kubectl delete against production contexts. A system-prompt instruction already says this, but in one run the agent ran terraform apply anyway.
questions.question: Which control should the team add?

options.A: A PreToolUse hook with matcher "terraform apply|kubectl delete" that returns a deny decision for each call
options.B: A rewritten system prompt that states the production rule first, in capitals, with three refusal examples
options.C: A PreToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command and returns deny with a reason that points to the change process
options.D: A PostToolUse hook on Bash that spots production-changing commands after they run and asks the agent to revert

questions.explanation: A PreToolUse hook blocks the call before it executes, which gives a deterministic guarantee where prompts only make compliance likely. Matching the Bash tool and checking tool_input.command inside the callback finds the forbidden commands, and the deny reason tells the agent what to do instead.

why_incorrect.A: Matchers match the tool name, not its arguments, so this pattern never matches a Bash call. The command must be checked inside the callback.
why_incorrect.B: Prompt wording makes compliance more likely, but the team has already seen it fail. A hard rule needs enforcement in code.
why_incorrect.D: PostToolUse fires after the command has run, which is too late to stop a production change.

questions.scenario: Silvergate Utilities' schema-helper agent generates database migrations. Any migration that drops a column must go to a human DBA for review instead of being written to the migrations folder. The agent can open review tickets through an MCP tool.
questions.question: Which design enforces this most reliably?

options.A: A PostToolUse hook that adds additionalContext reminding the agent of the review policy after each migration is written
options.B: A Stop hook that scans the working tree when the run finishes and deletes any migration containing a DROP COLUMN
options.C: A system-prompt rule telling the agent never to drop columns itself and to open a review ticket in such cases
options.D: A PreToolUse hook on Write|Edit that denies DROP COLUMN content, with a reason directing the agent to file a review ticket

questions.explanation: Intercepting the write before it happens enforces the policy deterministically. The deny reason redirects the agent to the approved alternative, opening a review ticket, so the workflow continues correctly instead of just failing.

why_incorrect.A: By the time PostToolUse fires, the migration is already in the folder. A reminder does not undo the write.
why_incorrect.B: Deleting files at the end is destructive clean-up, and the review request may never be filed.
why_incorrect.C: Prompt instructions make compliance likely but not certain. A rule with a mandatory human review needs enforcement in code.

questions.scenario: Brightwater Outfitters' support agent reads customer records through a vendor's MCP server, which returns full card numbers and dates of birth. Compliance requires that these values never enter the model's context or the stored transcripts. The team cannot change the vendor's server.
questions.question: What is the most reliable way to meet this requirement?

options.A: A PostToolUse hook on the CRM tools that masks card numbers and birth dates in each result before the model reads it
options.B: A PreToolUse hook that blocks any CRM lookup until the customer has confirmed their identity earlier in the chat
options.C: A system prompt rule telling the agent never to repeat card numbers or birth dates it sees in tool results to customers
options.D: A Stop hook that scans each final reply and removes any card numbers or birth dates before the customer sees the message

questions.explanation: A PostToolUse hook runs in the application after a tool returns and can replace an MCP tool's output before Claude sees it. Masking sensitive fields there is deterministic: the full values never reach the model's context or the transcript, regardless of what the model would do with them.

why_incorrect.B: Identity checks control who can trigger a lookup, but the full values still flow into context once the lookup runs.
why_incorrect.C: The data is already in context and the transcript; the rule only limits what the model repeats, and only probabilistically.
why_incorrect.D: By the time the reply is checked, the values have been in context and stored in the transcript, which is what compliance forbids.

questions.scenario: Thornbury Telecom's account-lookup MCP tool (on a server configured as 'billing') returns full card numbers that the model never needs. Compliance also wants an audit record of every MCP tool call the support agent makes.
questions.question: Which TWO hook configurations meet these needs? (Choose 2.)

options.A: A PreToolUse hook with a matcher such as "^mcp__" that logs each MCP tool call's name and input to the audit store
options.B: A hook whose matcher is just "billing", relying on the server's name matching the full names of its tools
options.C: A PreToolUse hook matched to the account-lookup tool that removes card numbers from the result before the model sees it
options.D: A PostToolUse hook matched to the account-lookup tool that returns a redacted replacement of the tool output
options.E: A UserPromptSubmit hook that strips card numbers from customer messages, which also covers data returned by tools

questions.explanation: PostToolUse hooks can replace a tool's output before Claude processes it, which makes them the right place to redact sensitive fields. PreToolUse hooks see every outgoing call with its input, and a matcher like ^mcp__ selects all MCP tools, so they suit audit logging. Hook matchers compare against tool names, and MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<action>.

why_incorrect.B: MCP tool names follow the mcp__<server>__<action> pattern, so a bare server name does not match them as an exact name.
why_incorrect.C: PreToolUse runs before the tool executes, so there is no result yet to redact.
why_incorrect.E: UserPromptSubmit sees submitted prompts, not tool results, so card numbers from the lookup would still reach the model.

questions.scenario: Thornbury Telecom's policy says any account credit above $300 needs human approval. The support agent's prompt states the limit, but last month it issued four credits above $300 while trying to calm angry customers.
questions.question: Which control best enforces the policy?

options.A: A system prompt rule stating the $300 limit, backed by few-shot examples of the agent escalating larger requests
options.B: A Stop hook that scans the finished conversation and alerts a supervisor whenever a credit above $300 was issued
options.C: A PreToolUse hook on the credit tool that denies amounts above $300 and gives a reason telling the agent to open a handoff instead
options.D: A PostToolUse hook on the credit tool that flags any credit above $300 for a supervisor to review and reverse the next day

questions.explanation: A PreToolUse hook intercepts the outgoing call before it runs. Returning a deny decision blocks the credit deterministically, and the reason text lets the model redirect to the escalation workflow. Prompt rules and after-the-fact checks cannot guarantee compliance.

why_incorrect.A: This is what failed already: prompt guidance is probabilistic, and the rule must hold every time.
why_incorrect.B: It detects violations only after the conversation ends, when the money has already moved.
why_incorrect.D: PostToolUse runs after the credit is issued, so the policy is breached first and fixed later.

questions.scenario: Wren Retail asks Claude Code to 'add comprehensive tests' to a 200,000-line legacy order service with about 5% coverage. Some modules are heavily changed each sprint, others have not been touched in years, and dependencies between them are poorly documented.
questions.question: Which decomposition strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Split the top-level directories evenly across parallel subagents straight away and merge whatever tests they return
options.B: Issue a single prompt asking for tests across the whole service so that Claude can judge coverage holistically
options.C: Map the structure and dependencies first, rank high-risk modules, then follow a prioritised plan that adapts as you learn
options.D: Work through the source files in alphabetical order, writing one test file per source file in a fixed sequence

questions.explanation: An open-ended task with unknown dependencies calls for adaptive decomposition. Map the structure, find where tests reduce the most risk, and let the plan change as dependencies and test seams emerge.

why_incorrect.A: Splitting before mapping assigns work blindly. Directory size says nothing about where coverage matters most.
why_incorrect.B: One prompt over 200,000 lines cannot hold the detail needed and gives no way to prioritise or check progress.
why_incorrect.D: A fixed order ignores risk and dependencies, so effort goes to stable code while fragile, high-churn modules wait.

questions.scenario: Quillon Media used Claude Code to review a 30-file refactoring pull request in one pass. The review left shallow comments on each file and missed that two files now disagree on a shared event payload's field names.
questions.question: Which restructuring of the review is most likely to fix both problems?

options.A: Review the files twice in different random orders and keep the union of the comments from both runs
options.B: Run the same single-pass review again with a longer, more detailed checklist so that nothing gets skipped
options.C: Skip per-file analysis and run one integration pass over a summary of the diff, since that is where the bugs are
options.D: Run a focused pass per file, then a separate integration pass over each file's interfaces and shared contracts

questions.explanation: Splitting the review into per-file passes gives each file full attention. A separate integration pass that compares interfaces and contracts across files then catches mismatches that a diluted single pass misses.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating a diluted pass in another order does not deepen per-file analysis or make cross-file checks systematic.
why_incorrect.B: A longer checklist adds to the same attention dilution across 30 files and does not create a cross-file comparison step.
why_incorrect.C: Dropping per-file analysis gives up the local defects, and a diff summary may leave out the field names that conflict.

questions.scenario: Ironbark Logistics' boilerplate tool must create 12 new event consumers from the team's standard template. Each consumer goes through the same steps: scaffold the code, add configuration, generate tests, write the README. Each step's output can be checked before the next starts.
questions.question: Which decomposition strategy is the best fit?

options.A: An autonomous agent that decides for each consumer which steps it needs and in what order it should run them
options.B: A fixed sequential chain for each consumer, with a validation check between steps before the next step starts
options.C: A single prompt that generates all 12 consumers' code, configuration, tests and documentation in one response
options.D: Dynamic decomposition, where the agent rebuilds the plan for every consumer from what it discovers on the way

questions.explanation: When the steps are known and identical every time, prompt chaining is predictable, cheap and easy to test. Gates between steps catch problems early. Adaptive planning adds variability without benefit here.

why_incorrect.A: Autonomy suits open-ended work. Here it adds cost and inconsistency to a fixed, well-understood procedure.
why_incorrect.C: One huge response removes the checkpoints, so a template error spreads into all 12 consumers before anyone sees it.
why_incorrect.D: Re-planning per consumer when the plan never changes adds variability and makes outputs harder to compare and validate.

questions.scenario: An engineer at Halyard Bank asks the team's codebase assistant: 'Why does the nightly reconciliation job sometimes post the same transaction twice?' Nobody on the team knows the job's code well.
questions.question: Which task decomposition strategy fits this request best?

options.A: Parallel subagents, one per top-level directory, each asked the same question, with the answers merged
options.B: One large prompt containing the whole reconciliation package so Claude can reason over everything at once
options.C: A fixed chain: list every file in the repository, summarise each in turn, then answer from the summaries
options.D: Investigate adaptively from the job's entry point and logs, choosing each next subtask from what turns up
