questions.explanation: Open-ended debugging calls for dynamic decomposition. Each finding, such as a retry wrapper, suggests the next question, such as whether posting is idempotent. A fixed plan cannot anticipate that path.

why_incorrect.A: Most directories have nothing to do with the bug, and identical questions without shared findings cannot follow a trail across components.
why_incorrect.B: Bulk context dilutes attention and does not reach the runtime evidence (logs, retries) that guides the investigation.
why_incorrect.C: Summarising everything in a fixed order spends most effort on irrelevant code and delays following the actual evidence.

questions.scenario: Linwood Capital's document-analysis subagent receives forty quarterly filings, about 300 pages in total, in one request and is asked to extract key metrics and flag inconsistencies between filings. Reviewers find missed per-filing details and missed cross-filing contradictions.
questions.question: How should the task be decomposed?

options.A: Send all forty filings in one request with a longer instruction that lists every field and every comparison to be made
options.B: Analyse each filing in its own pass with a fixed checklist, then run a separate pass comparing the per-filing results
options.C: Split the filings into four batches of ten and join the four batch summaries by concatenation at the end of the run
options.D: Analyse only the twelve most-cited filings in depth and sample the rest, because those filings drive most conclusions

questions.explanation: Large multi-document reviews benefit from a local pass per document (focused attention, consistent checklist) followed by a separate integration pass over the structured per-document results to find cross-document issues. That avoids attention dilution while still catching contradictions between documents.

why_incorrect.A: More instructions do not fix attention spread across 300 pages; the same details and comparisons will still be missed.
why_incorrect.C: Batching helps local detail, but concatenating summaries never compares filings across batches, so cross-filing contradictions are lost.
why_incorrect.D: Sampling leaves most filings unexamined and cannot find inconsistencies involving the ones that were skipped.

questions.scenario: Meridian Public Health Observatory has two workloads: a weekly digest that always fetches regulator feeds, extracts changes, summarises them and formats a bulletin; and ad hoc investigations such as 'Why did childhood vaccine uptake fall in one district this year?'
questions.question: Which decomposition strategy fits these workloads?

options.A: A fixed prompt chain for both, with each investigation's steps drafted in advance by an analyst before the run starts
options.B: An adaptive coordinator for both, so the weekly digest can also add steps whenever a regulator publishes something unusual
options.C: A fixed prompt chain for the weekly digest, and an adaptive plan for investigations that adds subtasks as findings emerge
options.D: An adaptive plan for the digest, since the feeds change weekly, and a fixed chain for investigations to keep them auditable

questions.explanation: Prompt chaining suits predictable work whose steps are known in advance; it is cheap, testable and consistent. Dynamic decomposition suits open-ended investigation, where the next subtask depends on intermediate findings, so the plan must adapt as evidence comes in.

why_incorrect.A: Open-ended investigations cannot be fully planned up front; what to look at next depends on what is found.
why_incorrect.B: The digest's steps are known and stable; dynamic planning adds cost and variability without benefit.
why_incorrect.D: This inverts the fit: changing content does not make the digest's steps change, and fixed chains suit the investigation least.

questions.scenario: Yesterday an engineer at Tallis Travel started a session with claude -n ledger-refactor and spent hours analysing the ledger module. Overnight a colleague merged changes to two of the files that session had read.
questions.question: What is the best way to continue today?

options.A: Start a new unnamed session and repeat the full analysis of the ledger module from scratch to be completely safe
options.B: Run claude --resume ledger-refactor, then name the two changed files and ask Claude to re-read them before continuing
options.C: Run claude --continue so the most recent conversation in the directory reloads, and carry on from the last step
options.D: Resume the named session and carry on as before, since a resumed session re-reads the files it used automatically

questions.explanation: Resuming the named session keeps the still-valid analysis. Because sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem, Claude must be told which files changed so it re-reads only those instead of relying on stale tool results.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating hours of analysis throws away context that is mostly still valid. Targeted re-reading is enough here.
why_incorrect.C: --continue picks the most recent conversation in the directory, which may not be ledger-refactor, and it still leaves the stale file contents unaddressed.
why_incorrect.D: A resumed session restores the conversation, including old tool results. Files are not re-read automatically.

questions.scenario: An Agent SDK session at Copperline Energy has finished a detailed analysis of a legacy billing module. The team wants to compare two refactoring strategies, a strangler adapter and an in-place rewrite, starting from that same analysis without either line of work contaminating the other.
questions.question: What is the best approach?

options.A: Resume the analysis session twice in a row, first exploring the adapter strategy and then the rewrite
options.B: Use continue: true for both runs so each one picks up the most recent session and its full analysis
options.C: Start two fresh sessions and repeat the full analysis in each, so the two strategies share no history
options.D: Fork the analysis session once per strategy, giving each fork its own working copy for any file edits

questions.explanation: Resuming with fork_session (forkSession in TypeScript) creates a new session that starts from a copy of the original history, which stays unchanged. Forks branch the conversation, not the filesystem, so separate working copies keep each strategy's edits apart.

why_incorrect.A: Sequential resumes put both strategies in one history, so the second is influenced by the first.
why_incorrect.B: continue picks the most recent session. The second run would continue the first strategy's thread instead of the clean baseline.
why_incorrect.C: Repeating the analysis wastes the work already done and may produce a different baseline for each strategy.

questions.scenario: A week ago an engineer at Basalt Systems ran a long analysis session over the order service. Since then a large merge has rewritten about 40% of its modules. She wants to pick the investigation back up.
questions.question: What is the most reliable way to continue?

options.A: Resume the session and ask Claude to refresh its memory of the codebase before it answers anything else
options.B: Fork the old session so that the stale analysis stays preserved while the fork continues the investigation
options.C: Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of still-valid conclusions, then re-explore the changes
options.D: Resume the session as it is, since the earlier tool results still describe how most of the service behaves

questions.explanation: When many earlier tool results are stale, resuming brings outdated file contents back into context as if they were current. A fresh session seeded with a curated summary of conclusions that still hold, followed by targeted re-exploration, is more reliable.

why_incorrect.A: A vague refresh request does not say what changed, so Claude may re-read nothing or everything, and stale results remain in context.
why_incorrect.B: A fork inherits the same stale history, so it has the same problem as resuming.
why_incorrect.D: With 40% of modules rewritten, stale results would mislead the analysis. Resuming suits cases where prior context is mostly valid.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Research finished a costly analysis session on regional energy prices. The director wants two drafts from it, a short policy brief and a technical appendix, explored independently, keeping the analysis intact for later questions. Both drafts are written to the project's working directory.
questions.question: How should the team run the two drafts?

options.A: Fork the analysis session once per draft and let both branches write report.md, since each fork has its own file snapshot
options.B: Fork the analysis session once per draft and have each branch write to its own output file, because forks share the filesystem
options.C: Start two new sessions and have each one repeat the full search and document analysis before it drafts its own version of the report
options.D: Resume the analysis session, write the policy brief, then ask the same session to rewrite it as a technical appendix

questions.explanation: Forking creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original history; the original stays unchanged and each branch can be resumed separately. Forks do not branch the filesystem, though: file edits are real and shared, so parallel branches need separate output paths (or file checkpointing).

why_incorrect.A: Forking branches the conversation, not the filesystem, so the two drafts would overwrite each other's file.
why_incorrect.C: This throws away the costly analysis and may produce two inconsistent evidence bases.
why_incorrect.D: The second draft is shaped by the first, and the original analysis session is changed instead of kept intact.

questions.scenario: Lumenwise Telecom's support service, built on the Agent SDK, handles thousands of customers at once. When a customer returns the next day to the same open ticket, the agent should continue with full knowledge of the earlier conversation.
questions.question: How should the service continue the conversation?

options.A: Start a new session and replay the stored transcript as one large user message containing the entire earlier conversation
options.B: Use the continue option, which returns to the most recent session, so the returning customer picks up where they left off
options.C: Store each ticket's session ID when the result arrives, and pass it to the resume option when that customer comes back
options.D: Fork the most recent session for every returning customer, so the original history stays unchanged for auditors

questions.explanation: Resume takes a specific session ID and restores that session's full context. Continue finds the most recent session in the current directory, which only works when one conversation runs at a time. Multi-user services should capture session_id from the result message and store it against the ticket.

why_incorrect.A: This loses the structure of the earlier tool calls and results and costs more than resuming the existing session.
why_incorrect.B: Continue picks the most recent session in the directory, which in a multi-user service is probably someone else's conversation.
why_incorrect.D: Forking the most recent session copies the wrong conversation, and forking is for exploring alternatives, not routine continuation.

questions.scenario: A Lumenwise Telecom customer paused a chat for twenty minutes to find the serial number on her router. Nothing on the account changed in that time. The saved session holds the order and line-status lookups and the troubleshooting steps already agreed with her.
questions.question: What is the best way to continue the case?

options.A: Start a new session seeded with a summary of the case, and have the agent re-fetch all order and line data first
options.B: Fork the saved session so the original is kept as a backup, then add the customer's reply only in the new fork
options.C: Resume the saved session and carry on, since its lookups and the agreed troubleshooting steps are still current
options.D: Start an empty session and ask the customer to describe the problem again, so the agent works only from fresh input

questions.explanation: Resuming is the right choice when the prior context is still valid: the session restores the full history, including tool results and agreed steps, at no extra cost. A fresh start with a summary is worth it when earlier tool results have gone stale; forking suits exploring an alternative approach while keeping the original line intact.

why_incorrect.A: Nothing has changed, so re-fetching and summarising adds cost and can drop detail from the agreed steps for no benefit.
why_incorrect.B: There is no alternative path to explore; forking only creates a second copy of the same valid conversation.
why_incorrect.D: Discarding valid context makes the customer repeat herself and throws away lookups that are still correct.

questions.scenario: Copperline Energy's code assistant has clear tool descriptions. Its system prompt includes: 'Whenever the user mentions documentation, call search_api_docs first.' Requests such as 'update the README documentation for the CLI flags' now trigger irrelevant API searches before Claude edits the file.
questions.question: What should the team change first?

options.A: Reword the keyword-triggered instruction to state when an API search is needed, not to fire on a word
options.B: Remove search_api_docs from the tool set, since the editing tools already cover most documentation work
options.C: Lengthen the search_api_docs description so that it clearly states the tool is unrelated to README edits
options.D: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks search_api_docs whenever the user's request mentions the README file

questions.explanation: Keyword-sensitive system prompt instructions can override well-written tool descriptions and create unintended tool associations. The fix is to rewrite the instruction around the real condition (an API question) rather than a trigger word.

why_incorrect.B: Removing the tool loses a capability that real API questions still need.
why_incorrect.C: The description is already clear. The system prompt's keyword rule overrides it, so a longer description treats the symptom.
why_incorrect.D: A hook keyed on another keyword repeats the original mistake and leaves the faulty instruction in place.

questions.scenario: Wren Retail's engineering assistant has two custom tools: lookup ('Looks up information') and find_info ('Finds information'). One returns the code owners for a path; the other searches internal API documentation. The agent often calls the wrong one.
questions.question: Which change most directly fixes the misrouting?

options.A: Merge them into one tool with a mode parameter, keeping the description short so it uses fewer tokens
options.B: Rename them get_code_owners and search_api_docs, each describing its inputs, outputs and when to use it
options.C: Add a system-prompt paragraph listing a few example requests that belong with each of the two tools
options.D: Remove find_info and let the agent answer API documentation questions from its general knowledge

questions.explanation: Near-identical names and descriptions give Claude nothing to choose by. Purpose-specific names, plus descriptions that state inputs, outputs and when to use each tool rather than the other, remove the overlap at its source.

why_incorrect.A: A merged tool with a terse description moves the ambiguity into the mode parameter. Selection stays unreliable.
why_incorrect.C: Examples in the system prompt help a little, but the tool definitions stay ambiguous everywhere else they are used.
why_incorrect.D: Dropping a needed capability trades misrouting for wrong or invented API answers.

questions.scenario: Sorrel Partners' coordinator has well-described tools for its internal document library and for web search. Its system prompt says 'Always search for the latest data before answering.' When users ask about reports already in the library, the coordinator still runs web searches and sometimes cites outdated press coverage instead of the report itself.
questions.question: What should the architect change first?

options.A: Narrow the 'always search' instruction to questions that need current external data, so library questions go to the document tools
options.B: Lengthen the document tools' descriptions further, so they outweigh the system prompt instruction about searching
options.C: Remove the web-search tool from the coordinator, so the document tools become the only option for every question
options.D: Add a PreToolUse hook that denies every web search whenever the user has uploaded at least one document to the library, for the rest of the session

questions.explanation: System prompt wording can override good tool descriptions. A broad, keyword-like instruction ('always search') creates an unintended association with the web-search tool. Reviewing and narrowing that instruction lets the tool descriptions do their job.

why_incorrect.B: The descriptions are already good; the conflicting instruction remains and keeps pulling the model towards search.
why_incorrect.C: This fixes library questions but breaks every question that genuinely needs current external information.
why_incorrect.D: A blanket rule blocks legitimate searches for any user with documents, and hides the real cause in the prompt.

questions.scenario: Orrin Analytics' research system has one generic analyze_document tool that is used to extract figures, summarise sections and check whether a source supports a claim. Its output shape varies with how the model phrases the request, and the synthesis step often cannot tell which kind of result it received.
questions.question: What should the team do?

options.A: Keep one tool and add a free-text 'mode' string, with no output schema, that the model fills in itself
options.B: Split it into tools for extracting data points, summarising content and checking a claim against a source, each with an output schema
options.C: Keep one tool and lengthen its description with a paragraph covering each of the three uses and the output shape that each one returns
options.D: Keep one tool and have the synthesis agent post-process its output with patterns that guess which task was run

questions.explanation: Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools gives each a clear purpose and a defined input/output contract. Selection gets easier, and downstream agents receive predictable, typed results they can rely on. Consolidating into one tool with an enum action parameter can also work, but the distractor's free-text mode and missing output contract keep results unpredictable; separate tools with defined output schemas give the synthesis step typed results.

why_incorrect.A: A free-text mode recreates the ambiguity inside an argument, and with no output schema the result shape still varies from call to call.
why_incorrect.C: Better text helps selection, but one tool still returns differently shaped results that downstream steps must guess at.
why_incorrect.D: Guessing after the fact is brittle and pushes a tool-design problem onto every consumer.

questions.scenario: Brightwater Outfitters' support agent calls a create_return tool whose input schema declares reason and items as plain strings with no further detail. The warehouse API rejects about one call in ten because the reason is free text such as 'too small' instead of a known code, or the items are not in the SKU:quantity format it expects.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Add a few-shot example of a correct return to the system prompt, and leave the tool's input schema as it is today
options.B: Retry each rejected call with the API's error message appended, until the warehouse API finally accepts the request
options.C: Make reason an enum of the API's codes, items an array of {sku, quantity} objects, and set strict: true on the tool
options.D: Add a system prompt line listing the valid return codes, and keep the reason field in the schema as a free-text string

questions.explanation: The schema is the tool's input contract. Declaring the allowed reason codes as an enum, giving items a typed structure, and setting strict: true (with required fields and additionalProperties: false) means every tool_use input validates against that contract, so malformed calls stop at the source instead of reaching the warehouse API.

why_incorrect.A: One example helps on similar cases, but the loose schema still permits any string, so malformed calls continue.
why_incorrect.B: Retries treat the symptom, add latency and cost, and may still fail; the schema keeps allowing invalid input.
why_incorrect.D: Prompt guidance lowers the error rate, but a free-text field still lets invalid codes through some of the time.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Research's document-store MCP server exposes load_filings, which takes a filing_date. The analysis subagent sometimes sends '14/03/2026' instead of the required YYYY-MM-DD format.
questions.question: How should the server respond to this input?

options.A: Silently convert the date to the nearest valid value and return the filings, noting nothing about the change
options.B: Return a JSON-RPC invalid-params error, since protocol errors are the intended channel for any problem with a tool call's arguments
options.C: Return a tool result with isError true that names the bad field and the expected date format, so the model can fix it and retry
options.D: Return an empty filing list with isError false, so the coordinator treats the request as a query with no matches

questions.explanation: The MCP specification separates protocol errors (unknown tool, request that does not match the call schema, server errors) from tool execution errors (API failures, input validation errors such as a wrongly formatted date, business logic errors). Tool execution errors are returned with isError true and actionable text so the model can self-correct.

why_incorrect.A: Silent coercion can return the wrong filings while the agent believes it got exactly what it asked for.
why_incorrect.B: The specification reserves protocol errors for unknown tools and malformed requests; argument validation failures belong in tool results.
why_incorrect.D: This disguises a bad request as a valid empty result and misleads the coordinator about the evidence.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Home Goods' MCP tool issue_store_credit returns isError true with the text 'Operation failed' for every failure: backend timeouts, malformed order IDs, orders past the 90-day credit window and agents lacking permission. The support agent retries policy failures again and again and tells customers to 'try again later'.
questions.question: How should the tool report failures?

options.A: Keep the generic message but add a system prompt rule capping retries at three, so repeated attempts on the same failure stop sooner
options.B: Raise a JSON-RPC protocol error for every failure, so the client stops the call before the model ever sees the failure
options.C: Return isError with a category (transient, validation, business, permission), a retryable flag and a short explanation to relay
options.D: Return policy failures as successful results with an empty body, so the agent stops retrying and moves on to the next step

questions.explanation: MCP tool execution errors are reported in the result with isError true so the model can act on them. A uniform message stops the agent from choosing the right recovery. Structured metadata (error category, whether retrying can help, and a human-readable explanation) lets it retry transient faults, fix bad input, and explain policy limits instead of retrying them.

why_incorrect.A: The agent still cannot tell retryable failures from final ones or explain the actual rule to the customer.
why_incorrect.B: MCP treats business and validation failures as tool execution errors that the model should see so it can respond.
why_incorrect.D: Reporting a failure as success hides it; the agent may tell the customer the credit was issued.

questions.scenario: Fernvale Mobile's find_account MCP tool looks up customers by email. Two situations keep causing confusion: the CRM sometimes times out, and some emails genuinely match no account.
questions.question: Which TWO responses should the tool return? (Choose 2.)

options.A: When an email matches no account, return isError true marked transient, so the agent retries the same lookup a few more times before giving up
options.B: When an email matches no account, return a normal result stating zero matches, so the agent can ask for another identifier
options.C: When the agent sends a malformed email, return a JSON-RPC protocol error, so the model never has to see the failure
options.D: When the CRM times out, return isError true marked transient and retryable, so the agent can retry before telling the customer
options.E: When the CRM times out, return an empty result list, so the agent's flow continues without needing an error branch

questions.explanation: An access failure (timeout) and a valid empty result mean different things and need different recovery: the first may be retried, the second means the lookup worked and the agent should ask for a different identifier. Returning each honestly, with retryability metadata on the error, prevents both wasted retries and false 'no account' answers.

why_incorrect.A: A query that ran and found nothing is a valid result; retrying it wastes calls and delays asking for another identifier.
why_incorrect.C: Input validation problems should come back as tool execution errors so the model can correct the argument and retry.
why_incorrect.E: This makes a failed lookup look like 'no such customer', so the agent may wrongly tell a real customer they have no account.

questions.scenario: In Brackenfield Insights' research system, the synthesis subagent has only its drafting tools. While writing, it sends dozens of requests back through the coordinator to confirm single figures in sources the search subagents already collected. Each request starts a new search subagent, and report latency has tripled. Requests that need genuinely new research are rare.
questions.question: What tool distribution should the architect adopt?

options.A: Give synthesis a read-only lookup tool over already-collected sources; keep new research with the coordinator
options.B: Give the synthesis agent the full web-search and fetch toolset, so that it never needs to involve the coordinator again
options.C: Have the synthesis agent queue its questions and send them to the coordinator in one batch at the end of each section
options.D: Tell the synthesis agent in its system prompt to stop confirming figures and to trust the numbers in its own draft

questions.explanation: The frequent need is a cheap lookup in material the system already gathered, not new research. A narrowly scoped, read-only tool over the collected sources lets the synthesis agent resolve those checks itself without new searches, while anything that needs fresh sources still goes through the coordinator, which keeps control of scope and source quality.

why_incorrect.B: A full search toolset invites the synthesis agent to start its own research, duplicating work and citing pages no other agent checked.
why_incorrect.C: Batching cuts the number of round trips but still launches searches for facts that are already on hand, and it stalls drafting.
why_incorrect.D: This trades latency for accuracy; figures go into the report unchecked.

questions.scenario: Thornbury Telecom's support agent now has 22 tools covering billing, shipping, loyalty points and internal admin tasks such as bulk account merges. Since the last few tools were added, the agent picks the wrong tool more often.
questions.question: Which TWO changes are most likely to improve tool selection? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Split the work so a billing agent and a shipping agent each get only the handful of tools their role needs
options.B: Combine all 22 tools into one generic action tool that takes an operation name and a free-form payload
options.C: Remove admin tools that support never needs, such as bulk account merges, from the agent's tool set entirely
options.D: Keep all 22 tools and reorder them so the most frequently used ones appear first in the list sent to the model
options.E: Keep all 22 tools and set tool_choice to any, so the model always picks a tool instead of replying with text

questions.explanation: Selection reliability drops as the number of tools grows. Scoping each agent to the few tools its role needs, and removing tools that the role should never use, cuts decision complexity and also limits the damage a wrong choice can do.

why_incorrect.B: This hides the choice inside an argument, removes per-tool schemas and makes misuse harder to detect.
why_incorrect.D: Order does not reduce the number of similar options the model must choose between.
why_incorrect.E: Forcing some tool call does not help the model pick the right one, and many current models reject forced tool_choice.

questions.scenario: Larchmont Utilities' triage step ran on Claude Haiku 5.5 with tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "classify_ticket"} so classification always came first. After moving the step to Claude Sonnet 5.5, every request fails with a 400 error about tool_choice.
questions.question: Which TWO changes restore reliable classification on Claude Sonnet 5.5? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Switch to tool_choice any, which still guarantees a tool call on Claude Sonnet 5.5 without naming one particular tool
options.B: Keep the forced tool_choice and add an assistant prefill that begins the classify_ticket call on the model's behalf
options.C: If the forced call only existed to get JSON back, drop the tool and request the classification through structured outputs
options.D: Keep the forced tool_choice and catch the 400 error, retrying the same request until the model accepts the call
options.E: Use tool_choice auto, tell the model in the prompt to call classify_ticket first, and set strict true on that tool

questions.explanation: On Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, forced tool use (tool_choice "any" or "tool") returns a 400; Claude Haiku 5.5 still accepts it. The replacements are tool_choice auto with a clear instruction naming the tool (plus strict true for schema-valid arguments), or structured outputs when the call only existed to obtain JSON.

why_incorrect.A: Claude Sonnet 5.5 rejects both forced forms, "any" and "tool", with a 400.
why_incorrect.B: The forced tool_choice still returns a 400, and assistant prefill is also rejected on this model family.
why_incorrect.D: The rejection is deterministic for this model, so retries fail every time and only add latency.

questions.scenario: Every Quillon Media engineer should get the team's error-tracking MCP server automatically in the web-platform repository. The server needs a per-user API token that must never be committed.
questions.question: Which TWO configuration choices together meet these requirements? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Define the server in a project-scoped .mcp.json at the repository root and commit that file
options.B: Write the header as "Authorization": "Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}" so each user's environment supplies it
options.C: Commit .mcp.json with the token written in literally, given that the repository is private to the company
options.D: Have every engineer run claude mcp add for the server with the default scope on their own machine
options.E: Register the server at user scope through an onboarding script so it lands in each user's ~/.claude.json

questions.explanation: Project scope (.mcp.json) is the version-controlled way to share a server with the team. Environment-variable expansion in fields such as headers lets each developer supply their own token without committing it.

why_incorrect.C: Committing a secret exposes it to everyone with repository access and to its history, whether or not the repository is private.
why_incorrect.D: The default scope is local, which is private to that user and project. Nothing is shared, so each engineer must repeat the setup.
why_incorrect.E: User scope is stored outside the repository, so the setup is not versioned with the project and drifts across machines.

questions.scenario: Tallis Travel's engineering agent has a code-search MCP tool, search_symbols, that resolves symbols across 30 repositories using a semantic index. Its description reads only 'Searches code.' The agent almost always uses Grep in the local checkout instead and misses cross-repository callers.
questions.question: What is the most effective first fix?

options.A: Expand the MCP tool's description to explain cross-repo coverage, inputs, outputs and when to prefer it
options.B: Remove Grep from the agent's tools so that the MCP search tool is the only search option left to use
options.C: Rename the MCP tool to grep_all_repos so that its name looks like a more capable version of Grep
options.D: Add a system-prompt line telling the agent to use the MCP tools whenever it would otherwise search code

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose between tools. A two-word description cannot compete with a familiar built-in. Stating the tool's unique coverage, its inputs and outputs, and when to choose it over Grep fixes the selection problem at its source.

why_incorrect.B: Grep is still the right tool for literal text in the local checkout. Removing it trades one blind spot for another.
why_incorrect.C: A new name alone gives little information about capabilities and may suggest the tool behaves like Grep.
why_incorrect.D: A blanket instruction pushes all searches to the MCP tool, including the local literal searches that Grep handles better.

questions.scenario: Ironbark Logistics wants its developer-productivity agent to read and update Jira issues, and to query an in-house deploy-ledger service that records which build is running in each environment.
questions.question: Which TWO integration decisions are most appropriate? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Have the agent use WebFetch on the Jira web UI to avoid adding another MCP server
options.B: Adopt an existing, maintained MCP server for Jira rather than writing a new one
options.C: Skip MCP and have the agent call both systems with curl through Bash, tokens in prompts
options.D: Build a small custom MCP server for the deploy ledger with the team's own operations
options.E: Write custom servers for both systems so that auth and tool naming are consistent

questions.explanation: Standard integrations such as Jira are well served by existing MCP servers, which saves building and maintaining one. Custom servers are best kept for team-specific systems like the deploy ledger, where no ready-made server exists.

why_incorrect.A: Scraping a web UI is brittle, may break authentication flows, and gives unstructured results compared with a proper integration.
why_incorrect.C: Tokens in prompts leak credentials into context and logs, and raw curl gives no typed tool contract.
why_incorrect.E: Rebuilding a standard integration costs effort and upkeep for little gain. Consistency does not justify maintaining a second Jira client.

questions.scenario: Silvergate Utilities' data-explorer agent connects to an MCP server for a warehouse with about 400 tables. Before answering most questions, the agent makes dozens of list_tables and describe_table calls just to find out what data exists.
questions.question: Which change most directly reduces these exploratory calls?

options.A: Add a PostToolUse hook that caches describe_table results so that repeated calls return immediately
options.B: Paste the definitions of all 400 tables into the system prompt so the agent never needs to discover them
options.C: Have the server expose its schema catalog as MCP resources so the agent can see what data is available
options.D: Raise MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS so that list_tables can return every table definition in a single call

questions.explanation: MCP resources let a server expose content catalogs, such as schemas, that the client can list and read. This gives the agent visibility into the available data without probing through repeated tool calls.

why_incorrect.A: Caching speeds up repeated calls, but the agent still makes the same exploratory calls to learn what exists.
why_incorrect.B: Loading every definition up front spends a large share of context on every request, including those that touch two tables.
why_incorrect.D: A larger output limit allows bigger responses but still relies on exploratory tool calls, and it adds bulk to the context.

questions.scenario: An engineer at Marlowe Publishing wants to try an experimental MCP server that indexes her personal engineering notes. She wants it in every project on her laptop, and teammates should never see it.
questions.question: Which configuration fits best?

options.A: Run claude mcp add with --scope user, which stores it in ~/.claude.json for all of her projects
options.B: Commit it to every repository's .mcp.json and ask teammates to disable it in their own settings
options.C: Run claude mcp add with no --scope flag inside each repository she works in, one project at a time
options.D: Add it to each repository's .mcp.json and list that file in .gitignore so it is never committed

questions.explanation: User scope makes a server available in all of one person's projects and stores it in ~/.claude.json, outside any repository, which suits a personal or experimental server.

why_incorrect.B: Committing a personal server pushes it onto everyone and puts the burden of opting out on teammates.
why_incorrect.C: The default local scope applies to one project only, so she would repeat the setup per repository and still miss new ones.
why_incorrect.D: Gitignoring .mcp.json in each repository is per-project setup, and it blocks the team from sharing project servers through that file.

questions.scenario: Claude is changing one return null; statement inside parseHeader() in a 2,400-line file. The Edit call fails because return null; appears seven times in the file.
questions.question: What should Claude do next?

options.A: Retry Edit with replace_all: true so that every occurrence is updated and the uniqueness check is satisfied
options.B: Read the file and then Write the full 2,400 lines back with the one change applied somewhere in the middle
options.C: Use Bash to run sed -i with a regular expression that targets the statement by its approximate line number
options.D: Retry Edit with an old_string that includes the surrounding lines of parseHeader() so that it matches once

questions.explanation: Edit requires old_string to match exactly once. Adding enough surrounding context from parseHeader() makes the match unique and keeps the change targeted. replace_all is only for changing every occurrence.

why_incorrect.A: replace_all would change all seven statements when only one should change.
why_incorrect.B: Rewriting a large file to change one line risks unintended changes. A full Write is a fallback when no unique anchor can be found, and here one can.
why_incorrect.C: Line-number regex edits are fragile and skip the exact-match safety check that Edit provides.

questions.scenario: Claude needs to create a new file config/feature-flags.ts and add one import line to the import block of an existing 1,500-line module, src/app.ts, which it has already read.
questions.question: Which TWO tool choices are most appropriate? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Use Write on src/app.ts, regenerating all 1,500 lines with the import added in place
options.B: Use Write to create config/feature-flags.ts with its full contents
options.C: Use Edit with replace_all: true on the word import to add the line after each import
options.D: Use Edit on src/app.ts with an old_string that uniquely anchors the import block
options.E: Use Bash to append the import with echo >> src/app.ts after the module's last line

questions.explanation: Write creates new files or replaces whole files. Edit makes targeted changes to existing files by exact, unique string replacement, which suits a one-line insertion into a large module.

why_incorrect.A: Regenerating a 1,500-line file for a one-line change risks accidental changes. Edit is designed for partial changes.
why_incorrect.C: replace_all would insert the line after every occurrence of import, corrupting the module.
why_incorrect.E: Appending puts the import at the end of the file rather than in the import block, and it bypasses Edit's exact-match checks.

questions.scenario: At Saltmarsh Robotics, legacy/index.js re-exports a dozen motor-control functions, several under aliases (for example, export { setTorqueV2 as setTorque }). An engineer asks the agent to find every place that uses any of these functions.
questions.question: Which TWO steps produce the most complete result? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Grep only for the original function names, since every alias resolves to the same symbol
options.B: Grep the codebase for each exported alias as well as for the original function names
options.C: Read legacy/index.js to list every name and alias that the wrapper module exports
options.D: Glob for files whose names match the original function names in the legacy folder
options.E: Read every file under src/ up front so that no indirect reference to them can be missed

questions.explanation: Tracing usage through a wrapper starts with the full set of exported names, aliases included. Each name then needs its own content search, because callers use whichever name they imported.

why_incorrect.A: Callers that import the alias never write the original name, so those call sites would be missed.
why_incorrect.D: File names do not show where a function is called. Usage is a content question.
why_incorrect.E: Reading everything up front is costly and fills context. Targeted searches find the same references more efficiently.

questions.scenario: A new engineer at Juniper Rail asks the onboarding agent (Read, Grep, Glob and Bash available) to explain how a ticket-refund request travels through an unfamiliar 1,800-file service.
questions.question: Which exploration strategy should the agent follow?

options.A: Read every file in the service first, so that its explanation rests on complete knowledge of the code
options.B: Glob all source files and infer the request flow from the directory names and the file names alone
options.C: Grep for the refund route registration, Read that handler, then follow its imports step by step
options.D: Ask the engineer to point out the relevant files first, since the agent cannot rank them on its own

questions.explanation: Incremental exploration scales. Use Grep to find an entry point, Read it, then follow imports and calls only as far as the flow requires. This builds an accurate picture without filling the context.

why_incorrect.A: Reading 1,800 files up front exhausts context and buries the relevant path among unrelated code.
why_incorrect.B: Names suggest structure but do not show the actual call flow, so the explanation would be guesswork.
why_incorrect.D: The agent's search tools exist precisely to locate entry points. Handing that back to a newcomer defeats the purpose.

questions.scenario: An engineer at Pinecrest Freight asks the codebase assistant (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob enabled) to list every place that calls computeLateFee( so she can judge the impact of a signature change.
questions.question: Which tool is the best first choice?

options.A: Write, saving a list of likely callers to review
options.B: Read, opening every file under billing/ one by one
options.C: Glob, with the pattern **/*computeLateFee*
options.D: Grep, searching file contents for computeLateFee\(

questions.explanation: Finding call sites is a content search, which is what Grep does. Content mode returns the matching lines with file paths and line numbers. Because Grep uses ripgrep regex syntax, the parenthesis is escaped.

why_incorrect.A: Writing a guessed list produces no evidence. The callers have to be found in the code.
why_incorrect.B: Reading files one by one is slow and spends context, and callers outside billing/ would be missed.
why_incorrect.C: Glob matches file names, not file contents. Callers live in files with unrelated names.

questions.scenario: An Agent SDK tool at Orchard Analytics has Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep and Glob enabled. An engineer asks it to find every Gherkin file in the repository; they are all named *.feature.yaml and spread across many directories.
questions.question: Which tool should the agent use first?

options.A: Grep, searching file contents for the word Feature
options.B: Bash, running ls -R and reading through the listing
options.C: Glob, with the pattern **/*.feature.yaml
options.D: Read, pointed at the repository root directory

questions.explanation: Glob finds files by name pattern, and ** matches at any depth. That is exactly a search by naming convention.

why_incorrect.A: Grep searches inside files. It would match unrelated files that contain the word and could miss feature files that do not.
why_incorrect.B: A recursive listing returns a large volume of irrelevant output that the agent must then filter.
why_incorrect.D: Read reads files, not directories, so it cannot list the repository.

questions.scenario: At Marrowstone Bank, the platform lead wrote the team's review rules (no raw SQL in handlers, every endpoint needs an audit log call) into `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on her laptop. Her local reviews follow the rules, but reviews from the CI job and from teammates' machines ignore them.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Bake a copy of her `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the CI runner image so that pipeline runs pick up the same rules
options.B: Move the rules into the project's CLAUDE.md and commit it, so every clone and the CI checkout load them
options.C: Paste the rules into the prompt string of the CI workflow and ask teammates to paste them into their sessions
options.D: Ask each teammate to add an `@import` in their own user file pointing to the path of the lead's personal file

questions.explanation: User-level CLAUDE.md applies only to that user on that machine and is not shared through version control. Rules the whole team and CI must follow belong in project-level memory (root CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md), committed with the code so every checkout gets them.

why_incorrect.A: This covers CI only, leaves teammates without the rules, and creates a second copy that drifts from the lead's file.
why_incorrect.C: Duplicating rules into prompts and manual pastes is error-prone and leaves no single versioned source of truth.
why_incorrect.D: The lead's home-directory path does not exist on other machines or runners, so the import cannot resolve there.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Grid keeps a payments service and embedded firmware in one monorepo. Its root CLAUDE.md has grown to about 1,800 lines mixing payments rules (idempotency keys, PCI logging limits) with firmware rules (no heap allocation in interrupt handlers). CI reviews of firmware pull requests sometimes cite payments rules, and the maintainers of each area want to own their own standards.
questions.question: Which organisation of project memory best fits these needs?

options.A: Keep a short root CLAUDE.md with repo-wide rules, and give each package a CLAUDE.md that uses `@import` to pull in its own standards files
options.B: Keep the single root file but add a line at the top telling Claude to ignore any rules that do not apply to the package being reviewed
options.C: Move every standard into one large review skill that the CI job invokes on each run, and delete the root CLAUDE.md entirely
options.D: Split the monorepo into two repositories so that each one has its own root CLAUDE.md, owned by the relevant team

questions.explanation: A modular hierarchy keeps universal standards at the root and lets each package's CLAUDE.md import the standards files its maintainers choose. Package-level files load when Claude works in that directory, so firmware reviews see firmware rules, and each team can own its imported files.

why_incorrect.B: All 1,800 lines still load on every run, and an instruction to ignore some of them does not reliably stop cross-contamination.
why_incorrect.C: A single skill bundles both domains again and drops the always-loaded repository-wide conventions that belong in CLAUDE.md.
why_incorrect.D: Restructuring repositories is a large, disruptive change to solve what memory organisation already handles.

questions.scenario: At Tidewell Insurance, payments/CLAUDE.md holds conventions for the payments package. A developer starts Claude Code at the repository root, asks a general design question about payments, and the answer ignores those conventions. Running /context lists the root CLAUDE.md under Memory files but not payments/CLAUDE.md. Teammates say the conventions apply once Claude edits payment code.
questions.question: What is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.A: The external-import approval dialog was declined earlier, which disables every nested CLAUDE.md file in the project for this user
options.B: Nested CLAUDE.md files are honoured only when Claude Code is started from inside that directory, so she must relaunch from payments/
options.C: The file needs YAML frontmatter with a paths field before Claude Code will recognise it as an instruction file for that directory
options.D: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand, when Claude reads or edits a file in that directory, so the file is not listed at launch

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md files above the working directory load at launch. Files in subdirectories load only when Claude reads, writes or edits a file in that subdirectory, so they do not appear under Memory files in /context at startup. Having Claude open a payments file first, or moving conventions that apply everywhere up a level, fixes the gap.

why_incorrect.A: The approval dialog covers imports that resolve outside the working directory. It does not switch off nested CLAUDE.md files.
why_incorrect.B: Launching from payments/ would load the file at startup, but it is not required. The file already loads on demand during a root-level session.
why_incorrect.C: Only rule files in .claude/rules/ use paths frontmatter. CLAUDE.md files need none, and teammates already see the file take effect.

questions.scenario: A Fernhill Education developer added notes for her own setup (her local database port, her preferred test-watch command) to the repository's CLAUDE.md. Teammates complain that Claude now suggests her port and command in their sessions. She wants the notes to apply only to her, and only in this repository.
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Move the notes to CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root and keep that file out of version control with .gitignore
options.B: Move the notes to her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so they load for her in every session on her laptop and nowhere else
options.C: Move the notes from the root CLAUDE.md into .claude/CLAUDE.md, so they sit apart from the team's shared instructions
options.D: Move the notes to a new CLAUDE.md inside the src/ directory, so they load only when Claude opens files under src/

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.local.md is the place for personal, project-specific instructions: it loads alongside the project's CLAUDE.md for her sessions in this repository, and because it is gitignored it never reaches teammates. The shared project CLAUDE.md should hold only what the whole team needs.

why_incorrect.B: User-level memory applies to all of her projects, so a port and command specific to this repository would leak into unrelated work.
why_incorrect.C: .claude/CLAUDE.md is still project memory that is committed and shared, so teammates keep getting her notes.
why_incorrect.D: A subdirectory CLAUDE.md is still committed and shared, and it loads for anyone whose session touches src/.

questions.scenario: Copperline Energy's monorepo contains billing/, telemetry/ and ui-kit/ packages. The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines, adherence is slipping, and each package's maintainers want only the standards relevant to their package to apply.
questions.question: Which TWO changes best restructure the instructions? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Move the guidance into every developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so the repository file shrinks and each person keeps only the parts they need
options.B: Convert the 900 lines into @imports from the root CLAUDE.md, because imported files load only when Claude decides to follow the reference
options.C: Keep only universal facts in the root CLAUDE.md, and let each package's own CLAUDE.md @import the shared standards files its maintainers choose
options.D: Move topic guidance into files under .claude/rules/, giving package-specific files a paths field so they load only when Claude works on matching files
options.E: Replace the file with one skill holding every standard, marked disable-model-invocation so it costs no context unless someone types it

questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ load only when Claude touches matching files, which cuts irrelevant context. Package-level CLAUDE.md files with selective @imports let maintainers choose which shared standards apply to their package, while the root file keeps only what every session needs.

why_incorrect.A: User-level files are not version-controlled, so the team loses a shared source of truth and new members receive nothing.
why_incorrect.B: Imported files are expanded and loaded together with the CLAUDE.md that imports them. Imports help organisation but do not reduce context cost.
why_incorrect.E: With disable-model-invocation, Claude never loads the skill on its own. Standards that should apply to every edit would then be absent unless someone remembered to type the command.

questions.scenario: Pinecrest University's research software team built a 'deep review' workflow that maps call graphs across the codebase before judging a change. They want developers to run it on demand from their sessions and the CI job to run the identical workflow. Developers complain that when they try it, the long call-graph output floods their working session.
questions.question: How should the team package this workflow?

options.A: As a personal skill under `~/.claude/skills/` on each developer laptop, with the CI job carrying its own copy of the steps
options.B: As a project skill in `.claude/skills/` with `context: fork`, committed to the repo and run in CI by putting `/deep-review` in the `-p` prompt
options.C: As a section of the root CLAUDE.md, so that the workflow is always loaded and available in every session and CI run
options.D: As a project skill without forking, ending with an instruction to summarise the call graph once the review is complete

questions.explanation: A project skill is shared through version control, so developers and CI use the same definition. `context: fork` runs the skill in its own subagent context, keeping the verbose analysis out of the developer's main conversation. In print mode, putting `/skill-name` in the prompt invokes the skill.

why_incorrect.A: Personal skills are not shared, so developers and CI would maintain separate copies that drift apart.
why_incorrect.C: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded standards; putting a long task workflow there spends context on every session that does not need it.
why_incorrect.D: Without forking, the full call-graph output still lands in the main session before any summary is written.

questions.scenario: At Halyard Bank, an engineer wants a terser variant of the team's project skill release-notes for her own use, without changing what teammates get. Separately, the team wants its db-reset skill never to start unless a person explicitly types it.
questions.question: Which TWO actions meet these needs? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Create ~/.claude/skills/release-notes-terse/SKILL.md, a personal skill with a different name that sits beside the team's version
options.B: Add a CLAUDE.md line asking Claude never to run db-reset unless an engineer explicitly asks it to in the prompt
options.C: Set disable-model-invocation: true in db-reset's SKILL.md so only a person typing /db-reset can start that skill
options.D: Set user-invocable: false on db-reset so it disappears from the slash menu and therefore cannot start by itself
options.E: Add a 'terse mode' paragraph to the committed release-notes SKILL.md, since only she will ever ask for that mode

questions.explanation: A personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ with a distinct name gives her a variant without touching the shared file or shadowing the team version. disable-model-invocation: true removes Claude's ability to invoke db-reset, so only a typed /db-reset can run it.

why_incorrect.B: A CLAUDE.md instruction is guidance Claude usually follows, not a control. disable-model-invocation removes the possibility entirely.
why_incorrect.D: user-invocable: false does the opposite of what is needed. It hides the skill from people while still letting Claude invoke it.
why_incorrect.E: Editing the committed skill changes the shared definition and the context every teammate loads with it.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Pharma's team has a dependency-audit skill that walks the lockfile and prints every transitive package with its licence. After an engineer runs it, the main conversation is full of package listings and Claude's later answers about the feature in progress get vaguer.
questions.question: Which change to the skill best addresses this?

options.A: Set disable-model-invocation: true so the skill runs only when an engineer types it, keeping the listings out of the session
options.B: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter so it runs in a subagent and only its summary returns to the main conversation
options.C: Add allowed-tools: Read so the skill cannot run shell commands, which keeps the size of each package listing much smaller
options.D: Set user-invocable: false so the skill is hidden from the slash menu and can only be triggered when Claude judges it is needed

questions.explanation: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent context. The verbose package walk stays inside that context and the main conversation receives only the result, so the working session is not crowded out.

why_incorrect.A: This controls who can invoke the skill, not where its output goes. A manual run would still flood the main conversation.
why_incorrect.C: allowed-tools pre-approves tools for the skill's turn; it does not shrink output. The listing would be just as long.
why_incorrect.D: This changes who can invoke the skill, not where its output lands, so the main context still fills up.

questions.scenario: Larkspur Games' release manager finds that about a third of the changelog entries Claude Code drafts for the game-server repository have no ticket reference. Engineers paste an ad-hoc prompt from a wiki page into their sessions, and many skip its ticket field.
questions.question: What should the team set up?

options.A: Copy the wiki prompt into each engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, adding a line that says a ticket ID is always required
options.B: Expose a changelog-entry prompt from an MCP server that each engineer registers with claude mcp add, using the default scope
options.C: Add a CLAUDE.md section telling Claude that when someone types /changelog-entry it should ask for the ticket ID and draft
options.D: Commit .claude/skills/changelog-entry/SKILL.md with argument-hint [ticket-id], $ARGUMENTS, and a rule to ask if none given

questions.explanation: A project skill in .claude/skills/ is shared through version control, replacing the copy-paste prompt with one versioned command. argument-hint shows the expected ticket ID in autocomplete, $ARGUMENTS places what the engineer typed into the instructions, and an explicit instruction to ask for the ID when none is given closes the gap that produced entries without a ticket.

why_incorrect.A: Personal files drift between machines, need a manual copy for every engineer, and load into every unrelated session rather than defining a command.
why_incorrect.B: The default scope of claude mcp add is local, which is private to one user and project, so it is not shared with the team. It also adds a server where a file would do.
why_incorrect.C: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded guidance, not a command definition. Typing an undefined slash command does not invoke anything reliably.

questions.scenario: Corvid Labs added .claude/rules/terraform.md. Its frontmatter is the single line paths: [terraform/**/*.tf, with the closing bracket missing, between --- markers. Engineers notice the Terraform conventions are in context even while Claude edits Python services.
questions.question: What explains this behaviour?

options.A: Path-scoped rules load at launch for every session and only become active once a matching file is opened
options.B: The root CLAUDE.md mentions `terraform.md` inside backticks, which imports the rule file for every session
options.C: Path scoping applies only to the Edit tool, so Read calls on any file still bring every rule into the context
options.D: The YAML does not parse, so Claude Code ignores the frontmatter and loads the rule as though it had no paths

questions.explanation: When the frontmatter YAML fails to parse, Claude Code ignores it and treats the file as an unconditional rule, which loads at launch. Fixing the list syntax restores path scoping, and claude --debug shows the parse error.

why_incorrect.A: A correctly scoped rule is not loaded at launch at all. It loads when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file.
why_incorrect.B: Import parsing skips Markdown code spans, so a path wrapped in backticks stays literal text and imports nothing.
why_incorrect.C: Path-scoped rules load on Read as well as Write and Edit of a matching file. Reading Python files would not match terraform/**/*.tf.

questions.scenario: Saltmarsh Robotics' root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines, a third of it SQL migration conventions (reversible steps, no column renames in place). Migrations live in services/*/db/migrations/, and few sessions touch them. The team reports that Claude follows the general rules less reliably as the file grows.
questions.question: What is the best way to restructure these conventions?

options.A: Move them to .claude/rules/migrations.md with paths: ["services/*/db/migrations/**"] in its frontmatter
options.B: Move them to a separate file and reference it with an @import from the root CLAUDE.md, so that the root file reads shorter
options.C: Move them into a CLAUDE.md inside services/, so they load only when Claude works on files somewhere under that directory
options.D: Package them as a skill whose description says to use it for database work, and rely on Claude to invoke it when needed

questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule in .claude/rules/ with a glob loads only when Claude works with matching files. That takes the migration conventions out of every session's context, which shortens the always-loaded instructions, while still applying them every time a migration file is touched.

why_incorrect.B: Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch, so the conventions still use context in every session.
why_incorrect.C: A subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads for any file under services/, which is most service work, not only migrations.
why_incorrect.D: Auto-invocation depends on Claude judging the skill relevant. A path-scoped rule loads automatically when a matching file is touched.

questions.scenario: Orchard Analytics wants SQL migration conventions to load only when Claude works on files matching db/migrations/**/*.sql. The rule lives in the project's .claude/rules/migrations.md.
questions.question: Which TWO statements about how this rule behaves are correct? (Choose 2.)

options.A: The rule loads at session start whenever at least one matching file exists anywhere in the repository, so it is present from the first prompt
options.B: The rule loads when Claude uses Read, Write or Edit on a matching file, and when it views one with a single-file command such as cat
options.C: Scoping is declared with an applies_to key, because paths is reserved for skill frontmatter and is ignored inside rule files
options.D: Adding a description field to the rule's frontmatter helps Claude decide when the rule is relevant enough to load
options.E: The rule's patterns resolve relative to the directory that contains the project's .claude folder, so they target the repository's migrations

questions.explanation: A path-scoped rule loads when Claude reads, writes or edits a matching file, including a single-file view through Bash that counts as a read. Patterns in project rules resolve relative to the directory containing the rule's .claude folder.

why_incorrect.A: Loading depends on Claude touching a matching file, not on matching files existing somewhere in the repository.
why_incorrect.C: paths is the documented field for rules. Claude Code reads no other frontmatter field in a rule file.
why_incorrect.D: paths is the only field Claude Code reads from a rule. Other fields, description included, are ignored.

questions.scenario: Juniper Rail wants to retire a home-grown date library used in about 60 files. Two approaches are on the table: wrap the new library behind an adapter, or replace calls directly. Each has different testing and rollout costs.
questions.question: How should the engineer run this task in Claude Code?

options.A: Start in plan mode so Claude explores call sites and compares both approaches, review and edit the plan, then approve it to begin editing
options.B: Use acceptEdits from the start, since the change is mechanical and Claude can correct mistakes as it moves from one file to the next
options.C: Have Claude convert one file directly, then ask it to repeat the same edit across the remaining files using that file as the pattern
options.D: Open about 60 short direct-execution sessions, one per file, so that each change stays small and the history is easy to review

questions.explanation: Large, multi-file changes with more than one valid approach and an architectural choice are where plan mode pays off. Claude explores read-only, proposes a plan you can edit (Ctrl+G opens it in your editor), and edits begin only after approval, which avoids costly rework.

why_incorrect.B: Editing immediately commits to an approach before the call sites and trade-offs are understood, which is the rework plan mode prevents.
why_incorrect.C: One file is not a representative sample. Edge cases in other call sites, and the adapter-versus-direct decision, stay unexamined.
why_incorrect.D: Per-file sessions lose the shared view needed to choose between approaches and keep the migration consistent.

questions.scenario: Basalt Systems is moving its services from one message-queue client to another. There are two integration options with different infrastructure needs. On a previous attempt, the discovery of every producer and consumer filled the context window before any design was agreed.
questions.question: Which TWO practices should the team combine? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Skip planning and use acceptEdits so Claude can try both integrations in place and keep whichever passes tests
options.B: Ask the Plan subagent to edit the files in parallel while the main session is still writing up the plan
options.C: Use plan mode to investigate and choose the approach, then approve the plan and implement it in an editing mode
options.D: Delegate the verbose producer and consumer discovery to the Explore subagent so only a summary returns
options.E: Run all discovery in the main conversation in plan mode, which keeps tool output out of the context window

questions.explanation: Plan mode handles the design decision before any edits, and the approved plan then drives implementation. Sending verbose discovery to the Explore subagent keeps the main context for the design work, because only a summary comes back.

why_incorrect.A: Trying both integrations by editing in place is the costly rework that planning is meant to avoid, especially with infrastructure differences.
why_incorrect.B: The built-in Plan subagent is read-only, with Write and Edit denied, so it cannot make edits.
why_incorrect.E: Plan mode blocks edits, but tool output from exploration still accumulates in the main context, which is the problem seen last time.

questions.scenario: A failing test at Wren Retail produces a stack trace pointing to an off-by-one error in a single paginate() function. The fix is clearly confined to that function and its test file.
questions.question: Which way of working is most appropriate?

options.A: Enter plan mode and have Claude produce a written plan for approval before it changes paginate()
options.B: Ask Claude directly to fix the off-by-one using the stack trace, then run the failing test to confirm
options.C: Spawn an Explore subagent to map the codebase's pagination patterns before any fix is attempted
options.D: Set defaultMode to plan in the project settings so that every bug fix goes through a reviewed plan

questions.explanation: Direct execution suits a small, well-scoped change with a clear diagnosis. Planning or wide exploration adds overhead without lowering risk, and the test gives immediate verification.

why_incorrect.A: A formal plan for a one-function fix with a known cause adds a step without reducing any meaningful risk.
why_incorrect.C: The stack trace has already located the defect. Mapping the wider codebase spends time and context on nothing.
why_incorrect.D: Making plan mode the project default slows every small fix, which is the wrong trade-off for well-understood changes.

questions.scenario: Vellum Analytics uses Claude Code in CI to generate tests for a utility that parses user-entered durations. The prompt says the tests should 'cover edge cases properly'. Each run picks different cases, and none of them so far has checked empty strings, null input or values such as '1h 90m'.
questions.question: What is the most effective refinement?

options.A: Expand the prose description of edge cases into a longer paragraph that explains why careful edge-case testing matters
options.B: Run test generation three times per change and keep only the test cases that appear in at least two of the three runs
options.C: Raise the effort level so Claude reasons more carefully about which edge cases deserve tests before writing any of them
options.D: Give two or three concrete inputs with their expected outputs, including empty, null and overflowing minute values

questions.explanation: When prose is interpreted inconsistently, concrete input and expected-output examples communicate the requirement far more precisely. Naming the exact edge cases with their expected results removes guesswork and makes later runs consistent.

why_incorrect.A: More prose about importance still leaves the actual cases unspecified, so different runs keep making different choices.
why_incorrect.B: Voting across runs triples cost and still cannot produce cases that none of the runs thought of.
why_incorrect.C: Deeper reasoning does not tell Claude which specific behaviours the team expects for these inputs.

questions.scenario: Marlowe Publishing asks Claude to write a function that converts legacy citation strings into a structured record. After three rounds of prose explanation, the output still varies: sometimes the year is parsed as a volume number and sometimes editors are dropped.
questions.question: What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Give two or three concrete input strings with the exact expected records, including one with editors and a volume
options.B: Rewrite the explanation in more detail with the key rules in capitals so the requirements stand out more clearly
options.C: Ask Claude to keep regenerating the function until two consecutive attempts produce the same parsed output
options.D: Switch to plan mode so that Claude writes out its parsing approach in detail before it attempts the code again

questions.explanation: When prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently, a few concrete input/output pairs remove the ambiguity. Pairs that cover the confusing cases (year versus volume, editors) pin down the transformation precisely and double as test cases.

why_incorrect.B: More emphatic prose keeps the ambiguity that caused the variation. Examples state the expected mapping directly.
why_incorrect.C: Two matching outputs show consistency, not correctness. Both attempts can share the same misreading.
why_incorrect.D: A written plan restates the same prose understanding. Without examples the year and volume ambiguity remains.

questions.scenario: Northgate Telecom's engineers are adding a cache in front of a pricing service. Nobody on the team has designed cache invalidation before, and they want Claude to improve the solution in steps rather than produce one big untested change.
questions.question: Which TWO techniques best support this? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Have Claude interview the engineer about invalidation triggers, acceptable staleness and failure modes before any code is written
options.B: Fix each failing test in a brand-new session so that earlier attempts cannot bias how Claude approaches the next one
options.C: Write tests for expected behaviour, edge cases and the latency budget first, then iterate by sharing the specific failures
options.D: Ask for the complete implementation at once, then reply that it still does not feel right until the design settles down
options.E: Let Claude pick an invalidation strategy on its own and document the assumptions it made after the code is merged

questions.explanation: The interview pattern surfaces considerations the team has not anticipated, such as invalidation events and failure behaviour, before implementation. Test-first iteration then gives concrete, shareable failures that drive each refinement.

why_incorrect.B: Fresh sessions throw away useful context about the design and earlier failures, which slows convergence.
why_incorrect.D: Vague feedback gives Claude nothing specific to correct, so iterations wander instead of converging.
why_incorrect.E: Unexamined assumptions in an unfamiliar domain are what lead to stale-data bugs. Documenting them after merge is too late.

questions.scenario: Saltmarsh Payments added `--bare` to its `claude -p` review step so runs behave the same on every runner. Since the change, reviews no longer enforce the rules in the repository's root CLAUDE.md, such as 'monetary amounts must use Decimal, never float'. Nothing else in the job changed.
questions.question: What explains the change, and what is the best fix?

options.A: Bare mode removes the file read tool, so Claude cannot open CLAUDE.md; add `--allowedTools "Read"` to restore access to the file
options.B: Bare mode skips CLAUDE.md discovery, so pass the review rules explicitly, for example with `--append-system-prompt-file`
options.C: CLAUDE.md is only read in interactive sessions, so move the review rules into `.claude/settings.json` where print mode reads them
options.D: Bare mode switches to a smaller default model that follows instructions less closely, so pin a larger model with `--model`

questions.explanation: `--bare` skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, which is what makes runs reproducible. Context the job needs must then be passed explicitly, for example with `--append-system-prompt-file` pointing at a committed rules file. Without `--bare`, `claude -p` does load CLAUDE.md as an interactive session would.

why_incorrect.A: In bare mode Claude still has the Bash, file read and file edit tools; the rules are missing because CLAUDE.md is not auto-loaded, not because files cannot be read.
why_incorrect.C: Print mode without `--bare` does load CLAUDE.md, and settings.json holds configuration such as permissions, not review instructions.
why_incorrect.D: The documented effect of bare mode is on what is discovered and loaded, not on model selection, so pinning a model leaves the rules missing.

questions.scenario: Brackenridge Logistics posts review findings with `jq '.structured_output.findings[]'` after a `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema ...` step. Most runs work, but a few each week end with a jq error about iterating over null, and the job then reports 'no findings' on the pull request. In one failing run the result text shows Claude declined part of the request.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate fix in the pipeline?

options.A: Check that `structured_output` exists before posting, and report a missing field as a failed review instead of as zero findings
options.B: Make every property in the findings schema optional so that whatever Claude returns always validates and the field is filled
options.C: Raise `--max-turns` for the review step so that Claude has enough turns left to produce output that matches the schema
options.D: When the field is missing, fall back to scanning the `result` text with a regular expression and post whatever findings it can recover

questions.explanation: When a run ends without valid structured output, for example because Claude declined, the JSON result has no `structured_output` field. Scripts should check for the field before using it. Treating its absence as success is the real defect: a pull request is told it is clean when no review happened. Surfacing it as a failed review keeps the signal honest.

why_incorrect.B: Loosening the schema does not make the field appear when the run produced no structured output, and it weakens the guarantees the posting script relies on.
why_incorrect.C: Nothing indicates the run hit a turn limit; the evidence points to a declined request, which more turns would not change.
why_incorrect.D: This reintroduces the fragile text parsing the schema was meant to remove, and may post partial or garbled findings from a run that did not finish properly.

questions.scenario: Larkspur Legal added `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` to a workflow triggered on pull_request events. The workflow passes a plain-text `prompt` input asking Claude to run `npm ls --all` and flag dependencies with disallowed licences. Every run finishes with Claude explaining that it was not able to run the command.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?

options.A: With a plain-text prompt, Claude has no shell access until the needed tools are granted with `--allowedTools` in `claude_args`
options.B: The action only responds to @claude mentions in comments, so a `prompt` input on a pull_request event is ignored
options.C: Shell access needs a Claude subscription token, so the workflow must use `claude_code_oauth_token` instead of an API key
options.D: The checkout step must run after the action, because the action resets the working directory when it starts up

questions.explanation: With a `prompt` input the action runs in automation mode on any event. For a plain-text prompt, Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until the workflow grants the tools it needs, through `--allowedTools` in `claude_args` or a `permissions.allow` rule in the `settings` input. Adding a scoped rule such as `Bash(npm ls *)` fixes the run.
