why_incorrect.B: Interactive @claude mode applies when no `prompt` is given; with a prompt, the action runs automatically on the configured event.
why_incorrect.C: Both authentication methods are supported, and the choice of credential does not control which tools Claude may use.
why_incorrect.D: Checkout has to happen before the action so the code is present; moving it after would make things worse, not fix tool access.

questions.scenario: Quillfeather Labs runs Claude Code in its pipeline to review pull requests. A Python script turns the review into inline PR comments and needs the file, line, severity and message for every finding. Today the script runs a regular expression over Claude's free-text answer, and it breaks whenever the wording or layout of the review changes.
questions.question: Which change gives the posting script reliable input?

options.A: Keep text output, add a strict instruction to print one finding per line as file:line:severity:message, and harden the regular expression against stray whitespace
options.B: Add `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` describing the findings array, and read the findings from the `structured_output` field
options.C: Use `--output-format stream-json` and rebuild the review by joining the text deltas, then parse the joined text once the final result event arrives
options.D: Ask Claude to write its findings to a findings.json file in the workspace, and have the posting script load that file once the run exits

questions.explanation: In print mode, `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` returns schema-conforming data in the `structured_output` field of the result, alongside session metadata. The posting script then reads typed fields instead of guessing at prose, so wording changes no longer break it. This is the documented way to get machine-parseable findings from a CI run.

why_incorrect.A: A format instruction makes the layout more likely but not guaranteed, so the script still depends on a regular expression that fails on the next unexpected variation.
why_incorrect.C: Streaming changes how the text arrives, not what it is; the script would still be parsing free text after reassembling it.
why_incorrect.D: A file written by the model has no schema check, and needs file-write permission in the job; malformed or missing files remain possible.

questions.scenario: Orchid Freight's pipeline uses one `claude -p` session to write a database migration, then runs `claude -p --continue` with 'Now review the changes you just made for bugs'. The review step almost never reports problems, yet human reviewers keep finding several issues per migration.
questions.question: Which change is most likely to make the automated review catch more issues?

options.A: Ask the continued session to review the migration twice in a row and merge the findings of both passes into one list
options.B: Run the review as a separate `claude -p` invocation that receives the diff and review criteria but not the generator's history
options.C: Keep `--continue` and raise the effort level for the review turn so that Claude reasons longer about its changes
options.D: Keep `--continue` but add 'review critically, as if a different engineer wrote this code' to the review prompt

questions.explanation: A session that generated the code carries its own reasoning and assumptions, which makes it less likely to question its decisions. A fresh instance that sees only the diff and the review criteria has no such anchoring and catches more subtle problems. Session isolation between generation and review is the design principle.

why_incorrect.A: Repeating the review in the same anchored context tends to repeat the same blind spots, while doubling cost.
why_incorrect.C: Longer reasoning inside the same session still starts from the generator's own justification for each choice.
why_incorrect.D: A role instruction does not remove the generator's reasoning from context, so the same assumptions still shape the review.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Robotics runs an automated Claude Code review on every push to an open pull request. Developers complain that after each push the bot posts the same nine comments again, including ones about code they have already fixed, so long pull requests fill with duplicates.
questions.question: Which two changes best address this? (Select 2)

options.A: Raise the severity threshold on later pushes so that only critical findings are posted after the first review
options.B: Pass the findings from the previous review run, with their locations, into the context of the new review run
options.C: Run the review only on the first push of each pull request and skip it for every push that comes after
options.D: Instruct Claude to report only issues that are new or still unaddressed, and to mark earlier findings as resolved
options.E: Delete every earlier bot comment before posting so that each pull request shows only the latest full set of findings

questions.explanation: Each CI run starts without memory of earlier runs, so the reviewer cannot know what it already said. Supplying the prior findings and asking for only new or still-open issues lets it compare against history, which removes duplicates while still catching problems introduced by the new commits.

why_incorrect.A: This hides important non-critical issues introduced later and does not stop critical findings from being repeated.
why_incorrect.C: Later commits can introduce new defects, so skipping them removes review coverage exactly where the code is changing.
why_incorrect.E: Deleting comments throws away discussion threads and still reposts fixed issues, so noise moves rather than disappears.

questions.scenario: Ferngrove Pharma's nightly job asks Claude Code to propose unit tests for recently changed modules. Reviewers reject most proposals: many repeat scenarios already in the test suite, others test trivial getters, and several build their own fake database instead of using the shared fixtures the team maintains.
questions.question: Which two changes would most improve the generated tests? (Select 2)

options.A: Add the sentence 'generate only high-quality tests that do not duplicate existing ones' to the start of the prompt
options.B: Document the testing standards, what makes a test valuable, and the available fixtures in the project CLAUDE.md
options.C: Ask for twice as many tests per run and keep only the ones that raise line coverage when the suite is executed
options.D: Raise `--max-turns` so Claude has more turns to explore the repository before it writes any new tests
options.E: Include the module's existing test files in the context so Claude can see which scenarios are already covered

questions.explanation: Duplicate scenarios come from Claude not seeing the existing tests, so putting them in context fixes that directly. Low-value tests and home-made fakes come from missing team knowledge; CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude Code persistent project context such as testing standards and fixture conventions.

why_incorrect.A: A general quality instruction gives no information about which tests exist or which fixtures to use, so the same failures recur.
why_incorrect.C: Coverage gain rewards tests that touch lines, not tests that check meaningful behaviour, and doubling output doubles cost and review load.
why_incorrect.D: More turns may help exploration, but nothing tells Claude what counts as valuable or which fixtures are expected, so output quality does not reliably improve.

questions.scenario: Tidewater Insurance is hardening its `claude -p` pull-request review job. The job should only read the code and the diff and report findings. It must never edit files or run arbitrary commands, and finance wants a hard ceiling on what a single run can spend.
questions.question: Which two configuration choices best meet these requirements? (Select 2)

options.A: Pass `--allowedTools "Bash"` so git commands and any helper scripts run without prompting in the unattended job
options.B: Set `--max-budget-usd` on the review step so the run stops once its estimated spend reaches the agreed cap
options.C: Rely on a prompt line saying 'do not modify files or run commands' as the main control, since review prompts are trusted
options.D: Pass `--permission-mode acceptEdits` so the job never stalls on an edit approval while it is running unattended
options.E: List only the needed tools, such as `Read` and `Bash(git diff *)`, and run with `--permission-mode dontAsk` so other calls are denied

questions.explanation: Scoped `--allowedTools` entries pre-approve only what the review needs, and `dontAsk` denies every call that would otherwise need approval, which suits locked-down CI. `--max-budget-usd` stops a print-mode run once estimated spend reaches the cap; it is an estimate and can be slightly exceeded, so leave headroom.

why_incorrect.A: A bare `Bash` allow rule approves any shell command, including destructive ones, which breaks the never-run-arbitrary-commands requirement.
why_incorrect.C: Prompt instructions guide behaviour but are not an enforcement boundary; permission settings are what actually block disallowed calls.
why_incorrect.D: acceptEdits auto-approves file writes, which is the opposite of what a read-only review job needs.

questions.scenario: Saltmarsh Payments' review bot classifies findings as critical, major or minor. The same unchecked null dereference in a refund handler was rated critical on Monday and minor on Thursday. The prompt currently says 'assign an appropriate severity to each finding'.
questions.question: What change will most improve severity consistency?

options.A: Have the model output a confidence score for each finding and derive the severity level from that score in code
options.B: Run each review three times and keep the severity that appears most often across the three runs for each finding
options.C: Define each severity level with explicit criteria and a concrete code example of a finding that belongs at that level
options.D: Add a reminder to the prompt that severity ratings must be consistent across pull requests and over time

questions.explanation: Inconsistent classification comes from undefined criteria. Spelling out what makes a finding critical, major or minor, and anchoring each level with a concrete code example, gives the model a stable rubric to apply across reviews.

why_incorrect.A: Confidence measures how sure the model is that something is a problem, not how severe the problem is, so it cannot stand in for severity.
why_incorrect.B: Majority voting triples cost and can still be inconsistent, because the underlying rubric is unchanged.
why_incorrect.D: Asking for consistency without saying what each level means leaves the same subjective judgment in place.

questions.scenario: Vellum Analytics' review bot has an instruction 'Check that code comments are accurate.' It now posts comment-related findings on 40% of pull requests, mostly about grammar, outdated TODO wording and stylistic phrasing. Developers have started ignoring the bot.
questions.question: Which rewrite of the instruction will best reduce false positives?

options.A: Be conservative with comment findings and report only the comment issues that you are highly confident about
options.B: Flag a comment only when the behaviour it describes contradicts what the code does; skip grammar, wording and TODO style
options.C: Rate every comment for accuracy on a scale of one to ten and report only those comments that score below four
options.D: Check comment accuracy only on public API functions, because internal comments matter less to most readers

questions.explanation: Explicit categorical criteria tell the model exactly what to report and what to skip. 'Contradicts actual behaviour' targets the comments that mislead readers, and naming the excluded categories removes the noise. General instructions such as 'be conservative' do not improve precision because they do not define what counts as an issue.

why_incorrect.A: Confidence wording does not define what an issue is, so the model remains confident about stylistic findings.
why_incorrect.C: A numeric score without criteria just moves the same subjective judgment into a number with an arbitrary cut-off.
why_incorrect.D: Narrowing scope cuts volume but still reports grammar and wording on public functions, and misses misleading internal comments.

questions.scenario: Norvale Health Records' automated reviewer reports in three categories: security, logic bugs and style. Telemetry shows developers dismiss 70% of style findings, while security findings are accurate. Engineers now say they skim past all bot comments, including security ones.
questions.question: Which two actions should the team take? (Select 2)

options.A: Temporarily stop posting style findings while the criteria for that category are rewritten and tested
options.B: Label style findings as optional in their text but keep posting them inline beside the other two categories
options.C: Add an instruction to report only findings that the model is at least 90% confident about in every category
options.D: Rewrite the prompt with explicit criteria for what to report and what to skip, such as patterns used consistently in the repo
options.E: Collect all findings into one summary comment at the end so that they seem less noisy on the pull request

questions.explanation: A high false-positive category erodes trust in accurate categories too. Disabling it temporarily restores trust in security and bug findings, and explicit report-or-skip criteria are what actually raise precision when the category returns. Confidence thresholds expressed in prose do not.

why_incorrect.B: Developers still see the noisy findings inline, so the habit of skimming past bot comments continues.
why_incorrect.C: Self-stated confidence thresholds are a general instruction and do not reliably separate valid findings from noise.
why_incorrect.E: Bundling the same noisy findings changes presentation, not accuracy, and makes the valuable security findings harder to spot.

questions.scenario: Cobaltline Clinical extracts adverse events from trial site notes into a safety database. The prompt says 'extract all adverse events'. Safety reviewers find that a third of extracted events are wrong: phrases such as 'denies chest pain', 'history of migraine' and 'mother had seizures' are all being recorded as events.
questions.question: Which prompt change will most improve precision?

options.A: Tell the model to extract only adverse events that it is sure about, and to leave out anything it is uncertain of
options.B: Record an event only when the note says it occurred in the participant after first dose; exclude negated, historical and family mentions
options.C: Ask the model to give each extracted event a confidence score and keep only events whose score is above 0.8
options.D: Shorten each note to its assessment section before extraction so that fewer incidental mentions reach the model

questions.explanation: The errors fall into identifiable categories, so explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria fix them directly. Defining an adverse event as something that happened to the participant after dosing, and naming negation, history and family history as exclusions, removes the false positives without relying on vague confidence wording.

why_incorrect.A: The model is confident that 'denies chest pain' mentions chest pain; without criteria, certainty does not filter these cases.
why_incorrect.C: Uncalibrated confidence scores do not encode the negation and history rules, so the same errors can score highly.
why_incorrect.D: Events are often recorded outside the assessment section, so truncation loses real events and still keeps negated ones.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Robotics' review job posts a markdown summary for human readers. The prompt already lists, in detail, that every finding needs a location, the issue, a severity and a suggested fix. Output still varies: some findings omit the location, and suggested fixes are often vague, such as 'consider refactoring this'.
questions.question: What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Add two or three complete example findings that show a precise location, a clear issue, a severity and a concrete fix
options.B: Restate the formatting rules in capital letters at both the start and the end of the prompt so they are harder to miss
options.C: Filter out incomplete findings in a post-processing script so that only well-formed ones reach the pull request
options.D: Move the review job to a larger model, on the basis that a stronger model follows long instructions more consistently

questions.explanation: When detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results, a few well-chosen examples are the most effective way to show the exact output expected. Examples also demonstrate what an actionable fix looks like, which prose struggles to convey.

why_incorrect.B: Emphasis repeats the same instructions the model already has without showing what a good finding looks like.
why_incorrect.C: Dropping incomplete findings hides real issues rather than making the model produce complete ones.
why_incorrect.D: A larger model costs more and may still vary in format; the gap is a missing demonstration, not model capability.

questions.scenario: Brackenridge Logistics' codebase wraps raw SQL in helpers named `unsafe_query_*`, but every call site validates inputs with a shared guard first. The review bot flags each of these calls as SQL injection. The team wants these false positives to stop while the bot still catches genuinely unsafe queries, including new patterns no one has listed.
questions.question: Which two prompt changes best achieve this? (Select 2)

options.A: State the criterion: flag raw SQL only when untrusted input can reach it without passing the shared guard
options.B: Add examples contrasting a guarded `unsafe_query_*` call with an unguarded variant, each with a short rationale
options.C: Add dozens of examples, one for each helper name in the codebase, so the model memorises every acceptable call
options.D: Add a list of file paths where SQL injection findings are suppressed, covering every file that uses these helpers
options.E: Instruct the model not to raise security findings on any code that calls an internal helper function

questions.explanation: Two changes work together but each stands on its own. An explicit reporting criterion tells the model what actually makes a call unsafe (untrusted input reaching the query without the guard), so it can judge new patterns no one has listed. Few-shot examples that contrast a guarded call with an unguarded one, with a short rationale, show that distinction in practice. Both teach the model to reason about the guard rather than react to the helper's name.

why_incorrect.C: Exhaustive name lists encourage pattern matching on names instead of reasoning about guards, and cost context on every run.
why_incorrect.D: Path suppression hides every injection finding in those files, including a future call that skips the guard.
why_incorrect.E: A blanket exemption removes coverage for exactly the helpers that execute raw SQL.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Wholesale extracts supplier invoices from many layouts. Tabular invoices extract well, but for letter-style invoices the model returns null for `due_date` and `payment_terms`, even though a human can see sentences such as 'Settlement is expected by the 14th of the month after delivery'.
questions.question: What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Make `due_date` and `payment_terms` required in the schema so that the model always has to return a value for both
options.B: Add a paragraph explaining that payment terms can appear in prose, and that the model should read prose carefully
options.C: Add few-shot examples that show correct extraction from a letter-style invoice alongside a tabular one
options.D: Run OCR on every invoice and convert it into a table before it is sent to the model for extraction

questions.explanation: Empty or null extraction of fields that are present usually means the model has not seen how those fields look in that format. Few-shot examples demonstrating correct extraction from varied document structures, including prose-style terms, are the most effective way to close that gap.

why_incorrect.A: Forcing required fields pushes the model to invent values on invoices where the terms really are absent.
why_incorrect.B: General prose guidance helps less than a concrete demonstration of what to extract from a letter-style invoice.
why_incorrect.D: Converting letters to tables does not turn a sentence about settlement into a structured field, and adds a lossy step.

questions.scenario: Orchid Freight extracts cargo quantities from shippers' free-text booking emails. Many quantities are informal, such as 'roughly half a container', 'approx 3t' or 'two pallets-ish'. The current extraction returns exact-looking numbers like 14,500 kg for 'half a container', which then drive load planning.
questions.question: Which two changes best reduce these fabricated values? (Select 2)

options.A: Add few-shot examples showing informal quantities recorded with the original wording, an approximate flag and a value only when stated
options.B: Give the schema a nullable normalised value plus fields for the raw phrase and whether the quantity is approximate
options.C: Add a lookup table that converts every informal phrase into kilograms using the average weight of past shipments
options.D: Make the quantity field a required number, so that every booking yields a value usable by the load planner
options.E: Tell the model to round informal quantities to the nearest thousand kilograms so that false precision is avoided

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are effective at reducing hallucination for informal measurements because they demonstrate exactly how to treat them. A schema that keeps the raw phrase, marks approximation and allows a null normalised value gives the model a valid place to put uncertainty instead of inventing a precise figure.

why_incorrect.C: Average-based conversions manufacture precision from history and can be badly wrong for a specific booking.
why_incorrect.D: A required number forces a value even when the email only implies one, which is the cause of the fabrication.
why_incorrect.E: Rounding a guessed number still presents a guess as data, and hides that the source was informal.

questions.scenario: Tidewater Insurance extracts policy data with structured outputs. The schema marks `policy_end_date` as a required string. Auditors find that open-ended rolling policies, which have no end date, come back with plausible but invented dates such as the first anniversary of the start date.
questions.question: What is the best schema change?

options.A: Keep the field required and add a prompt rule that rolling policies should use the end date 9999-12-31
options.B: Make `policy_end_date` nullable, and instruct the model to return null when the document gives no end date
options.C: Remove `policy_end_date` from the schema and compute it later in code from the start date and policy type
options.D: Keep the field required but add a `format: date` constraint so that any value returned must at least be a valid date

questions.explanation: Required fields pressure the model to produce a value even when the source has none. Making the field nullable and stating when to use null gives the model an honest option, which prevents fabrication while keeping the field for policies that do have an end date.

why_incorrect.A: A sentinel date is easy to mistake for real data downstream, and it hides missing information in a date field.
why_incorrect.C: Fixed-term policies state their end dates; deriving them in code ignores the document and can be wrong.
why_incorrect.D: A date format constraint still requires a value, so invented dates remain valid output.

questions.scenario: Ironbark Media's contract pipeline runs on Claude Haiku 5.5. Its first step uses `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` so metadata is always extracted before enrichment, and it works. The team is moving this step to Claude Sonnet 5.5 for better accuracy on complex contracts.
questions.question: What must the team change in this step?

options.A: Replace forced tool choice, for example with `output_config.format` using the metadata schema, since Sonnet 5.5 returns a 400
options.B: Nothing, because forcing a named tool behaves the same on every current model, so the step moves over unchanged
options.C: Add a beta header that re-enables forced tool choice on Sonnet 5.5, keeping the rest of the request as it is now
options.D: Change `tool_choice` to `{"type": "any"}`, which still guarantees a tool call on Sonnet 5.5 where naming a tool does not

questions.explanation: Claude Haiku 5.5 accepts forced tool choice, but Claude Sonnet 5.5 returns a 400 for both `any` and a named `tool`. When the forced call only existed to get schema-shaped data, structured outputs with `output_config.format` is the direct replacement; `auto` plus a `strict: true` tool and an explicit instruction is another option.

why_incorrect.B: Forced tool choice behaves differently across current models; Sonnet 5.5 rejects it.
why_incorrect.C: No documented beta header restores forced tool choice on this model; the supported paths are auto with strict tools or structured outputs.
why_incorrect.D: `any` is also rejected on Claude Sonnet 5.5, so the step would still fail.

questions.scenario: Larkspur Legal categorises expense lines from client disbursement reports into an enum: travel, court_fees, expert_fees, courier, printing. New kinds of expense keep appearing, such as translation and e-discovery hosting, and the model squeezes them into the closest category. Some lines are also too vague to classify.
questions.question: Which schema design best handles this?

options.A: Replace the enum with a free-text category string so the model can name any category it sees in the report
options.B: Add every newly observed category to the enum each month, and re-run extraction on reports from the past month
options.C: Add `other` with a `category_detail` string for new kinds, plus `unclear` for lines too vague to classify
options.D: Keep the enum unchanged and instruct the model to pick the closest category whenever a line does not fit

questions.explanation: An `other` value with a detail string keeps the category set controlled while capturing new kinds of expense for later review, and an `unclear` value lets the model say a line is ambiguous instead of guessing. Both keep downstream reporting clean.

why_incorrect.A: Free text produces many spellings of the same category and breaks reporting that relies on fixed values.
why_incorrect.B: Constant enum churn and re-runs are costly, and lines arriving between updates are still miscategorised.
why_incorrect.D: This is the current behaviour that silently miscategorises new expense types.

questions.scenario: Cobaltline Clinical moved its lab-invoice extraction from free-text JSON to structured outputs with a strict schema. JSON parse errors dropped to zero. A manager now proposes removing the downstream checks that compare line items with the invoice total, arguing that the schema guarantees correct data.
questions.question: Which statement about this proposal is accurate?

options.A: The proposal is sound, because strict schemas stop the model from returning numbers that are inconsistent with each other
options.B: Keep the checks, because the schema guarantees shape and types, not that values are correct or consistent
options.C: The checks are needed only on models without strict mode, so they can be removed once the current model is in use
options.D: Keep the checks only for invoices above a value threshold, since low-value invoices are rarely extracted wrongly

questions.explanation: Structured outputs and strict tools guarantee that output matches the schema, which removes syntax errors. They do not guarantee semantic correctness: line items can still fail to sum to the total, or values can land in the wrong field. Business-rule validation stays necessary.

why_incorrect.A: A schema cannot express that line items must sum to a total, so inconsistent numbers remain possible.
why_incorrect.C: Semantic errors are independent of model or strict mode; constrained decoding governs shape only.
why_incorrect.D: Error rates are not known to depend on invoice value, and the checks are cheap compared with silent bad data.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Wholesale's invoice pipeline runs on Claude Haiku 5.5 with adaptive thinking and `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}`. Requests succeed, but on messy multi-currency invoices the extracted totals are often wrong, and the responses contain no thinking block at all.
questions.question: Which two changes let the model reason before extracting while keeping schema-valid output? (Select 2)

options.A: Use `tool_choice` auto with `strict: true` on the tool, and instruct the model to call extract_invoice once per document
options.B: Drop the tool and request the invoice through structured outputs, with `output_config.format` set to the invoice schema
options.C: Keep the forced tool choice and raise effort to `max`, so that the model spends more thinking on each forced extraction call
options.D: Switch to `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}`, which lets the model think first and then choose a tool, unlike naming the tool
options.E: Keep the forced tool choice and add an assistant prefill containing a worked reasoning step before the extract_invoice call

questions.explanation: Claude Haiku 5.5 accepts forced tool choice, even with thinking on, but a forced call makes the response start with the tool call and skip thinking. Using `auto` with a clear instruction (and `strict: true` for schema-valid arguments) lets the model think before calling the tool; structured outputs via `output_config.format` also keep a schema guarantee while letting the model think before it writes the JSON.

why_incorrect.C: Effort cannot add thinking to a forced call, because the response still opens directly with the tool call.
why_incorrect.D: `any` is also forced tool use, so the response still starts with a tool call and skips thinking.
why_incorrect.E: Assistant prefill returns a 400 on Claude Haiku 5.5, and it would not change how a forced call behaves.

questions.scenario: Ironbark Media's reviewer posts structured findings, and developers can dismiss each one. About a quarter are dismissed. The team wants to learn systematically which code constructs cause false positives so it can fix the prompt rather than guess.
questions.question: Which change gives the team the data it needs?

options.A: Replace dismissals with a thumbs-up or thumbs-down vote, and track the overall approval rate of the bot over time
options.B: Add a `detected_pattern` field to each finding and log dismissals against it, then compare dismissal rates by pattern
options.C: Lower the number of findings posted per pull request until the dismissal rate drops below ten percent
options.D: Ask developers to type a free-text reason whenever they dismiss a finding, and read through those reasons each month

questions.explanation: Recording which construct triggered each finding turns dismissals into analysable data: dismissal rates per pattern show exactly which detections are noisy. That points prompt changes at specific patterns instead of overall volume.

why_incorrect.A: An overall approval rate says the bot is noisy but not which detections are responsible.
why_incorrect.C: Cutting volume hides the symptom without showing which constructs cause the false positives.
why_incorrect.D: Free-text reasons are inconsistent and patchy, so systematic analysis by construct is hard.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Wholesale validates each extracted invoice in code. About 5% fail: dates are in DD/MM/YYYY instead of ISO 8601, or tax amounts are placed in the discount field. On failure, the pipeline simply sends the identical request again, and most retries fail the same way.
questions.question: How should the retry be redesigned?

options.A: Retry the identical request up to five times instead of once, and keep the first attempt that passes validation
options.B: Send a follow-up with the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors to correct
options.C: Send failing invoices straight to manual entry, since a model that erred once is likely to repeat the same mistake
options.D: Retry with a shorter prompt that removes the general instructions, so the model concentrates on the fields themselves

questions.explanation: Retry with error feedback works because it tells the model exactly what was wrong. Including the source document, the failed output and the concrete validation errors lets the model correct format and placement mistakes, which are the kind of errors retries fix well.

why_incorrect.A: An identical request carries no new information, so the same errors tend to recur while cost grows.
why_incorrect.C: These are correctable format and placement errors; sending them all to people wastes reviewer capacity.
why_incorrect.D: Removing instructions gives the model less guidance, not information about what failed.

questions.scenario: Cobaltline Clinical extracts lab invoices where the printed total sometimes does not match the line items, because of supplier errors or unprinted surcharges. In testing, the model sometimes 'fixes' the total to match the lines, and finance loses the evidence of supplier errors.
questions.question: Which extraction design best supports self-correction while preserving evidence?

options.A: Reject any invoice whose total does not match its lines and ask the supplier to send a corrected document
options.B: Instruct the model to always trust the printed total and adjust line items as needed so that both agree
options.C: Extract the printed total as `stated_total`, the line sum as `calculated_total`, and a `conflict_detected` flag
options.D: Extract only the line items and compute the total in code, discarding the printed total entirely from the record

questions.explanation: Capturing both the stated and calculated totals, plus an explicit conflict flag, lets validation detect discrepancies without the model silently resolving them. Finance keeps the evidence and can route conflicts for review.

why_incorrect.A: Many mismatches have legitimate explanations; blanket rejection delays payment and does not record the conflict.
why_incorrect.B: Adjusting line items to fit the total fabricates data and hides real discrepancies.
why_incorrect.D: Discarding the printed total removes exactly the evidence finance needs to detect supplier errors.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Grid extracts supply contracts. For about 8% of purchase orders, `payment_terms` fails validation three times in a row. Each of these orders says only 'terms as per Master Supply Agreement MSA-2291', and the agreement itself is not part of the input.
questions.question: Which two actions are most appropriate? (Select 2)

options.A: Route the record to fetch the referenced agreement, or to a reviewer, with the reason and the reference recorded
options.B: Retry at a higher effort level, since deeper reasoning may let the model infer the most likely terms in the agreement
options.C: Append the validation error to the prompt and retry up to three more times, since error feedback fixes most failures
options.D: Make `payment_terms` required so that the model has to produce terms rather than returning null for these orders
options.E: Classify these as information-absent failures and stop retrying them once the external reference is detected

questions.explanation: Retries help with format and structural errors, but not when the information is missing from the input. Recognising that case stops wasted retries, and routing the record to obtain the referenced document, or to a person with the reason, is the only way to get correct terms.

why_incorrect.B: More reasoning produces a better guess at most, and a guess about contract terms is not acceptable data.
why_incorrect.C: Error feedback cannot supply terms that exist only in a document the model has not seen.
why_incorrect.D: Requiring the field pushes the model to fabricate plausible terms, which is worse than an honest null.

questions.scenario: Tidewater Insurance is deciding which validation failures to send back to the model with error feedback, and which to route elsewhere. It reviews five failure examples from claim-form extraction.
questions.question: Which two failures are most likely to be fixed by a retry that includes the specific validation error? (Select 2)

options.A: The form never states when the claimant first reported the loss to the insurer's call centre
options.B: The policy number appears only in a separate cover letter that was not sent with the form
options.C: Page three of the scanned form is blank apart from a smudge, so the witness section is missing
options.D: The incident date was returned as 03/04/2026 when the schema rules require ISO 8601 format
options.E: Repair-cost line items were placed in the `deductibles` array instead of the `repairs` array

questions.explanation: Format mismatches and structural placement errors are correctable when the model is told what went wrong, because the information is present in the source. Failures caused by information that is absent, illegible or held in another document cannot be fixed by retrying.

why_incorrect.A: The fact is not in the form at all; retrying invites fabrication rather than correction.
why_incorrect.B: The value is in a document the model never saw, so a retry can only guess or return null again.
why_incorrect.C: The missing section is not legible in the source, so no amount of feedback can recover it.

questions.scenario: Quillfeather Labs runs a nightly test-gap analysis with `claude -p`, letting Claude read source and test files with tools as it goes. To halve the cost, the team plans to move the job to the Message Batches API, one request per module, with results needed by the next morning.
questions.question: What must the team change for the batch version to work?

options.A: Order the requests by module name so results come back in the same order and can be matched to modules by position
options.B: Split the work into batches of one module each so every request completes within a few minutes of submission
options.C: Nothing structural; batch requests run the same agentic tool loop as Claude Code, only at a lower price per token
options.D: Put each module's source and existing tests in the request itself, since a batch cannot run your own file tools

questions.explanation: A batch request is processed as a single Messages call: it cannot pause to run your client-side tools (such as reading source files) and feed their results back to the model. Server tools such as code execution can still run inside a request, but they cannot see Quillfeather's repository, so everything the model needs, here each module's source and tests, has to be included up front. Batches cost 50% less, complete within 24 hours, and return results in any order keyed by `custom_id`.

why_incorrect.A: Batch results can arrive in any order and must be matched by `custom_id`, never by position.
why_incorrect.B: Batch latency is not guaranteed for small batches, and many tiny batches add overhead without solving the tool issue.
why_incorrect.C: A batch request cannot pause to run client-side tools such as Claude Code's file reads and feed the results back, so a job that depends on them will not work unchanged.

questions.scenario: Ferngrove Pharma is about to batch-extract 250,000 archived supplier certificates in a new format that nobody has tried before. Last year a similar job was submitted in full, then corrected and resubmitted twice after systematic errors were discovered, nearly tripling its cost.
questions.question: What is the best way to plan this run?

options.A: Submit all 250,000 at once to secure the batch discount, then fix systematic errors by resubmitting the affected documents
options.B: Refine the prompt on a representative sample until it meets the quality bar, then submit the full volume as a batch
options.C: Process every certificate through the synchronous API instead, so errors are visible immediately as each one returns
options.D: Split the full volume into twenty batches and submit them all at the same time to finish sooner and spot errors earlier

questions.explanation: Testing and refining the prompt on a representative sample before batch-processing large volumes maximises first-pass success and avoids paying for repeated resubmissions. The batch discount applies only to work that does not have to be redone.

why_incorrect.A: This repeats last year's pattern, paying for a full run before systematic errors are found.
why_incorrect.C: Synchronous processing gives up the 50% batch discount on 250,000 documents without improving the prompt.
why_incorrect.D: Submitting every batch at once still processes all documents before anyone checks quality.

questions.scenario: Marrowstone Bank must extract data from mortgage documents within 32 hours of arrival. It plans to use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours to finish a batch. After results arrive, validation and loading take up to 2 hours. Documents arrive continuously through the day.
questions.question: What is the longest interval between batch submissions that still guarantees the 32-hour deadline?

options.A: Every 8 hours
options.B: Every 6 hours
options.C: Every 30 hours
options.D: Every 12 hours

questions.explanation: A document that arrives just after a submission waits a full interval before it is batched, then up to 24 hours for processing, then up to 2 hours for validation. The interval plus 26 hours must not exceed 32 hours, so the interval can be at most 6 hours.

why_incorrect.A: 8 + 24 + 2 = 34 hours, which misses the deadline for documents that arrive just after a submission.
why_incorrect.C: This treats the deadline as if only the submission interval mattered and ignores batch processing time.
why_incorrect.D: 12 + 24 + 2 = 38 hours; this ignores both the worst-case wait and the validation time.

questions.scenario: Larkspur Legal submitted a batch of 40,000 discovery documents for extraction. When it ended, 39,620 had succeeded, 310 had errored (many because the document exceeded the context limit) and 70 had expired. The team's loader currently writes results into the database by their position in the results stream.
questions.question: Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2)

options.A: Resubmit only the errored and expired `custom_id`s, chunking the oversized documents before resubmission
options.B: Match every result to its document by `custom_id`, because results can come back in any order
options.C: Keep position-based loading but sort the submitted requests first so that results come back sorted too
options.D: Resubmit the entire batch of 40,000 so that every result comes from the same run and the same prompt
options.E: Send the 380 failed documents unchanged through the synchronous API, one at a time, to get faster results

questions.explanation: Batch results are returned in any order, so `custom_id` is the only reliable link back to the source document. Failures should be handled by resubmitting just those IDs, with fixes such as chunking where the cause was size, rather than reprocessing everything.

why_incorrect.C: Sorting requests does not make results arrive in order; position-based matching stays unsafe.
why_incorrect.D: Reprocessing 39,620 successful documents doubles cost for no benefit.
why_incorrect.E: Oversized documents will fail again unchanged, and synchronous calls give up the batch discount.

questions.scenario: Norvale Health Records now reviews pull requests with an independent Claude instance. Precision is better, but some findings are still wrong, and the team does not want to drop real issues just to cut noise. Reviewers have six months of history showing which findings were accepted or dismissed.
questions.question: Which design best routes reviewer attention?

options.A: Have the reviewing instance post only its first five findings per pull request, ordered by the severity it assigns them
options.B: Add a verification pass that rechecks each finding against the code and reports confidence, with thresholds tuned on the history
options.C: Have the generating session confirm or reject each finding before posting, since it knows the intent behind the code
options.D: Post every finding inline but sort them so that the ones the reviewer rated as most severe appear at the top of the thread

questions.explanation: A verification pass that reports confidence per finding enables routing: high-confidence findings go inline, low-confidence ones to a summary for triage. Calibrating the thresholds against labelled outcomes (accepted versus dismissed) makes the confidence values meaningful rather than raw self-assessment.

why_incorrect.A: A fixed cap drops real issues on large pull requests and does nothing about wrong findings in the top five.
why_incorrect.C: The generator is anchored by its own reasoning and is likely to reject valid criticism of its choices.
why_incorrect.D: Sorting changes order but every wrong finding is still posted inline, so noise remains.

questions.scenario: Ironbark Media reviews a 38-file refactor of its subscription billing code in a single Claude pass. The output contradicts itself: one comment says `prorate_credit` is now unused, another flags a bug in a caller of that function. Files near the end of the diff get only superficial comments.
questions.question: Which review architecture best addresses these problems?

options.A: Keep a single pass but first ask Claude to summarise the whole diff, then review all 38 files with that summary in context
options.B: Split the files into random groups of ten and review each group independently, then concatenate all of the findings
options.C: Run focused per-file passes for local issues, then a separate integration pass that checks data flow across files
options.D: Move to a model with a larger context window so the whole diff fits comfortably in a single review pass

questions.explanation: Attention dilutes across a very large review, producing shallow coverage and contradictions. Per-file passes give each file focused attention, and a dedicated integration pass handles cross-file questions such as whether a function is still called, so local and cross-file findings stay consistent.

why_incorrect.A: A summary helps orientation but the review is still one diluted pass over all files.
why_incorrect.B: Random grouping splits related files apart and has no step that reasons about interactions across groups.
why_incorrect.D: Fitting in the context window is not the problem; attention spread across many files is, and it persists in a larger window.

questions.scenario: Ferngrove Pharma lets Claude Code open pull requests for routine dependency and lint fixes. Leadership wants automated review of these AI-generated pull requests to catch subtle problems before a human looks at them.
questions.question: Which two architectural choices most improve detection of subtle issues? (Select 2)

options.A: For large changes, run per-file passes for local issues and a separate pass for cross-file interactions
options.B: Review with a second, independent Claude instance that sees the diff but not the generator's reasoning
options.C: Have the generator write a detailed rationale into the pull request description for reviewers to trust
options.D: Run the generating session at maximum effort and ask it to double-check every change that it makes
options.E: Instruct the generating session to critique its own work thoroughly before it opens the pull request

questions.explanation: Independent review without the generator's context avoids the anchoring that makes self-review weak, and splitting large reviews into local and integration passes avoids attention dilution. Together they catch more subtle issues than self-critique within the generating session.

why_incorrect.C: A rationale may help humans, but it can make reviewers more likely to accept flawed reasoning rather than detect it.
why_incorrect.D: More effort in the generator improves generation somewhat, but its checking remains anchored to its own reasoning.
why_incorrect.E: Self-critique in the same session inherits the generator's assumptions and is less likely to question them.

questions.scenario: Saltmarsh Payments extracts obligations from 120-page merchant agreements in one request. Clauses in the middle of the document are often missed, and the output sometimes lists a fee that a later amendment schedule removed. Definitions in section 1 change the meaning of covenants in section 14.
questions.question: Which extraction architecture best addresses these problems?

options.A: Split the agreement into fixed 20-page chunks, extract each chunk independently, and append all of the results together
options.B: Run one extraction pass but repeat the most important instructions at both the start and the end of the long prompt
options.C: Extract section by section in focused passes, then run an integration pass that applies definitions and amendments
options.D: Ask the model to self-review its single-pass output in the same conversation and add anything that it missed

questions.explanation: Focused per-section passes give each part of a long document full attention, which addresses missed middle clauses. A separate integration pass handles cross-section relationships such as definitions and amendments, which per-section passes cannot see on their own.

why_incorrect.A: Fixed chunks cut through clauses and have no step that applies definitions or amendments across chunks.
why_incorrect.B: Prompt placement helps a little but the single pass still spreads attention over 120 pages.
why_incorrect.D: Self-review in the same context is anchored to the first pass and tends to repeat its omissions.

questions.scenario: Tidewater Insurance uses a long-running extraction agent that works through a 300-page claim file over many turns, summarising history as it goes. By the end, its summary says 'several repair invoices of varying amounts', and the final report is missing invoice numbers, amounts and the date the claimant said repairs started.
questions.question: What is the best fix?

options.A: Summarise history less often, so that each summary covers more turns and keeps more of the original wording
options.B: Keep a structured case-facts block of invoice numbers, amounts and dates outside the summary, included in every turn
options.C: Ask the summariser to be thorough and to keep every important detail whenever it condenses earlier turns
options.D: Increase `max_tokens` on the final report request so the agent has room to list all of the invoices it saw

questions.explanation: Progressive summarisation tends to blur exact numbers, dates and stated expectations into vague prose. Extracting transactional facts into a persistent structured block that is included in every prompt, outside the summarised history, preserves them for the whole session.

why_incorrect.A: Less frequent summarisation delays the loss but still compresses specifics into prose eventually.
why_incorrect.C: A general instruction does not define which facts must survive, so compression still drops them.
why_incorrect.D: Output length is not the problem; the facts are no longer in context when the report is written.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Wholesale extracts 60 supplier contracts separately, then sends all 60 full extraction records, each with about 45 fields, to a final step that reconciles pricing terms. The reconciliation reliably covers the first and last contracts but often omits contracts from the middle of the input.
questions.question: Which two changes best improve coverage in the reconciliation step? (Select 2)

options.A: Move the contracts with the highest annual spend into the middle of the input where attention is lowest
options.B: Raise `max_tokens` on the reconciliation request so the model has room to write about every contract
options.C: Sort the contracts alphabetically by supplier name so the order of the input is predictable for the model
options.D: Put a summary of the key findings at the start of the input and give each contract its own labelled section
options.E: Trim each extraction record to the pricing fields the reconciliation needs before combining all of them

questions.explanation: Long aggregated inputs suffer from position effects, with middle sections more likely to be missed. A key-findings summary at the start and clear section headers make every contract easy to locate, and trimming records to relevant fields cuts the volume that dilutes attention.

why_incorrect.A: Putting the most important contracts where attention is weakest would make the most costly omissions more likely.
why_incorrect.B: The model is omitting content it was given, not running out of output space.
why_incorrect.C: Alphabetical order does not change the length or structure that causes the middle to be missed.

questions.scenario: Pinecrest Pharmacy Online is adding a case-facts block to its support agent. The block is kept outside the summarised history and sent with every request, so that long chats do not lose what was agreed with the customer.
questions.question: What should the case-facts block contain?

options.A: The verbatim transcript of the latest twenty turns, so that nothing the customer said recently can be lost again
options.B: The model's running notes on the customer's mood and likely intent, refreshed after every turn of the conversation
options.C: A prose recap of the whole conversation so far, rewritten by the summariser in full each time history is condensed
options.D: Order numbers, agreed amounts, promised dates and open commitments, each stored as an exact, labelled value

questions.explanation: The case-facts block exists to keep transactional facts exact while the narrative history is condensed. It should hold compact, structured values such as identifiers, amounts, dates and commitments, updated as they change, rather than prose or raw transcript, which is exactly what summarisation blurs or what grows without limit.

why_incorrect.A: Raw turns grow the block without limit and bury the few exact facts among everything else said.
why_incorrect.B: Impressions are interpretive and change often; they do not protect the exact figures and promises that were lost.
why_incorrect.C: A prose recap is another summary, so exact amounts and dates get blurred in the same way as the history.

questions.scenario: Brightwater Outfitters' fetch_order_history tool returns about 45 fields per order, and a typical returns conversation loads 20 orders. Context fills quickly, cost per conversation has doubled, and the agent sometimes overlooks the delivery date it needs for return eligibility.
questions.question: What is the most effective change?

options.A: Return order results as compressed base64, so each lookup uses fewer tokens while still keeping every field
options.B: Ask the agent in the system prompt to ignore irrelevant fields whenever it reads an order lookup result
options.C: Move to a model with a larger context window, so all 45 fields of every order fit in context comfortably
options.D: Trim each order result to the fields the returns flow uses, such as status, delivery date and amount, before it enters context

questions.explanation: Tool results accumulate in context and can use tokens far out of proportion to their relevance. Trimming verbose outputs to the fields the task needs (in the tool itself or with a PostToolUse hook) cuts cost and keeps the key facts easy for the model to find.

why_incorrect.A: Encoded data is hard for the model to read reliably and does not remove the irrelevant content.
why_incorrect.B: The tokens are still consumed, and the relevant fields remain buried among the irrelevant ones.
why_incorrect.C: More room does not make irrelevant fields less distracting, and cost keeps rising with every lookup.

questions.scenario: Marrowstone Bank's CI job asks Claude Code to generate tests for changed functions. For `close_account`, the docstring says it returns None when the account has a pending transfer, but the code raises `PendingTransferError`. The job runs unattended and posts its tests as a pull request.
questions.question: How should the job be instructed to handle cases like this?

options.A: Treat the code as the source of truth and write tests that expect the exception, since the code is what runs in production
options.B: Test the unambiguous behaviour, and flag the contradiction in the pull request as a question rather than encoding either answer
options.C: Skip any function whose documentation and code disagree, so that the generated suite only contains reliable tests
options.D: Treat the docstring as the specification and write tests expecting None, letting the failing tests reveal the bug

questions.explanation: When the specification is ambiguous, the agent should not resolve it by guessing. Encoding either behaviour as the expected result either locks in a possible bug or breaks the build. Testing what is clear and surfacing the conflict to a human gets the decision made by someone who knows the intent.

why_incorrect.A: If the code is the bug, the tests now lock it in and make the wrong behaviour harder to change.
why_incorrect.C: Silently skipping hides the discrepancy, so nobody learns that the docs or the code need fixing.
why_incorrect.D: Deliberately failing tests break the pipeline on a guess about intent that may be wrong.

questions.scenario: Halcyon Grid's invoice pipeline looks up each extracted supplier name in the vendor master. For 'Northwind Services', the lookup returns three records in different regions. The current code picks the record with the most recent invoice, and finance has found payments posted to the wrong legal entity.
questions.question: How should the pipeline handle multiple matches?

options.A: Have the model choose the most likely record based on the invoice's wording and its knowledge of each region
options.B: Keep the most-recent-invoice rule, but log every case in which more than one candidate record matched the name
options.C: Match on further identifiers from the invoice, such as tax ID or remittance account, and route to review if none decide it
options.D: Pick the record whose region matches the region of the purchasing site that raised the original order

questions.explanation: Multiple matches need disambiguation from additional identifiers, not a heuristic choice. The invoice usually carries a tax ID or bank details that identify the entity; if it does not, a person should decide, because a wrong legal entity has financial consequences.

why_incorrect.A: A model guess is still a heuristic and cannot be relied on to identify the correct legal entity.
why_incorrect.B: Logging records the problem but still posts payments to a guessed entity.
why_incorrect.D: This is another heuristic; suppliers often invoice from a regional entity that differs from the purchasing site.

questions.scenario: A Fernvale Mobile customer opens a chat with: 'I just want to speak to a person, please.' Their underlying request is a simple billing address change that the agent could complete in seconds.
questions.question: How should the agent respond?

options.A: Check the customer's sentiment score and hand off only if it shows strong frustration rather than a mild preference
options.B: Hand off to a person straight away with a structured summary, without first trying to resolve the address change
options.C: Make the address change first, since it takes seconds, then offer a human if the customer still wants to speak to one
options.D: Acknowledge the request, explain that the agent can do it faster, and escalate only if the customer asks a second time

questions.explanation: An explicit request for a human is an escalation trigger in its own right and should be honoured immediately, with a handoff summary so the person does not start from scratch. Offering to resolve first is appropriate when a customer is frustrated but has not asked for a human.

why_incorrect.A: Sentiment is an unreliable escalation proxy, and the customer's explicit request already settles the question.
why_incorrect.C: This overrides an explicit request; customers who ask for a person should not be made to go through the agent first.
why_incorrect.D: Offering to help first suits a frustrated customer who has not asked for a person; an explicit request should be honoured at once.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Home Goods is writing explicit escalation criteria, with examples, for its support agent's system prompt.
questions.question: Which TWO situations should lead the agent to escalate to a human? (Choose 2.)

options.A: The customer wants a refund paid to another retailer's gift card, and the refund policy says nothing about third-party cards
options.B: The agent's self-rated confidence in its own answer falls below 0.7 on a routine customer question about delivery tracking
options.C: A name lookup returns three possible accounts, so the agent escalates rather than asking for a postcode or order number
options.D: The customer writes in capitals and uses angry language about a late delivery that the agent is able to rebook
options.E: After several attempts the order system keeps returning conflicting statuses, and the agent cannot make further progress

questions.explanation: Good escalation triggers include explicit requests for a human, policy gaps or exceptions (the policy is silent on the request), and being unable to make meaningful progress. Sentiment and self-rated confidence are unreliable proxies, and ambiguous matches should be resolved by asking for more identifiers.

why_incorrect.B: Self-reported confidence is a poor proxy for real complexity, and a routine tracking question does not need a human.
why_incorrect.C: Several matches call for more identifiers from the customer, not escalation or a guess.
why_incorrect.D: Anger alone is not a trigger when the issue is within the agent's ability; it should acknowledge the frustration and offer the fix.

questions.scenario: Linwood Capital's document-analysis subagent uses an OCR service that intermittently returns HTTP 503. When 4 of 15 scanned filings fail, the subagent reports only {"status": "analysis unavailable"}, and the coordinator abandons the whole report.
questions.question: How should the failure be handled?

options.A: Return the eleven successful analyses marked as complete, and leave out any mention of the four filings that failed
options.B: Abort the whole research run whenever any subagent fails, so no report is ever built on incomplete evidence
options.C: Have the coordinator re-run the full document-analysis subagent from scratch up to five times whenever it reports any kind of failure
options.D: Retry transient failures in the subagent, then return the failure type, files tried, partial results and alternatives for the rest

questions.explanation: Subagents should recover locally from transient faults, and propagate only what they cannot resolve, with structured context: what failed and why, what was attempted, the partial results, and possible alternatives. That lets the coordinator decide to retry, use another source or proceed with clear caveats, instead of seeing a generic status that hides everything.

why_incorrect.A: Silently dropping failures makes the report look complete when a quarter of the evidence is missing.
why_incorrect.B: Ending the whole workflow on one recoverable failure wastes the successful work and leaves the user with nothing.
why_incorrect.C: Blind full retries repeat work that succeeded and ignore whether the failure is transient or not.

questions.scenario: For a question on battery-recycling patents, Sorrel Partners' web-search subagent queried a patent database that returned no matches, while a trade-news archive returned HTTP 403. Both were reported as 'no results', and the report concluded that there was 'no evidence of recent activity'.
questions.question: How should the subagent report these two outcomes?

options.A: Report both as errors, so the coordinator re-runs every query that came back without any matching documents
options.B: Drop both sources from the subagent's output, so the coordinator only sees the sources that returned documents
options.C: Report both as successful empty results, so the report is not delayed by sources that turned up nothing useful
options.D: Report the query that ran and found nothing as a successful empty result, and the 403 as an access failure with what was attempted

questions.explanation: An access failure and a valid empty result mean different things. A successful query with no matches is evidence; a 403 means that source was never searched. Reporting them distinctly, with what was attempted, lets the coordinator retry or substitute the inaccessible source and avoid claiming absence of evidence.

why_incorrect.A: A query that ran correctly and found nothing is valid evidence; treating it as an error wastes retries.
why_incorrect.B: Hiding both outcomes removes the coordinator's ability to judge coverage or try another route into the archive.
why_incorrect.C: This is what produced the false conclusion: an unread source is not evidence of absence.

questions.scenario: Meridian Public Health Observatory's report on clinic waiting times draws on six regional data portals. Two portals were unavailable for the whole run, despite retries, and the subagents returned structured failure details for them.
questions.question: Which TWO behaviours should the system show? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Fill the two missing regions with estimates from neighbouring regions, so the published report has no visible gaps
options.B: Annotate the report's coverage, marking which findings are well supported and which regions have gaps from unavailable sources
options.C: Keep the gaps out of the report text, but list the failed portals in an internal log that engineers can review
options.D: Withhold the whole report until every one of the six regional portals is available again, however long that outage turns out to last
options.E: Have the coordinator decide from the failure details whether to try an alternative source for those regions or proceed with partial data

questions.explanation: When some sources stay unavailable, the coordinator should use the structured error context to choose a recovery path, and the output should carry coverage annotations so readers can see which findings are solid and where gaps exist. Hiding gaps, inventing data or halting everything are all worse outcomes.

why_incorrect.A: Invented estimates presented as findings mislead readers about what the evidence actually shows.
why_incorrect.C: Readers then cannot tell which conclusions rest on complete evidence and which do not.
why_incorrect.D: Blocking all output on a partial failure throws away well-supported findings for the other four regions.

questions.scenario: Two hours into exploring a 3,000-file codebase at Meridian Freight, Claude's answers have become generic. It now refers to 'the typical repository pattern' instead of naming the specific classes it found earlier, and the context is full of search output.
questions.question: Which TWO actions best restore precise answers while keeping the work done so far? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Switch the session into plan mode, which drops earlier exploration output from the context window
options.B: Have Claude record key findings such as class names, file paths and flows in a notes file it can refer back to
options.C: Repeat each question with the instruction 'be specific' in capitals until the class names reappear
options.D: Paste the earlier tool output back into the conversation so that the original details are fresh again
options.E: Run /compact to shrink the accumulated search output and keep working from a condensed context

questions.explanation: Context degradation in long exploration shows up as answers drifting to generic patterns. A scratchpad file keeps key findings outside the context window, and /compact reduces the verbose discovery output so the session can continue with the essentials.

why_incorrect.A: Plan mode restricts edits. It does not remove existing tool output from the context.
why_incorrect.C: Emphasis does not bring back details that have become hard to attend to in an overloaded context.
why_incorrect.D: Re-pasting output makes the context problem worse, adding more tokens to an already crowded window.

questions.scenario: A developer at Larkspur Outfitters asks Claude Code to find every place a legacy billing module is used across a monorepo of 40 packages. Earlier attempts filled the main session with hundreds of lines of search output before any code was changed.
questions.question: Before changing how invoices are rounded, how should the developer run this discovery step so the main session stays focused?

options.A: Delegate the search to a subagent that explores in its own context and returns a short list of call sites with file paths
options.B: Run the search in the main session with a larger output limit so that every match is visible at once
options.C: Ask Claude to read every file in the billing packages first so that it has the full picture loaded
options.D: Start a fresh session for every package and copy the results between them by hand

questions.explanation: A subagent does the verbose exploration in a separate context window and hands back only a summary, so the main session keeps room for the actual change. This is the standard way to keep exploration output from crowding the working context.

why_incorrect.B: More output in the main session is exactly what crowded the context in earlier attempts.
why_incorrect.C: Reading every file up front fills the context with material that is mostly irrelevant to the change.
why_incorrect.D: Manual copying across sessions is slow and error-prone, and it loses the link between findings.

questions.scenario: Ashgrove Pharma's Agent SDK explorer maps 14 services using one subagent per service. Halfway through a run the process crashed. Restarting began from zero, and the coordinator's context had already been close to full before the crash.
questions.question: Which TWO design changes best address recovery and context pressure? (Choose 2.)

options.A: On restart, resume the crashed session's ID and ask the coordinator to work out where it left off from history
options.B: Have each subagent write its findings to a known per-service state file, with a manifest tracking which services are done
options.C: Return every subagent's full exploration transcript to the coordinator so that nothing is lost if a crash recurs
options.D: On restart, have the coordinator load the manifest and pass the relevant summaries into new subagents' prompts
options.E: Raise maxTurns on every subagent so each service is mapped in one longer run that is less likely to stop early

questions.explanation: Structured state exports to a known location, tracked by a manifest, let the coordinator see what is done after a crash. Loading the manifest and injecting only the needed summaries into new subagent prompts recovers progress without refilling the coordinator's context.

why_incorrect.A: Resuming relies on a transcript that may end mid-operation and brings the near-full context straight back.
why_incorrect.C: Full transcripts in the coordinator are what crowd its context. Summaries and state files are the point of delegation.
why_incorrect.E: Longer runs do not prevent process crashes and make each lost run more expensive.

questions.scenario: Cobaltline Clinical's extraction of consent forms reaches 97% field-level accuracy on a validation set. The operations director wants to remove human review for all extractions next month. The validation set includes typed forms, scanned forms and handwritten site amendments.
questions.question: What should happen before human review is reduced?

options.A: Measure accuracy by document type and by field, and reduce review only for the segments that meet the bar
options.B: Keep review for every extraction until the model reaches 99% overall accuracy on the existing validation set
options.C: Expand the validation set to ten times its size and remove review if the overall figure stays at 97% or higher
options.D: Remove review now, since 97% overall accuracy is above the 95% target agreed with the clinical operations team

questions.explanation: An aggregate figure can hide poor performance in a segment, such as handwritten amendments or a specific consent field. Breaking accuracy down by document type and field shows where automation is safe and where review must stay.

why_incorrect.B: A higher overall target keeps the same blind spot and may hold back segments that are already safe to automate.
why_incorrect.C: A bigger sample tightens the overall estimate but still masks weak segments.
why_incorrect.D: A 97% average can include a segment performing far below target, which removing review would let through unchecked.

questions.scenario: Orchid Freight auto-approves customs declarations when the extractor's field-level confidence is high, and sends the rest to a small review team. It wants to keep measuring the error rate of auto-approved records and to notice new kinds of error early.
questions.question: Which two practices should it adopt? (Select 2)

options.A: Audit the first 100 records processed each day, as a simple and consistent sample of the day's extraction traffic
options.B: Audit only low-confidence records, since high-confidence records are by design the ones least likely to be wrong
options.C: Audit a stratified random sample of high-confidence records across document types and fields on an ongoing basis
options.D: Calibrate the confidence thresholds against a labelled validation set, and recalibrate as the document mix changes
options.E: Use 0.9 as the auto-approval threshold for every field, since it is a widely used default in extraction systems

questions.explanation: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence output measures the real error rate of auto-approved records and surfaces new error patterns across segments. Confidence scores are only useful for routing when thresholds are calibrated against labelled data and kept current.

why_incorrect.A: The first records of each day are not representative of document types or later traffic, so the sample is biased.
why_incorrect.B: Low-confidence records already get review; auditing only them never measures errors in what is auto-approved.
why_incorrect.E: An uncalibrated default threshold may be far too lenient or strict for particular fields.

questions.scenario: Brackenfield Insights' research pipeline extracts claims from sources and attaches a confidence score to each. Analysts have time to review about 15% of extracted claims before reports are published.
questions.question: Which TWO practices make the best use of reviewer time? (Choose 2.)

options.A: Calibrate the routing threshold against a labelled set of claims, so the score used for routing reflects observed accuracy
options.B: Stop reviewing high-confidence claims entirely once the first month of reviews shows few errors among them
options.C: Send low-confidence claims, and claims whose sources contradict each other, to analysts ahead of other claims
options.D: Spread analyst time at random across all claims, ignoring confidence, so reviewers always see a representative mix
options.E: Route claims to analysts only when the model's raw confidence is below 0.5, without checking how scores relate to accuracy

questions.explanation: Confidence scores are useful for routing only once calibrated against labelled data. Limited reviewer capacity should go first to low-confidence items and items with ambiguous or contradictory sources, while a smaller random sample of high-confidence items keeps measuring error rates.

why_incorrect.B: Without ongoing sampling, new error patterns in high-confidence claims would go unnoticed.
why_incorrect.D: Random sampling is useful for measuring error rates, but as the main routing rule it wastes scarce reviewer time.
why_incorrect.E: An uncalibrated score may not track real accuracy, so the threshold could miss many errors or waste review time.

questions.scenario: Lumenwise Telecom's agent proposes refund decisions that human reviewers approve. Over three months, reviewers agreed with 96% of proposals. Leadership plans to stop reviewing proposals the model marks as high confidence. Damaged-goods claims are 8% of volume.
questions.question: What should happen before review is reduced?

options.A: Stop review for all proposals, and ask customers to report wrong decisions, using complaints as the error signal
options.B: Measure agreement separately for each claim type and amount band, and keep sampling approved cases after review is reduced
options.C: Keep reviewing every proposal indefinitely, because any automation of refund decisions carries an unacceptable risk
options.D: Stop review for every high-confidence proposal now, because 96% overall agreement already meets the quality target

questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can mask weak performance in specific segments. Accuracy should be checked by claim type and amount before automating, and stratified random sampling of automated decisions should continue afterwards to measure error rates and catch new failure patterns.

why_incorrect.A: Complaints are a biased, delayed signal; many wrong decisions, especially in the company's favour, never get reported.
why_incorrect.C: This ignores the evidence; segment-level validation plus ongoing sampling can safely free reviewer capacity.
why_incorrect.D: An aggregate figure can hide poor accuracy in smaller segments such as damaged-goods claims.

questions.scenario: Larkspur Legal's pipeline extracts claims from dozens of case documents, summarises them per matter, then synthesises a matter brief. Partners cannot trace statements in the brief back to a document or page, because the summary step drops that information. The extraction step uses structured outputs with a JSON schema.
questions.question: Which design best preserves provenance through to the brief?

options.A: Make every extracted claim carry its document name, page and excerpt, and require each later step to keep and merge them
options.B: Instruct the synthesis step to cite sources where possible, using document names it remembers from the summaries
options.C: Turn on the Citations feature for the documents while keeping `output_config.format`, so each JSON field gets a citation
options.D: Add a list of all source documents at the end of the brief so partners know which files were used to write it

questions.explanation: Attribution is lost when summarisation compresses claims without their sources. Structured claim-source mappings created at extraction time, which every later step must carry forward and merge, keep each statement traceable to its document, page and excerpt.

why_incorrect.B: The summaries no longer contain source details, so the synthesis step can only guess at citations.
